knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-lattice structure and strict-chain height of exact finite-domain information states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite universes \((U_i)_{i\in I}\), the state space \(\mathcal D=\prod_{i\in I}\mathcal P(U_i)\), ordered componentwise by inclusion, is a finite distributive lattice. Its meet and join are componentwise intersection and union. Every strict descending chain beginning at the top state \((U_i)_{i\in I}\) has at most \(\sum_{i\in I}|U_i|\) strict steps, and this bound is attained by deleting one value at a time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact finite-domain states form a finite distributive product lattice, and at most the total number of values can be deleted along a strict descending chain.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and every \(U_i\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{\text{strict steps below }(U_i)_{i\in I}\}=\sum_{i\in I}|U_i|,\quad(D\wedge E)_i=D_i\cap E_i,\quad(D\vee E)_i=D_i\cup E_i.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Domain State Lattice
Finite-Domain Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact domain states for variables whose ground universes are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite variable index set and let each \(U_i\) be a finite ground domain. A finite-domain information state is a tuple \(D=(D_i)_{i\in I}\) with \(D_i\subseteq U_i\). Its concretization is \(\gamma(D)=\prod_{i\in I}D_i\). The precision order is \(D\sqsubseteq E\) exactly when \(D_i\subseteq E_i\) for every \(i\in I\), so smaller component domains carry more information. The state is inconsistent exactly when some \(D_i=\varnothing\), equivalently \(\gamma(D)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-domain state lists the remaining values of each finite-domain variable; componentwise inclusion orders precision, and an empty component signals inconsistency.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and every \(U_i\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\sqsubseteq E\iff (\forall i\in I)\,D_i\subseteq E_i\), and \(\gamma(D)=\varnothing\iff (\exists i\in I)\,D_i=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: current admissible values of variable i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-domain constraint-programming information order

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no inspectable source establishes that this exact Cartesian-domain representation and precision orientation are intended here.

children.title: Interval Enclosures
children.top_down_role: Information states represented by interval-valued variable domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Enclosures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Axis-aligned real interval information, including empty and unbounded enclosures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For \(\ell,u\in\overline{\mathbb R}\) with \(\ell\le u\), define \([\ell,u]=\{x\in\mathbb R:\ell\le x\le u\}\), and also admit \(\varnothing\) as an interval. An interval enclosure is a box \(B=\prod_{i=1}^{n}B_i\), where each \(B_i\) is such an interval; if any \(B_i=\varnothing\), then \(B=\varnothing\) represents inconsistency. A set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is enclosed by \(B\) exactly when \(S\subseteq B\). For boxes \(B\) and \(C\), define \(B\sqsubseteq C\) exactly when \(B\subseteq C\), so the smaller box is the more precise enclosure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interval enclosure is an axis-aligned, possibly empty or unbounded real box. It encloses a set when it contains that set, and box inclusion orders precision.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb N\) is positive.
\(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ encloses }S\iff S\subseteq B\), and \(B\sqsubseteq C\iff B\subseteq C\).

notation.meaning: possibly empty or unbounded interval box
box-precision order, with the smaller box more precise

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smallest closed extended-real box enclosing an arbitrary real set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define \(\operatorname{box}(\varnothing)=\varnothing\). If \(S\ne\varnothing\), let \(\ell_i=\inf\{x_i:x\in S\}\) and \(u_i=\sup\{x_i:x\in S\}\) in \(\overline{\mathbb R}\), and set \(\operatorname{box}(S)=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\). Then \(S\subseteq\operatorname{box}(S)\), and every closed extended-real interval box containing \(S\) also contains \(\operatorname{box}(S)\). Moreover, \(S\subseteq T\) implies \(\operatorname{box}(S)\subseteq\operatorname{box}(T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinatewise infima and suprema produce the unique smallest closed interval box enclosing a real set, and this hull is monotone.
assumptions_latex: \(S,T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
Unbounded endpoints are admitted in \(\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{box}(S)=\bigcap\{B:B\text{ is a closed extended-real box and }S\subseteq B\}.

notation.meaning: least closed interval-box enclosure of S

knowledge_statements.title: Least Interval-Box Hull

children.title: Bound Abstractions
children.top_down_role: Information states retaining selected lower or upper domain limits.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical endpoint encoding and cardinality of interval states over a finite chain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=\{u_1<\cdots<u_k\}\). Every nonempty bound state is represented uniquely by an endpoint pair \((u_i,u_j)\) with \(1\le i\le j\le k\), denoting \([u_i,u_j]_U\); add one distinguished empty state \(\bot\). Hence there are \(1+k(k+1)/2\) bound states. Inclusion satisfies \([u_i,u_j]_U\subseteq[u_r,u_s]_U\) exactly when \(r\le i\) and \(j\le s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound state over a finite chain is uniquely represented by two endpoints, plus an empty marker.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a finite chain of cardinality \(k\).

notation.meaning: empty and nonempty interval states over U

knowledge_statements.title: Endpoint Representation of Bound States
Bound Abstractions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hull abstraction of exact finite ordered domains by endpoint bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a finite totally ordered set. For a nonempty exact domain \(D\subseteq U\), its bound abstraction is \(\alpha(D)=[\min D,\max D]_U\), where \([a,b]_U=\{u\in U:a\le u\le b\}\). Define \(\alpha(\varnothing)=\varnothing\), and let the concretization of an interval be \(\gamma([a,b]_U)=[a,b]_U\). Then \(D\subseteq\gamma(\alpha(D))\), and \(\alpha(D)\) is the least interval in \(U\) containing \(D\). Componentwise application gives the bound abstraction of a finite-domain state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bound abstraction replaces each exact ordered domain by its smallest interval hull, preserving endpoints but forgetting interior holes.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and totally ordered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(D)=\min\{J:J\text{ is an interval in }U\text{ and }D\subseteq J\}\).

children.title: Interval–Bound Precision Relations
children.top_down_role: Relative information precision across interval-based versus bound-based states.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hull Interaction with Union and Intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and inexact preservation laws for finite-domain interval hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For subsets \(D,E\) of a finite chain \(U\), let \(\alpha\) be the interval hull and let \(\operatorname{hull}(J\cup K)\) denote the least interval containing two interval states. Then \(\alpha(D\cup E)=\operatorname{hull}(\alpha(D)\cup\alpha(E))\), whereas only \(\alpha(D\cap E)\subseteq\alpha(D)\cap\alpha(E)\) holds in general. The latter inclusion can be strict: for \(U=\{1,2,3\}\), \(D=\{1,3\}\), and \(E=\{2,3\}\), one has \(\alpha(D\cap E)=\{3\}\) but \(\alpha(D)\cap\alpha(E)=\{2,3\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval hulls preserve union after rehulling, but abstract intersection can retain values absent from the hull of the exact intersection.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and totally ordered.
\(\alpha(\varnothing)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Hull Interaction with Union and Intersection
Interval–Bound Precision Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precision loss incurred when exact ordered domains are represented only by bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be finite and totally ordered, and let \(D,E\subseteq U\). Their interval hulls satisfy \(D\subseteq\alpha(D)\) and \(D\subseteq E\Rightarrow\alpha(D)\subseteq\alpha(E)\). Moreover, \(\alpha(D)=D\) exactly when \(D\) is empty or order-convex in \(U\). Hence the bound representation is exact on interval domains and otherwise strictly less precise by admitting the holes \(\alpha(D)\setminus D\). The converse implication \(\alpha(D)\subseteq\alpha(E)\Rightarrow D\subseteq E\) fails in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking interval hulls is monotone and exact precisely for hole-free domains; otherwise it loses information about excluded interior values.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and totally ordered.
\(\alpha\) is the interval-hull abstraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\subseteq E\Rightarrow\alpha(D)\subseteq\alpha(E)\), and \(\alpha(D)=D\iff D\text{ is empty or order-convex}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Domain Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact information states for variables whose possible values are themselves sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite index set and, for each \(i\in I\), let \(U_i\) be a ground universe for a set-valued variable \(S_i\). A set-domain information state is a tuple \(\mathcal D=(\mathcal D_i)_{i\in I}\) with \(\mathcal D_i\subseteq\mathcal P(U_i)\). It represents \(\gamma(\mathcal D)=\prod_{i\in I}\mathcal D_i\). Precision is componentwise inclusion: \(\mathcal D\sqsubseteq\mathcal E\) exactly when \(\mathcal D_i\subseteq\mathcal E_i\) for all \(i\). The state is inconsistent exactly when some \(\mathcal D_i\) is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-domain state records the admissible set values of each set-valued variable, ordered by componentwise removal of possibilities.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite.
Each set variable \(S_i\) ranges over \(\mathcal P(U_i)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal D\sqsubseteq\mathcal E\iff(\forall i\in I)\,\mathcal D_i\subseteq\mathcal E_i\).

notation.meaning: power set of ground universe U_i
admissible set values of variable i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact powerset-domain semantics for set-valued constraint variables
The title may alternatively intend lower-and-upper set bounds; a direct constraint-programming source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source resolves whether this leaf denotes exact families of admissible sets or the more usual lower-and-upper set-bound representation used by set-variable propagators.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-scope locality of a propagator associated with one constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\operatorname{var}(c)\) be the variables occurring in constraint \(c\), and let \(D=(D_x)_{x\in V}\) be a store. A constraint-local propagator \(p_c\) satisfies the frame condition when \((p_c(D))_x=D_x\) for every \(x\notin\operatorname{var}(c)\). Thus it changes only domains in the declared scope of \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint-local propagator leaves every variable outside its constraint's scope unchanged.
assumptions_latex: Stores have variable-indexed domain components.
\(\operatorname{var}(c)\subseteq V\) is the declared scope of \(c\).
knowledge_statements.title: Scope-Local Frame Condition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Idempotence Is Not Implied by Propagator Correctness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between a valid propagator and a saturated closure operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Contractivity, monotonicity, solution preservation, and scope locality do not imply \(p_c\circ p_c=p_c\). On a chain \(x_2\sqsubset x_1\sqsubset x_0\), define \(p(x_0)=x_1\), \(p(x_1)=x_2\), and \(p(x_2)=x_2\), and let all three states represent the same solution set. Then \(p\) has the stated correctness properties, but \(p^2(x_0)=x_2\ne x_1=p(x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A correct propagator need not reach its own closure in one call; idempotence is an additional property.
assumptions_latex: The abstract solution interpretation is identical on the three chain states.
knowledge_statements.title: Idempotence Is Not Implied by Propagator Correctness
Constraint-Local Propagators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contracting, monotone, solution-preserving reduction associated with one constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((L,\sqsubseteq)\) be an information-state poset ordered from more to less permissive states, let \(c\) be a constraint, and let \(\operatorname{Sol}_c(x)\) denote the solutions of \(c\) represented by \(x\in L\). A constraint-local propagator for \(c\) is a map \(p_c:L\to L\) satisfying contraction \(p_c(x)\sqsubseteq x\), monotonicity \(x\sqsubseteq y\Rightarrow p_c(x)\sqsubseteq p_c(y)\), and local solution preservation \(\operatorname{Sol}_c(p_c(x))=\operatorname{Sol}_c(x)\) for every \(x\in L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint-local propagator monotonically removes information-state possibilities without deleting any solution of its associated constraint.
assumptions_latex: \((L,\sqsubseteq)\) is an information-state poset.
\(\operatorname{Sol}_c(x)\) is defined for every \(x\in L\).

notation.meaning: solutions of c represented by x

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard contracting monotone solution-preserving propagator model
No supplied locator directly supports abstract constraint propagators.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed propagator axioms fit the leaf, but an inspectable constraint-propagation source is needed to confirm the solution-preservation formulation and precision-order convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Guard Stability for Monotone Rule Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition ensuring a guarded reduction remains monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let stores be ordered by inclusion, let \(a_r\) be contracting and monotone, and assume the guard is stable under refinement: \(D\subseteq E\land g_r(E)\Rightarrow g_r(D)\). Then the induced operator \(R_r(D)=a_r(D)\) when \(g_r(D)\) holds and \(R_r(D)=D\) otherwise is monotone and contracting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone contracting action induces a monotone guarded reduction when a true guard remains true after domain refinement.
assumptions_latex: \(a_r\) is contracting and monotone.
\(g_r\) is stable under refinement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\subseteq E\Rightarrow R_r(D)\subseteq R_r(E),\qquad R_r(D)\subseteq D.
knowledge_statements.title: Guard Stability for Monotone Rule Operators

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chaotic iteration of a finite family of monotone contracting rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\) be a finite family of monotone, contracting, solution-preserving rule operators on a finite-height poset. Starting from \(x_0\), repeatedly apply enabled rules under a fair schedule until none is enabled. The process performs at most \(H\) strict reductions, where \(H\) is the strict descending height below \(x_0\), preserves represented solutions, and returns the greatest common fixed point of \(\mathcal R\) below \(x_0\), independently of the fair rule order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fair chaotic application of valid rules terminates on finite-height states and reaches the greatest common rule fixed point below the initial state.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal R\) is finite.
Every rule operator is monotone, contracting, and solution-preserving.
Enabled updates are strict, and scheduling is fair.
The strict descending height below \(x_0\) is finite.

notation.meaning: strict descending height below the initial state

knowledge_statements.title: Fair Rule Saturation Theorem
Rule-Based Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational reduction induced by guarded domain-restriction rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reduction rule on an information-state poset \((L,\sqsubseteq)\) is a pair \(r=(g_r,a_r)\), where \(g_r:L\to\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}\) is a guard and \(a_r:L\to L\) is a contracting, solution-preserving action. Its induced operator is \(R_r(x)=a_r(x)\) when \(g_r(x)\) holds and \(R_r(x)=x\) otherwise. The rule is enabled at \(x\) exactly when \(g_r(x)\) and \(a_r(x)\ne x\). A rule-based reduction step selects an enabled rule and replaces \(x\) by \(R_r(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A guarded reduction rule changes a state only when its guard holds and its solution-preserving action makes a strict contraction.
assumptions_latex: \((L,\sqsubseteq)\) is an information-state poset.
Every action \(a_r\) is contracting and solution-preserving.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_r(x)=g_r(x)\mathbin{?}a_r(x):x\), with enablement equivalent to \(g_r(x)\land a_r(x)\ne x\).
review_flags: A propagation-rule source is needed to certify the guard and enablement convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The guarded operational form fits Rule-Based Reduction, but no source supports the chosen enablement convention, and the action's solution-preservation predicate is not formally tied to a represented solution set.

children.title: Reduction Composition
children.top_down_role: Compound reduction operators formed from multiple component reductions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Height Convergence of Repeated Composite Passes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination bound for iterating a sequential composite to quiescence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=p_m\circ\cdots\circ p_1\) be the composite of contracting maps on a poset whose strict descending height below \(x_0\) is \(H\). The iteration \(x_{t+1}=P(x_t)\) reaches a fixed point after at most \(H\) strict composite changes. If every constituent map is monotone, the result is the greatest common fixed point of \(p_1,\ldots,p_m\) below \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated full composite passes terminate after at most the available strict state reductions and, under monotonicity, yield the greatest common fixed point below the initial state.
assumptions_latex: Every \(p_i\) is contracting.
The strict descending height below \(x_0\) is finite.
The greatest-common-fixed-point conclusion additionally assumes every \(p_i\) is monotone.

notation.meaning: maximum number of strict descending transitions below the initial state

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Height Convergence of Repeated Composite Passes
Reduction Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential composition of contracting monotone solution-preserving reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_1,\ldots,p_m:L\to L\) be contracting, monotone, solution-preserving maps on a poset \((L,\sqsubseteq)\), and define \(P=p_m\circ\cdots\circ p_1\). Then \(P\) is contracting, monotone, and solution-preserving. Moreover, contraction implies \[\operatorname{Fix}(P)=\bigcap_{j=1}^{m}\operatorname{Fix}(p_j).\] Thus one complete composite pass is quiescent exactly when every constituent reduction leaves the input state unchanged, although repeated composite passes may still be required to reach such a state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequentially composing valid reductions preserves their properties, and a fixed point of the composite is precisely a common fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \((L,\sqsubseteq)\) is a poset.
Each \(p_j\) is contracting, monotone, and solution-preserving.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is contracting, monotone, and solution-preserving, with \(\operatorname{Fix}(P)=\bigcap_{j=1}^{m}\operatorname{Fix}(p_j)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary order-theoretic composition property for contracting maps
No supplied locator directly supports propagator composition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property and its content kind fit the leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied for the common-fixed-point equality under the stated contraction convention.

children.title: Staged Reduction
children.top_down_role: Reduction organized into semantically distinct processing stages.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeated-stage variant restoring global quiescence after cross-stage re-enablement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\) be the monotone contracting closures computed by the stages. Starting at \(x_0\), repeatedly set \(x\leftarrow C_k\circ\cdots\circ C_1(x)\) until a complete cycle makes no change. On a finite-height poset this terminates at the greatest state below \(x_0\) fixed by every \(C_j\). If the strict descending height below \(x_0\) is \(H\), at most \(H\) cycles can change the state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeating the full sequence of saturated stages until an unchanged cycle repairs re-enablement and computes the greatest common stage fixed point.
assumptions_latex: Each stage computes a monotone, contracting, idempotent closure.
The information order has finite descending height below the initial state.

notation.meaning: saturated closure effected by stage j
strict descending height below the initial state

knowledge_statements.title: Cyclic Staged Saturation
Staged Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successive saturation of prescribed groups of reduction operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an initial state \(x_0\in L\), ordered finite stages \(\mathcal P_1,\ldots,\mathcal P_k\), and a fair selector within each stage. Set \(x\leftarrow x_0\). For \(j=1,\ldots,k\), repeatedly choose \(p\in\mathcal P_j\) with \(p(x)\ne x\) and update \(x\leftarrow p(x)\); leave stage \(j\) when every \(p\in\mathcal P_j\) fixes \(x\). Output the final \(x\). On a finite-height information poset with contracting operators, every stage terminates; the output is fixed by the last stage, but not necessarily by earlier stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Staged reduction saturates one prescribed propagator group at a time; later stages can re-enable reductions from earlier stages.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) has finite descending height.
Every staged operator is contracting.
Selection within each stage is fair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{\mathrm{out}}\in\operatorname{Fix}(\mathcal P_k)\); membership in \(\operatorname{Fix}(\mathcal P_j)\) for \(j<k\) is not automatic.

notation.meaning: common fixed points of stage j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fair saturation algorithm on a finite-height reduction order
No supplied locator directly treats staged propagator scheduling.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits Staged Reduction and is internally plausible, but the precise stage-saturation and fairness conventions lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Composition–Staging Interactions
children.top_down_role: Effects of stage boundaries on composed reduction behavior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Later Stage Can Re-enable an Earlier Stage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete noncommuting stage closures requiring another cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(L=2^{\{a,b\}}\) ordered by inclusion, define \(C_1(D)=D\) if \(a\in D\) and \(C_1(D)=\varnothing\) otherwise, and define \(C_2(D)=D\cap\{b\}\). Both maps are contracting, monotone, and idempotent. Starting from \(\{a,b\}\), the order \(C_1\) then \(C_2\) returns \(\{b\}\), but \(C_1(\{b\})=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two valid stage closures can fail to commute, leaving a one-pass result that an earlier stage can still reduce.
assumptions_latex: The state lattice is the powerset ordered by inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Later Stage Can Re-enable an Earlier Stage

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-Set Preservation Suffices for One-Pass Staging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-sensitive sufficient condition weaker than pairwise commutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\) be contracting, monotone, idempotent stage closures. Suppose that for every \(i<j\), \(C_j(\operatorname{Fix}(C_i))\subseteq\operatorname{Fix}(C_i)\). Then \(C_k\circ\cdots\circ C_1(x)\) is fixed by every \(C_i\) for every input \(x\). Changing the stage order need not preserve this property or the result.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One ordered staged pass is sufficient when every later stage preserves every fixed-point set established by an earlier stage; pairwise commutation is sufficient but not necessary.
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_i\) is contracting, monotone, and idempotent.
Every later stage preserves every earlier fixed-point set.

notation.meaning: fixed-point set of stage closure i

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Set Preservation Suffices for One-Pass Staging
Composition–Staging Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient commutation condition for staged saturation to equal joint closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be a finite lattice and let \(C_1,ldots,C_k:L\to L\) be contracting, monotone, idempotent stage-closure operators. If they commute pairwise, so \(C_i\circ C_j=C_j\circ C_i\) for all \(i,j\), then the staged composite \(C=C_k\circ\cdots\circ C_1\) is contracting, monotone, and idempotent, and \[\operatorname{Fix}(C)=\bigcap_{j=1}^{k}\operatorname{Fix}(C_j).\] Consequently, one staged pass computes the common closure independently of stage order. Without commutation, a later stage may destroy fixedness under an earlier stage, so another cycle can be necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairwise commuting stage closures compose into the order-independent common closure; without commutation, later stages may re-enable earlier reductions.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is a finite lattice.
Each \(C_j\) is contracting, monotone, and idempotent.
The operators \(C_i\) and \(C_j\) commute pairwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_k\circ\cdots\circ C_1\) is an idempotent common closure with fixed points \(\bigcap_j\operatorname{Fix}(C_j)\), independent of stage order.

notation.meaning: fixed points of stage closure j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: commuting idempotent reductions have an order-independent composite closure
A direct order-theoretic or propagation source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the interaction leaf, but no source supports the stated commuting-closure result, and the opening expression contains the malformed text \(C_1,ldots,C_k\) instead of \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\).

children.title: Closure States
children.top_down_role: States closed under the relevant family of reductions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common-fixed-point characterization separated from the orientation used to select a closure result.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family \(\mathcal P\) of self-maps on a state space \(L\), a state \(x\in L\) is closed under \(\mathcal P\) exactly when \(p(x)=x\) for every \(p\in\mathcal P\). This predicate is independent of order orientation. If reductions move downward, a closure result from \(x_0\) may be selected as the greatest closed state below \(x_0\); under the reversed information order, the same state is described as the least closed state above \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed state is a common fixed point. Greatest-below and least-above descriptions are equivalent after reversing the information order.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is a family of self-maps on \(L\).
Greatest-below or least-above terminology is used only when the corresponding extremal closed state exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is closed under }\mathcal P\iff(\forall p\in\mathcal P)\,p(x)=x.
knowledge_statements.title: Order-Neutral Closed-State Predicate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic Laws of Greatest Common Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Laws of an extremal common-fixed-point closure under the downward order convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal P}(x)\) exists for every \(x\in L\) and is the greatest common fixed point of \(\mathcal P\) below \(x\). Then \(\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal P}(x)\sqsubseteq x\), \(\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal P}(\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal P}(x))=\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal P}(x)\), and \(x\sqsubseteq y\) implies \(\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal P}(x)\sqsubseteq\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal P}(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A greatest-common-fixed-point closure below each state is contractive, idempotent, and monotone.
assumptions_latex: Reductions are oriented downward under \(\sqsubseteq\).
The greatest common fixed point below every state exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal P}\text{ is contractive, idempotent, and monotone}.

notation.meaning: Greatest common fixed point below its argument.

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Laws of Greatest Common Closure
Closure States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greatest common fixed point below an initial information state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be a family of contracting reductions on a poset \((L,\sqsubseteq)\), and let \(x_0\in L\). A closure state of \(x_0\) under \(\mathcal P\) is a common fixed point \(x^\star\sqsubseteq x_0\) satisfying \(p(x^\star)=x^\star\) for every \(p\in\mathcal P\). When the set of such states has a greatest element under \(\sqsubseteq\), the closure is defined by \[\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal P}(x_0)=\max\{y\sqsubseteq x_0:(\forall p\in\mathcal P)\,p(y)=y\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closure state is unchanged by every reduction; the closure is the greatest such state below the initial state when it exists.
assumptions_latex: \((L,\sqsubseteq)\) is a poset.
Every \(p\in\mathcal P\) is contracting.
The displayed greatest common fixed point exists when closure is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal P}(x_0)\sqsubseteq x_0\) and \((\forall p\in\mathcal P)\,p(\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal P}(x_0))=\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal P}(x_0)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: common-fixed-point definition of propagation closure
The orientation of the project's information order should be checked against a direct source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional greatest-common-fixed-point definition fits Closure States, but a source is needed to confirm that greatest below the initial state is correct for the shard's chosen information-order orientation.

children.title: Quiescent States
children.top_down_role: States in which scheduled propagation has no further effective work.

knowledge_statements.title: Quiescent States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational states with no enabled reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family \(\mathcal P\) of reductions on an information-state space \(L\), a state \(x\in L\) is quiescent when no reduction can change it: \[\forall p\in\mathcal P,\qquad p(x)=x.\] In a rule-based system this is equivalent to saying that no rule is enabled, provided a rule is enabled exactly when its induced operator changes the current state. Quiescence is relative to the active family \(\mathcal P\); a state quiescent for one stage need not be quiescent after additional reductions are activated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state is quiescent when every active reduction leaves it unchanged, equivalently when no change-producing rule is enabled.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is the active reduction family.
Rule enablement means that the induced operator changes the state.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: operational quiescence as absence of enabled state-changing reductions
No supplied locator directly supports propagation quiescence.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Quiescent States, but its equivalence with absence of enabled rules depends on the stipulated change-producing enablement convention, for which no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Closure–Quiescence Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing when operational quiescence represents semantic closure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between an implementation worklist state and semantic common-fixed-point closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be the active propagator family at store \(D\), and let \(Q\) be an implementation worklist. The implication \(Q=\varnothing\Rightarrow(\forall p\in P)\,p(D)=D\) requires complete wake-up and reliable scheduling: every store change that can make \(p\) effective must schedule \(p\), and scheduled work must not be lost. Conversely, semantic closure does not imply \(Q=\varnothing\) unless stale queued entries are removed or executed to exhaustion. Without these invariants, queue state and semantic closure can differ in either direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An empty worklist certifies closure only with complete, reliable wake-ups; a closed store can still have stale queued work until the queue is drained.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is a worklist for the active family \(P\).
Semantic closure means \((\forall p\in P)\,p(D)=D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q=\varnothing\iff D\text{ is closed under }P\text{ only under complete wake-up, reliable scheduling, and queue-drain invariants}.
knowledge_statements.title: Worklist Emptiness Requires Scheduler Invariants
Closure–Quiescence Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence for a finite family of propagators acting on one ordered store space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\) be a poset of stores and let \(P=\{p_1,\ldots,p_m\}\) be self-maps of \(L\). Call \(D\in L\) closed under \(P\) when \(p_i(D)=D\) for every \(i\), and call it quiescent when no propagator application changes it. Then
\[
D\text{ is closed under }P\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D\text{ is quiescent for }P.
\]
Thus closure is exactly the common-fixpoint condition \(D\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{Fix}(p_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A store is closed under all propagators exactly when no propagator can change it; equivalently, it is their common fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is a poset and each \(p_i:L\to L\) is deterministic.
Quiescence means absence of any index \(i\) with \(p_i(D)\ne D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\text{ is closed under }P\iff D\text{ is quiescent for }P\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is a direct equivalence of the stated definitions and fits the leaf, but the record has no citation or inspectable locator supporting the propagation terminology.

children.title: Fair Propagator Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Coverage properties of repeated propagator selection.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worklist discipline realizing nonstarving propagator selection with sound dependency notifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a worklist \(Q\subseteq P\), initially \(Q=P\). Repeatedly select and remove some \(p\in Q\), replace \(D\) by \(p(D)\), and, after every change, insert each propagator whose result may have been affected. If dependency notifications are sound and no queued propagator is postponed forever, every continuously enabled propagator is eventually selected. Moreover, \(Q=\varnothing\) implies \(p(D)=D\) for every \(p\in P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonstarving worklist with complete dependency notifications provides fair scheduling, and an empty worklist certifies common quiescence.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is finite.
Initially \(Q=P\).
Every propagator affected by a store change is reinserted.
No queued propagator is postponed forever.
knowledge_statements.title: Fair Worklist Scheduling
Fair Propagator Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak fairness for sequential propagation schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For propagators \(P=\{p_1,\ldots,p_m\}\), a schedule \(\sigma:\mathbb N\to\{1,\ldots,m\}\) generating \(D_{n+1}=p_{\sigma(n)}(D_n)\) is fair if every propagator that remains continuously enabled is eventually selected:
\[
\forall i\,\forall N\;\Bigl[\forall n\ge N,\ p_i(D_n)\ne D_n\Bigr]\Longrightarrow\Bigl[\exists n\ge N,\ \sigma(n)=i\Bigr].
\]
A schedule selecting every index infinitely often is therefore fair, although this stronger condition is not necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A schedule is fair when any propagator that stays able to reduce the store is eventually applied.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is finite.
The sequential run satisfies \(D_{n+1}=p_{\sigma(n)}(D_n)\).

notation.meaning: propagator i is enabled at stage n

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the scheduling leaf and gives a coherent weak-fairness predicate, but fairness conventions vary; an authoritative source with a precise locator is required to validate this exact continuously-enabled formulation.

children.title: Termination Regimes
children.top_down_role: State-space or operator settings supporting finite propagation runs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative bound on changing propagator applications below an initial store.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every strict descending chain beginning at \(D_0\) has at most \(h(D_0)\) strict steps. For any sequence of contractive propagator applications \(D_{n+1}=p_{\sigma(n)}(D_n)\), the number of indices \(n\) satisfying \(D_{n+1}\subsetneq D_n\) is at most \(h(D_0)\), independently of the application order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The descending height below the initial store bounds the number of strict propagation reductions.
assumptions_latex: Every \(p_i\) is contractive.
Every strict descending chain beginning at \(D_0\) has at most \(h(D_0)\) strict steps.

notation.meaning: maximum number of strict steps in a descending chain beginning at the initial store

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Reduction Height Bound
Termination Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-height termination of strict contractive propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((L,\subseteq)\) have no infinite strictly descending chain, and let each \(p_i:L\to L\) be contractive. For any schedule, define \(D_{n+1}=p_{\sigma(n)}(D_n)\). Whenever an application changes the store, \(D_{n+1}\subsetneq D_n\); hence only finitely many changing applications occur. If the scheduler continues until every propagator has been tested without change, the returned store is a common fixed point of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a store order with no infinite descent, contractive propagation makes only finitely many strict reductions and terminates at quiescence when all propagators are checked.
assumptions_latex: \((L,\subseteq)\) satisfies the descending-chain condition.
Every propagator is contractive: \(p_i(D)\subseteq D\).
Termination is declared only after all propagators have been tested without change.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The run has finitely many strict reductions and terminates at \(D_*\) with \(p_i(D_*)=D_*\) for all \(i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-descent claim is mathematically plausible and the theorem kind fits, but no source supports the exact hypotheses or the scheduler-dependent stopping condition. The distinction between finitely many changing applications and actual termination also requires source-backed formulation.

children.title: Unfairness Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Closure losses attributable to persistently omitted propagation work.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample showing that selecting every propagator once does not ensure common quiescence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(L=\mathcal P(\{a,b\})\), define \(p(S)=S\setminus\{a\}\) and define \(q(S)=S\setminus\{b\}\) when \(a\notin S\), while \(q(S)=S\) when \(a\in S\). Both maps are monotone and contractive. Starting from \(D_0=\{a,b\}\), use the schedule \(q,p,p,p,\ldots\). It reaches \(D_2=\{b\}\) and remains there under \(p\), although \(q(\{b\})=\varnothing\). Thus selecting every propagator once does not prevent closure loss after a later store change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A propagator applied before it becomes effective may need to be scheduled again; one-time coverage is not fairness.
assumptions_latex: Stores are ordered by inclusion.
The schedule is \(q,p,p,p,\ldots\).
knowledge_statements.title: One-Time Coverage Is Insufficient
Unfairness Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite-store counterexample showing that contractiveness and monotonicity do not replace fairness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\mathcal P(\{a,b\})\), ordered by inclusion, and define \(p(S)=S\setminus\{a\}\) and \(q(S)=S\setminus\{b\}\). Both maps are monotone and contractive. Starting from \(D_0=\{a,b\}\), the unfair schedule applying only \(p\) reaches \(D_1=\{b\}\) and then remains there. However \(q(D_1)=\varnothing\ne D_1\), so the apparent limit is not quiescent and not a common fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ignoring an enabled propagator can stabilize a monotone, contractive run at a state that is not a common fixed point.
assumptions_latex: Stores are subsets of \(\{a,b\}\).
The schedule selects \(p\) at every step and never selects \(q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The run stabilizes at \(\{b\}\notin\operatorname{Fix}(q)\), demonstrating failure without fairness.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit example is internally correct and appropriately classified as a counterexample, but it has no cited source or registered evidence establishing its use as the intended unfairness boundary.

children.title: Infinite-Descent Regimes
children.top_down_role: Information-state settings in which reduction may continue indefinitely.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infinite Height Does Not Force Infinite Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the converse to a uniform finite-height termination condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}\) have the order \(0<1<2<\cdots<\infty\). Although strict descending chains in \(L\) have no uniform finite length bound, the map \(p(x)=0\) is monotone, contractive, and idempotent. From every \(x\in L\), iteration reaches \(0\) after at most one changing application. Thus unbounded finite height permits but does not imply an infinite propagation descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A store order without a uniform finite height bound can still have propagators that reach a fixed point immediately.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) has the displayed total order.
\(p(x)=0\) for every \(x\in L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^2=p\quad\text{and every orbit is stationary after at most one strict reduction}.

notation.meaning: store chain with unbounded finite descending lengths

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite Height Does Not Force Infinite Descent

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbounded Height Does Not Force Infinite Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the converse to a uniform finite-height termination condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}\) have order \(0<1<2<\cdots<\infty\). Although strict descending chains have no uniform finite length bound, \(p(x)=0\) is monotone, contractive, and idempotent. Every orbit reaches \(0\) after at most one changing application.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An order with unbounded finite descending lengths may still have a propagator that stabilizes immediately.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) has the displayed total order.
\(p(x)=0\) for every \(x\in L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^2=p\quad\text{and every orbit stabilizes after at most one strict reduction}.

notation.meaning: store chain of unbounded finite height

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Height Does Not Force Infinite Descent

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact orbit-based definition of the nonterminating convergence regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a contractive propagator \(p\) and initial store \(x_0\), an infinite descent is an orbit \(x_{n+1}=p(x_n)\) satisfying \(x_{n+1}<x_n\) for every finite \(n\). Such an orbit has no finite quiescent stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infinite descent means that every finite propagation iterate strictly reduces the preceding store, so no finite iterate is a fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \(p(x)\leq x\) for every store \(x\).
The order distinguishes strict reduction from equality.

notation.meaning: nth store in the propagation orbit

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite Propagation Descent

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit nonterminating orbit on an infinite-height interval-store order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\{[0,r]:r\in[0,1]\}\), ordered by inclusion, and define \(p([0,r])=[0,r/2]\). The map is monotone and contractive. From \(D_0=[0,1]\), \(D_n=[0,2^{-n}]\), so \(D_{n+1}\subsetneq D_n\) for every finite \(n\). Exact iteration therefore never terminates, although \(\bigcap_{n<\omega}D_n=[0,0]=\{0\}\in L\) and is fixed by \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval halving gives infinitely many strict reductions and approaches an already-present limiting fixed point without reaching it finitely.
assumptions_latex: Stores are exact real intervals of the displayed form.
Termination requires equality at a finite iterate.
knowledge_statements.title: Interval-Halving Infinite Descent

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limit Fixed Point of a Meet-Continuous Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit semantics for a descending orbit whose propagator preserves countable descending meets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) admit meets of descending countable chains, and let \(p:L\to L\) be monotone, contractive, and satisfy \(p(\bigwedge_nx_n)=\bigwedge_np(x_n)\) for every descending chain. For \(x_{n+1}=p(x_n)\), put \(x_\omega=\bigwedge_{n<\omega}x_n\). Then \(p(x_\omega)=x_\omega\), and every fixed point \(y\leq x_0\) satisfies \(y\leq x_\omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under descending-meet continuity, the meet of all finite iterates is the greatest fixed point below the initial store.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) has meets of descending countable chains.
\(p\) is monotone and contractive.
\(p\) preserves descending countable meets.

notation.meaning: meet of the finite propagation iterates

knowledge_statements.title: Limit Fixed Point of a Meet-Continuous Descent
Infinite-Descent Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nontermination when the store order admits infinitely many strict reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L=\{[0,r]:r\in[0,1]\}\), ordered by inclusion, and define the contractive monotone propagator \(p([0,r])=[0,r/2]\). From \(D_0=[0,1]\), iteration gives
\[
D_n=[0,2^{-n}],\qquad D_{n+1}\subsetneq D_n
\]
for every finite \(n\). Thus exact fixpoint iteration never terminates, although \(\bigcap_{n\ge0}D_n=\{0\}\) is the limiting fixed point after adjoining the degenerate interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone contractive propagator may reduce forever on an infinite-height store order, approaching a fixed point without reaching it finitely.
assumptions_latex: Exact real intervals are used as stores.
Termination requires equality after a finite number of applications.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration has infinitely many strict reductions and no finite quiescent stage.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The infinite strict-descent example is mathematically valid, but no source is cited. Moreover, the degenerate interval \([0,0]=\{0\}\) already belongs to the stated space because \(0\in[0,1]\), so the phrase 'after adjoining the degenerate interval' is incorrect and must be removed when sourced.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of unique closure for contractive idempotent reductions that are not monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=2^{\{a,b\}}\) be ordered by inclusion. Define \(p(\{a,b\})=\{a\}\) and \(q(\{a,b\})=\{b\}\), and let both maps fix every proper subset. The maps are contractive and idempotent but not monotone. From \(\{a,b\}\), applying \(p\) first reaches the common fixed point \(\{a\}\), whereas applying \(q\) first reaches \(\{b\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contractive idempotent but nonmonotone reductions can reach different common fixed points in different application orders.
assumptions_latex: \(L=2^{\{a,b\}}\) is ordered by inclusion.
The maps are defined as displayed and fix every proper subset.
knowledge_statements.title: Order Dependence Without Monotonicity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unfair Scheduling Can Miss Common Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of closure computation when an effective propagator is indefinitely omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On subsets of \(\{a,b\}\), let \(p(S)=S\setminus\{a\}\) and \(q(S)=S\setminus\{b\}\). Both maps are monotone, contractive, and idempotent, and their greatest common fixed point below \(\{a,b\}\) is \(\varnothing\). A schedule that applies only \(p\) reaches \(\{b\}\) and remains there, although \(q(\{b\})=\varnothing\). Thus a schedule that indefinitely omits an effective propagator need not compute the common closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even monotone contractive propagators can stop short of common closure when scheduling indefinitely ignores an effective propagator.
assumptions_latex: The initial store is \(\{a,b\}\).
The schedule may omit \(q\) indefinitely.
knowledge_statements.title: Unfair Scheduling Can Miss Common Closure
Order Independence of Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness of the terminating fair closure for monotone contractive propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((L,\subseteq)\) satisfy the descending-chain condition, and let \(P\) be a finite family of monotone, contractive self-maps. Starting from \(D_0\), every fair sequential propagation run terminates at the same store
\[
D^*=\max\{E\in L:E\subseteq D_0\text{ and }p(E)=E\text{ for every }p\in P\},
\]
provided this greatest common fixed point exists. Consequently, the closure is independent of the fair application order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every fair order of monotone contractive propagators reaches the same greatest common fixed point below the initial store.
assumptions_latex: \((L,\subseteq)\) satisfies the descending-chain condition.
\(P\) is finite and every member is monotone and contractive.
The displayed greatest common fixed point below \(D_0\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every fair run from \(D_0\) terminates at the same store \(D^*\).

notation.meaning: greatest common fixed point below the initial store

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and local topic match, and the result is plausible under the stated monotonicity, contractiveness, descending-chain, fairness, and existence assumptions. Its exact order-independence theorem nevertheless requires an authoritative propagation or fixpoint-theory locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contraction Alone Does Not Preserve Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp separation between state contraction and semantic soundness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=\{0,1\}\), \(C=\{1\}\), and \(p(D)=D\cap\{0\}\). The map \(p\) is contracting, monotone, and idempotent on \(2^U\), but for \(D=U\), \(C\cap D=\{1\}\) whereas \(C\cap p(D)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contracting, monotone, idempotent operator can delete the only solution, so solution preservation is an independent correctness requirement.
assumptions_latex: Stores are ordered by set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\text{ contracting, monotone, and idempotent}\centernot\Rightarrow C\cap p(D)=C\cap D.
knowledge_statements.title: Contraction Alone Does Not Preserve Solutions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifting constraint-local preservation to a conjunctive model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\) be a model's feasible set. If \(p_i\) satisfies \(C_i\cap p_i(D)=C_i\cap D\) for every store \(D\), then \(F\cap p_i(D)=F\cap D\). Consequently, every finite sequence of such propagators preserves \(F\cap D_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A propagator preserving its own constraint's solutions preserves all solutions of the conjunctive model, and finite heterogeneous propagation preserves the initial model solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(F=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\).
Every applied \(p_i\) preserves \(C_i\)-solutions in every store.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\cap D_n=F\cap D_0\text{ for every finite sequence }D_n.

notation.meaning: feasible set of the conjunctive model

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Solution Preservation by Heterogeneous Propagators
Solution Preservation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic soundness of domain reduction relative to a constraint solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be the universe of complete assignments, let \(C\subseteq U\) be the assignments satisfying the constraint, and let stores be subsets \(D\subseteq U\). A propagator \(p\) preserves solutions when
\[
C\cap p(D)=C\cap D
\]
for every store \(D\). If every applied propagator has this property, then every finite propagation sequence from \(D_0\) preserves exactly the feasible assignments initially represented by \(D_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sound propagator removes no satisfying assignment; any finite composition of such propagators preserves the initial store's solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq U\) is the solution set of the constraint.
Every propagator in the sequence satisfies \(C\cap p(D)=C\cap D\) for all \(D\subseteq U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every finite propagated store \(D_n\), \(C\cap D_n=C\cap D_0\).

notation.meaning: current store interpreted as represented assignments

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property precisely expresses extensional solution preservation and its finite-composition consequence, but the record supplies no authoritative constraint-propagation citation or locator.

children.title: Contractive Reduction
children.top_down_role: Propagator behavior that only removes information-state possibilities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of contractiveness under finite sequential composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((L,\leq)\) be a poset. If \(p,q:L\to L\) are contractive, then \((q\circ p)(x)\leq p(x)\leq x\) for every \(x\in L\). Hence every finite composition of contractive maps is contractive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequentially composing contractive reductions cannot reintroduce information.
assumptions_latex: \(p(x)\leq x\) and \(q(x)\leq x\) for every \(x\in L\).
knowledge_statements.title: Composition of Contractive Reductions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Descent of Repeated Contractive Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination of repeated application on a finite-height information order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((L,\leq)\) have finite height \(h\), let \(p:L\to L\) be contractive, and set \(x_{k+1}=p(x_k)\). Then \(x_{k+1}\leq x_k\), at most \(h-1\) transitions are strict, and some \(x_*\) is reached with \(p(x_*)=x_*\). For \(L=\mathcal P(U)\) and finite \(x_0\), at most \(|x_0|\) transitions are strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated contractive reduction reaches a fixed point after finitely many strict reductions on a finite-height order.
assumptions_latex: \((L,\leq)\) has finite height \(h\), measured as the maximum number of elements in a strict chain.
\(p(x)\leq x\) for every \(x\in L\).

notation.meaning: maximum number of elements in a strict chain

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Descent of Repeated Contractive Reduction
Contractive Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contractiveness under the information order given by set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let stores be subsets of a universe \(U\), ordered by inclusion. A map \(p:\mathcal P(U)\to\mathcal P(U)\) is a contractive reduction, or contracting propagator, if
\[
\forall D\subseteq U,\qquad p(D)\subseteq D.
\]
An application is strict at \(D\) when \(p(D)\subsetneq D\). Contractiveness alone prevents the reintroduction of assignments but does not imply monotonicity, solution preservation, termination, or order independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contractive reduction always returns a substore of its input, and it is strict when at least one represented assignment is removed.
assumptions_latex: Stores are ordered by ordinary set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\text{ is contractive}\iff(\forall D\subseteq U)\ p(D)\subseteq D\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically precise and fits the Contractive Reduction leaf, but neither it nor the additional claims distinguishing contractiveness from other properties has a cited locator.

children.title: Monotone Reduction
children.top_down_role: Propagator behavior ordered consistently with information-state refinement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of order preservation under finite sequential composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((L,\leq)\) be a poset. If \(p,q:L\to L\) are monotone, then \(q\circ p\) is monotone. Consequently every finite composition of monotone maps is monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite sequential compositions preserve monotonicity.
assumptions_latex: \(x\leq y\Rightarrow p(x)\leq p(y)\).
\(x\leq y\Rightarrow q(x)\leq q(y)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Composition of Monotone Reductions
Monotone Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order preservation for propagators under store inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let stores be ordered by inclusion. A reduction map \(p:\mathcal P(U)\to\mathcal P(U)\) is monotone if
\[
D_1\subseteq D_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p(D_1)\subseteq p(D_2)
\]
for all stores \(D_1,D_2\subseteq U\). Thus strengthening the input store cannot produce an output weaker than, or incomparable with, the output obtained from the original store. Monotonicity does not by itself require \(p(D)\subseteq D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone reduction preserves store inclusion: a stronger input yields an output contained in that produced from a weaker input.
assumptions_latex: Stores are subsets of a fixed universe \(U\) and are ordered by inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\text{ is monotone}\iff(\forall D_1\subseteq D_2)\ p(D_1)\subseteq p(D_2)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inclusion-preserving definition is correct and fits the Monotone Reduction leaf, but the record contains no source reference or inspectable locator for the propagator convention used.

children.title: Contraction–Monotonicity Interaction
children.top_down_role: Structural consequences of combining contractive behavior with monotone behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Contraction–Monotonicity Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistence of reductions under simultaneous strengthening of input and output stores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p:\mathcal P(U)\to\mathcal P(U)\) be contractive and monotone. For stores \(D_1\subseteq D_2\),
\[
p(D_1)\subseteq p(D_2)\subseteq D_2,
\qquad p(D_1)\subseteq D_1.
\]
Moreover, every fixed point below \(D\) is preserved by one reduction: if \(F\subseteq D\) and \(p(F)=F\), then \(F\subseteq p(D)\subseteq D\). Hence applying \(p\) cannot remove any fixed-point store already contained in the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a monotone contractive propagator, outputs remain nested, and every fixed point contained in an input remains contained after reduction.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is contractive.
\(p\) is monotone.
\(D_1\subseteq D_2\subseteq U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(D_1)\subseteq p(D_2)\subseteq D_2\), and \(F\subseteq D\land p(F)=F\Rightarrow F\subseteq p(D)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed nesting and fixed-point persistence statements follow from monotonicity and contractiveness and fit the property leaf, but no authoritative source or evidence locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Builder proposal rejected from this interaction leaf because its two components have separate canonical homes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p\) and \(q\) are both monotone and contractive, then \(q\circ p\) is both monotone and contractive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The combined class is closed under composition, but this is only the conjunction of two independently owned closure properties.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) and \(q\) are monotone and contractive self-maps of one poset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q\circ p\text{ is monotone and contractive}.
review_flags: Contractive composition belongs primarily to Contractive Reduction and monotone composition to Monotone Reduction.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Under Composition

intermediate_metadata.reason: The locally owned inventory is nested reduction and persistence of contained fixed points when contraction and monotonicity coexist. Standalone definitions, their separate composition laws, and nonmonotone counterexamples are excluded to sibling scopes.

children.title: Nonmonotone Propagation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Semantic limitations arising when refinement order is not respected.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Propagation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-dependent closure caused by contractive but nonmonotone propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(L=\mathcal P(\{a,b\})\), define \(p(\{a,b\})=\{a\}\), \(q(\{a,b\})=\{b\}\), and \(p(S)=q(S)=S\) for every proper subset \(S\). Both maps are contractive but nonmonotone. From \(\{a,b\}\), applying \(p\) first yields the common fixed point \(\{a\}\), whereas applying \(q\) first yields the common fixed point \(\{b\}\). Thus contractiveness without monotonicity permits order-dependent closures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two contractive nonmonotone propagators can reach different common fixed points solely because their application order differs.
assumptions_latex: Stores are subsets of \(\{a,b\}\).
Each run stops when both propagators leave the store unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(p(\{a,b\}))=\{a\}\ne\{b\}=p(q(\{a,b\}))\), and both outputs are common fixed points.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maps are indeed contractive and nonmonotone, and the two orders yield distinct common fixed points, so the counterexample fits the failure-boundary leaf. It nevertheless lacks a cited source or registered evidence.

children.title: Failure Status
children.top_down_role: Propagation outcomes signaling the absence of admissible states.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes sound empty-output reports from detection of every semantically inconsistent store.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq U\) and let \(p:\mathcal P(U)\to\mathcal P(U)\) preserve solutions: \(C\cap p(D)=C\cap D\). Then \(p(D)=\varnothing\) soundly certifies \(C\cap D=\varnothing\). The test is complete precisely when
\[
p(D)=\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C\cap D=\varnothing
\]
for every store \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solution preservation makes empty output a sound failure report; failure completeness additionally requires every inconsistent store to yield empty output.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq U\) is the exact solution relation.
\(C\cap p(D)=C\cap D\) for every store \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\text{ is failure-complete}\iff(\forall D)\,[p(D)=\varnothing\iff C\cap D=\varnothing].
knowledge_statements.title: Complete Failure Detection
Failure Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure as emptiness of the represented assignment store.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a store \(D\subseteq U\) represent its admissible complete assignments. The store has failure status exactly when
\[
D=\varnothing.
\]
A propagator application reports failure at input \(D\) when its output is empty. If the propagator preserves solutions for a constraint solution set \(C\), then \(p(D)=\varnothing\) certifies \(C\cap D=\varnothing\); hence no solution represented by the input store exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure means that the current store represents no assignment; a solution-preserving propagator may soundly report failure when its output is empty.
assumptions_latex: Stores are interpreted extensionally as sets of complete assignments.
For the certificate implication, \(p\) preserves solutions: \(C\cap p(D)=C\cap D\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The empty-store definition and the solution-preservation certificate implication are mathematically consistent, and definition is the correct primary kind for this status leaf. An authoritative propagator-status citation with a specific locator is missing.

children.title: Entailedness Status
children.top_down_role: Propagation outcomes signaling that further checking is unnecessary within the current state.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjoint status convention resolving vacuous entailment of an empty store.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq U\) be a store and \(C\subseteq U\) a constraint relation. The semantic entailment predicate is \(D\subseteq C\), which is vacuously true for \(D=\varnothing\). In a disjoint status taxonomy where failure has precedence, the reported entailed status is instead
\[
D\neq\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad D\subseteq C.
\]
Thus an empty store is reported failed, not entailed, while every nonempty represented assignment satisfies the constraint at an entailed store.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set-theoretic entailment includes the empty store, but a disjoint failure-first taxonomy reports entailed only for a nonempty store whose assignments all satisfy the constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq U\) is interpreted extensionally.
\(C\subseteq U\) is the exact constraint relation.
Failure has precedence over entailment in the reported taxonomy.
knowledge_statements.title: Entailedness with Failure Precedence
Entailedness Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic entailment status of a constraint relative to a finite-domain store.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the current store be \(D=\prod_{i=1}^{n}D_i\), and let \(C\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^{n}U_i\) be the assignments satisfying a constraint. The constraint has entailedness status at \(D\) precisely when every assignment represented by the store satisfies it:
\[
D\subseteq C.
\]
Equivalently, no completion compatible with the current domains violates the constraint. This is a semantic status; a particular propagator may fail to recognize it unless its entailment test is complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint is entailed at a store when every complete assignment allowed by the current domains satisfies the constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(D_i\subseteq U_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
\(C\) denotes the exact solution relation of the constraint.

notation.meaning: Cartesian-product store represented by the current domains
relation of assignments satisfying the constraint

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard semantic definition of constraint entailment over a finite-domain store.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No inspectable source is cited. A source must also clarify whether entailment is allowed vacuously at an empty store or whether failure takes precedence so that the status taxonomy is disjoint.

children.title: Undetermined Status
children.top_down_role: Propagation outcomes that establish neither failure nor entailedness.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit certificate for the semantic undetermined case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be a store and \(C\) a constraint relation. A pair \((s,v)\) certifies that \(C\) is undetermined at \(D\) when \(s,v\in D\), \(s\in C\), and \(v
otin C\). Such a pair exists if and only if \(D\cap C
eq\varnothing\) and \(D
subseteq C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A represented satisfying assignment together with a represented violating assignment is a necessary and sufficient witness for undetermined status.
assumptions_latex: Membership in \(D\) and satisfaction of \(C\) are checkable for the exhibited assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists s,v\in D:\ s\in C\land v\notin C\iff \operatorname{status}_C(D)=\mathsf{undetermined}.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Witness Certificate for Undetermined Status
Undetermined Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-valued semantic status when neither failure nor entailment has been established.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=\prod_{i=1}^{n}D_i\) be a store and \(C\) the solution relation of a constraint. The constraint is undetermined at \(D\) exactly when the store contains at least one satisfying assignment and at least one violating assignment:
\[
D\cap C\neq\varnothing
\quad\text{and}\quad
D\nsubseteq C.
\]
Thus the current domains neither refute nor entail the constraint. This semantic definition is independent of whether an implementation can exhibit the two assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint is undetermined when the store permits both a satisfying assignment and a violating assignment.
assumptions_latex: \(D_i\subseteq U_i\) for every \(i\).
\(C\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^{n}U_i\) is the exact constraint relation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard three-way semantic classification of a constraint at a store.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is a precise standard characterization of the nonterminal semantic case, but no source with a specific locator supports the adopted three-status convention.

children.title: Status Stability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Persistence of reported statuses under later information refinement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact narrowing transitions for a disjoint failure-first status taxonomy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D'\subseteq D\subseteq U\) and \(C\subseteq U\). Classify \(D\) as failed when \(D\cap C=\varnothing\), entailed when \(D\neq\varnothing\) and \(D\subseteq C\), and undetermined otherwise. Failure is downward stable. Entailedness remains entailed under every nonempty narrowing, but an empty narrowing is failed. An undetermined store may remain undetermined, become entailed by removing all violating assignments while retaining a satisfying assignment, or become failed by removing all satisfying assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure persists under narrowing; entailedness persists under nonempty narrowing but changes to failure at the empty store; undetermined status may reach any status.
assumptions_latex: \(D'\subseteq D\subseteq U\).
\(C\subseteq U\) is the exact constraint relation.
The taxonomy is disjoint and gives failure precedence.
knowledge_statements.title: Status Stability Under Failure Precedence
Status Stability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Behavior of semantic constraint statuses under domain narrowing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For stores \(D'\subseteq D\) and constraint relation \(C\), entailment and failure are downward stable:
\[
D\subseteq C\Longrightarrow D'\subseteq C,
\qquad
D\cap C=\varnothing\Longrightarrow D'\cap C=\varnothing.
\]
Undetermined status is not downward stable. If \(D\cap C\neq\varnothing\) and \(D\nsubseteq C\), a narrowing may remain undetermined, become entailed by deleting all violating assignments, or become failed by deleting all satisfying assignments. Hence only a nonempty undetermined store can cross either terminal-status boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Narrowing preserves entailment and failure, whereas an undetermined store may remain undetermined or become entailed or failed.
assumptions_latex: \(D'\subseteq D\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^{n}U_i\).
\(C\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^{n}U_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathsf{entailed}\) and \(\mathsf{failed}\) are stable under narrowing; \(\mathsf{undetermined}\) is not.

notation.meaning: a narrowed store and its predecessor

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Immediate standard status-stability property under set inclusion.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-inclusion claims are correct under the stated predicates, but the entailment stability claim depends on how an empty narrowed store is classified. An authoritative source must establish the status convention.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact enforcement of all unary constraints in a finite-domain network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each variable \(x_i\), replace its domain by \[D_i'=D_i\cap\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal U_i}C,\] where \(\bigcap\varnothing=U_i\). These domains are the unique greatest componentwise subdomain of \(D\) that is node consistent. The operation is contracting, monotone, idempotent, and independent of unary-constraint processing order. Naive direct enforcement uses at most \(\sum_i|D_i||\mathcal U_i|\) exact membership tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersect each domain with every unary relation on its variable; this gives the unique greatest node-consistent subdomain.
assumptions_latex: Each \(D_i\subseteq U_i\) is finite.
Unary-relation membership is tested exactly.
The intersection of an empty unary-constraint family is \(U_i\).

notation.meaning: unary constraint relations on variable x_i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Node Consistency Does Not Imply Satisfiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limitation of unary consistency when higher-arity constraints are present.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_x=D_y=\{0\}\), impose no nontrivial unary constraints, and impose \(x\ne y\). The network is node consistent but has no solution and is not arc consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unary consistency can hold even though an incompatible binary constraint makes the network unsatisfiable.
assumptions_latex: The only non-unary constraint is \(x\ne y\).
knowledge_statements.title: Node Consistency Does Not Imply Satisfiability
Node Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unary consistency for a finite-domain constraint network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite-domain constraint network is node consistent when every current value satisfies every unary constraint on its variable. Formally, for each variable \(x_i\) with domain \(D_i\) and unary constraint relation \(C\subseteq U_i\),
\[
D_i\subseteq C.
\]
If several unary constraints constrain \(x_i\), this condition is equivalent to \(D_i\subseteq\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal U_i}C\). Enforcing node consistency deletes precisely those values violating at least one unary constraint; an empty resulting domain signals inconsistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network is node consistent when every domain value satisfies all unary constraints imposed on its variable.
assumptions_latex: Each variable \(x_i\) has a finite domain \(D_i\subseteq U_i\).
\(\mathcal U_i\) is the family of unary constraint relations on \(x_i\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Classical finite-domain CSP definition of node consistency.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The classical definition is stated accurately, but it has no citation. The intersection formulation additionally requires a convention for variables having no unary constraints, normally an empty intersection equal to the universe.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local filtering operation for one directed binary arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed arc \((i,j)\), \(\operatorname{REVISE}(i,j)\) replaces \(D_i\) by \(\{a\in D_i:\exists b\in D_j,(a,b)\in C_{ij}\}\) and leaves every other domain unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: REVISE removes exactly the source-domain values lacking support in the target domain.
assumptions_latex: \(C_{ij}\) is a binary relation.
The current domains are finite.
knowledge_statements.title: Directed Revise Operator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary relation with constant-time membership testing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Testing each source value against every possible supporting value implements \(\operatorname{REVISE}(i,j)\) in \(O(|D_i||D_j|)\) time and constant auxiliary workspace apart from recording deletions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Naive directed revision scans at most the Cartesian product of the two current domains.
assumptions_latex: Membership in \(C_{ij}\) is testable in constant time.
