knowledge_statements.statement_title: Safety and Monotonicity of Directed Revision
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solution preservation and response to contraction of the supporting domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Directed revision deletes no source value used by a solution of the current network. If the supporting domain shrinks, no new support is created, so the revised source domain can only shrink.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Revision preserves solution values, and contraction of the supporting domain can only remove supports.
assumptions_latex: Solutions satisfy \(C_{ij}\) and use values from the current domains.
knowledge_statements.title: Safety and Monotonicity of Directed Revision
Directed Arc Support
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value support along one orientation of a binary constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_{ij}\subseteq U_i\times U_j\) be a binary constraint and let \(D_i,D_j\) be the current domains. A value \(b\in D_j\) supports \(a\in D_i\) along the directed arc \((i,j)\) when
\[
(a,b)\in C_{ij}.
\]
The directed arc \((i,j)\) is arc consistent exactly when every \(a\in D_i\) has at least one such support in \(D_j\). The reverse arc imposes a separate support condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value has directed arc support when it can be paired with a current value of the other variable satisfying the binary constraint; support in the reverse direction is a separate condition.
assumptions_latex: \(D_i\subseteq U_i\) and \(D_j\subseteq U_j\) are finite.
\(C_{ij}\subseteq U_i\times U_j\) is a binary relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((i,j)\text{ is arc consistent}\iff\forall a\in D_i\;\exists b\in D_j:\,(a,b)\in C_{ij}\).

notation.meaning: binary constraint relation between variables i and j
arc directed from the tested domain to the supporting domain

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arc Consistency Does Not Imply Satisfiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary finite-domain separation example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let three variables have domain \(\{0,1\}\), with disequality on every pair. Every value has the opposite value as support across each incident constraint, so the network is arc consistent. No assignment satisfies all three constraints because a triangle is not two-colorable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two-color disequality triangle is arc consistent but unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.title: Arc Consistency Does Not Imply Satisfiability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic safety of enforcing network arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Deleting a value solely because it lacks support on an incident binary constraint cannot remove a complete solution of the current network. Consequently, sound arc-consistency enforcement preserves the complete-solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arc-consistency filtering removes no value used by a complete solution.
assumptions_latex: Every deletion is justified by absence of directed support in a current neighboring domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution Preservation Under Arc Filtering

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-Projection Characterization of Network Arc Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relational-algebra formulation for each domain-restricted binary relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each binary constraint let \(R_{ij}=C_{ij}\cap(D_i\times D_j)\). The network is arc consistent exactly when \(\pi_i(R_{ij})=D_i\) and \(\pi_j(R_{ij})=D_j\) for every constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each binary relation restricted to current domains must project fully onto both endpoint domains.
assumptions_latex: The network is binary.
Current domains are finite.

notation.meaning: constraint relation restricted to the current endpoint domains

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Projection Characterization of Network Arc Consistency
Network Arc Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc consistency of an entire binary finite-domain network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A binary constraint network is arc consistent when every directed arc induced by every binary constraint is arc consistent. Thus, for each relation \(C_{ij}\subseteq U_i\times U_j\),
\[
\forall a\in D_i\;\exists b\in D_j:\,(a,b)\in C_{ij},
\qquad
\forall b\in D_j\;\exists a\in D_i:\,(a,b)\in C_{ij}.
\]
If a pair of variables has multiple binary constraints, support must satisfy each constraint separately unless those constraints have first been replaced by their relational intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary network is arc consistent when every value has support across every incident binary constraint in both directions.
assumptions_latex: The network has finite domains \(D_i\subseteq U_i\).
Every nonunary constraint is represented by a binary relation \(C_{ij}\).

notation.meaning: binary constraint relation on variables i and j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Classical definition of arc consistency for a binary constraint network.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly requires directed support in both orientations for every binary constraint, but no source with an inspectable locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Queue-based enforcement of arc consistency in a finite binary network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a queue with all directed arcs. On removing \((i,j)\), replace \(D_i\) by the values having support in \(D_j\). If values are deleted, enqueue each \((h,i)\) with \(h\ne j\). Stop with failure if a domain becomes empty; if the queue becomes empty, every directed arc is consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AC-3 repeatedly revises queued arcs and requeues arcs whose supports may have been invalidated, stopping at an empty domain or an arc-consistent fixpoint.
assumptions_latex: The binary network and all domains are finite.
Revision deletes exactly the values lacking current directed support.

notation.meaning: queue of directed arcs awaiting revision

Let \(x_1,x_2,x_3\) have domains \(\{0,1\}\), and impose \(x_1

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contractive, monotone, and idempotent behavior for a fixed finite binary network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed finite binary constraint network, let \(\operatorname{cl}_{AC}(D)\) denote the domains remaining after complete fair enforcement of arc consistency from domain vector \(D\). Under componentwise inclusion, \[\operatorname{cl}_{AC}(D)\subseteq D,\qquad E\subseteq D\Longrightarrow\operatorname{cl}_{AC}(E)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_{AC}(D),\qquad \operatorname{cl}_{AC}(\operatorname{cl}_{AC}(D))=\operatorname{cl}_{AC}(D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arc-consistency closure is contracting, monotone under domain inclusion, and idempotent.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic invariant of support-based value deletion in a finite binary network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) be a binary constraint network with domain vector \(D\). If \(a\in D_i\) has no support in the current domain \(D_j\) across an incident relation \(C_{ij}\), then no solution of the current network assigns \(x_i=a\). Consequently, every finite sequence of arc-consistency deletions preserves the complete solution set, and \[\operatorname{Sol}(N,D)=\operatorname{Sol}(N,\operatorname{cl}_{AC}(D)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting a value lacking support on an incident arc removes no solution, so complete arc-consistency enforcement preserves the solution set.
assumptions_latex: All current domains are finite.
A value is deleted only when it lacks support in a current neighboring domain.
The binary relations remain fixed during enforcement.

domains remaining after complete arc-consistency enforcement

knowledge_statements.title: Solution Preservation Under Arc-Consistency Deletion
Arc-Consistency Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greatest arc-consistent domain restriction of a finite binary network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite binary network with initial domain vector \(D=(D_i)_i\), its arc-consistency closure is the componentwise greatest vector \(D^*=(D_i^*)_i\) satisfying
\[
D^*\subseteq D
\]
and making every directed binary arc consistent. Equivalently, \(D^*\) is the common fixpoint reached by repeatedly deleting values lacking directed support. The closure is unique and independent of the order of fair deletion steps. Some component \(D_i^*=\varnothing\) certifies that arc-consistency enforcement has detected inconsistency, although nonempty closure does not generally certify global satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The arc-consistency closure is the unique largest subdomain network in which every binary arc is consistent.
assumptions_latex: All domains are finite.
Deletion repeatedly removes only values lacking support on some directed arc.
The deletion schedule is fair.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard greatest-fixpoint characterization of binary arc-consistency enforcement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Backtrack-Free Extension on an Ordered Forest
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficiency of directional arc consistency for binary forest networks under a root-to-leaf ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the binary constraint graph be a forest. Root each component and choose a total ordering in which every parent precedes its children. Under the earlier-to-later support convention, if every domain is nonempty and the network is directionally arc consistent, then every choice of one value for each component root extends recursively to a complete satisfying assignment by selecting for each child a value supporting its assigned parent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a rooted forest ordered from roots to leaves, directional arc consistency makes every tuple of root choices extendible without backtracking.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Order-Reversal Equivalence of DAC Orientation Conventions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation between earlier-to-later and later-to-earlier directional arc-consistency conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\prec\) be a total variable order and \(\prec^{\mathrm{rev}}\) its reverse. Define \(\operatorname{DAC}^{\rightarrow}_{\prec}\) by requiring support from every earlier variable to each later neighbor, and \(\operatorname{DAC}^{\leftarrow}_{\prec}\) by requiring support from every later variable to each earlier neighbor. With relation coordinates transposed consistently when orientation is reversed, \[\operatorname{DAC}^{\rightarrow}_{\prec}(N)\iff\operatorname{DAC}^{\leftarrow}_{\prec^{\mathrm{rev}}}(N).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Earlier-to-later DAC under one order equals later-to-earlier DAC under the reversed order.
assumptions_latex: \(\prec\) is a total order.

Directional Arc Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way arc consistency relative to a fixed variable ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a total ordering \(x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_n\) of the variables of a binary constraint network. The network is directionally arc consistent relative to this ordering when, for every binary relation \(C_{ij}\) with \(i<j\), every value of the earlier variable has support in the current domain of the later variable:

\forall a\in D_i\;\exists b\in D_j:\,(a,b)\in C_{ij}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and finite computation of the maximal GAC reduction of a finite network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from finite domains \(D\), repeatedly delete a value whenever it lacks full-tuple support in an incident constraint, and reconsider affected constraints fairly until no deletion is possible. This terminates after at most \(\sum_i|D_i|\) successful deletions and returns the unique greatest componentwise subdomain \(D^*\subseteq D\) on which every constraint is generalized arc consistent. Every fair exact revision order yields the same closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fair exact deletion of unsupported values terminates and yields the unique greatest generalized-arc-consistent subdomain.
assumptions_latex: All initial domains are finite.
Every support test is exact.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Arc-Consistency Closure
Generalized Arc Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-wise full-tuple support for constraints of arbitrary finite arity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a constraint with scope \(S\) have relation \(C\subseteq\prod_{j\in S}U_j\) and current domains \((D_j)_{j\in S}\). The constraint is generalized arc consistent when every value of every scoped variable extends to a satisfying tuple using only current-domain values:
\[
\forall i\in S\;\forall a\in D_i\;\exists t\in C\cap\prod_{j\in S}D_j:\;t_i=a.
\]
A network is generalized arc consistent when each of its constraints satisfies this condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every value of every variable in a constraint must extend to a complete satisfying tuple over the current domains.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a finite constraint scope.
Each \(D_j\subseteq U_j\) is finite.
\(C\) is the exact relation of the constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall i\in S\;\forall a\in D_i\;\exists t\in C\cap\prod_{j\in S}D_j:\;t_i=a\).

knowledge_statements.title: Hyper-Arc Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-tuple support definition for a nonbinary constraint hyperedge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Represent a nonbinary constraint as a hyperedge with scope \(S\) and relation \(C\subseteq\prod_{j\in S}U_j\). It is hyper-arc consistent with respect to domains \((D_j)_{j\in S}\) when every pair consisting of a scoped variable and one of its current values occurs in a feasible tuple:
\[
\forall i\in S\;\forall a\in D_i\;\exists t\in C\cap\prod_{j\in S}D_j:\;t_i=a.
\]
The supporting tuple may depend on both \(i\) and \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint hyperedge is hyper-arc consistent when each current value occurs in some satisfying tuple whose components all belong to the current domains.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite.
Each \(D_j\subseteq U_j\) is finite.
\(C\subseteq\prod_{j\in S}U_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall i\in S\;\forall a\in D_i\;\exists t\in C\cap\prod_{j\in S}D_j:\;t_i=a\).

knowledge_statements.title: Domain Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-wise support consistency for one finite-domain constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A constraint with scope \(S\), relation \(C\subseteq\prod_{j\in S}U_j\), and current domains \((D_j)_{j\in S}\) is domain consistent when every value remaining in every scoped domain belongs to at least one satisfying tuple compatible with all current domains:
\[
\forall i\in S\;\forall a\in D_i\;\exists t\in C\cap\prod_{j\in S}D_j:\;t_i=a.
\]
Consequently, removing any unsupported value is necessary to restore domain consistency; the definition does not require every combination of remaining values to satisfy the constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint is domain consistent when every remaining domain value participates in a satisfying tuple over the current domains.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) and all domains \(D_j\) are finite.
\(C\) is interpreted extensionally as its exact satisfying relation.

notation.meaning: component of tuple t for variable i

knowledge_statements.title: Terminology Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which three nonbinary consistency names denote one predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite-domain constraints interpreted by exact relations, suppose “generalized arc consistent,” “hyper-arc consistent,” and “domain consistent” are each defined by value-wise full-tuple support. Then, for every constraint relation \(C\) on scope \(S\), the three predicates are equivalent, because each requires exactly
\[
\forall i\in S\;\forall a\in D_i\;\exists t\in C\cap\prod_{j\in S}D_j:\;t_i=a.
\]
The equivalence is terminological rather than an implication between distinct consistency strengths and applies constraintwise, hence also networkwise when every constraint is tested.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the shared full-tuple-support convention, generalized arc, hyper-arc, and domain consistency are the same predicate.
assumptions_latex: All constraint scopes and domains are finite.
Constraints denote exact relations.
Each term uses value-wise support by a tuple covering the full constraint scope.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The equivalence follows from adopting the identical full-tuple-support predicate for all three terms.

knowledge_statements.title: Terminology Divergence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary governing comparisons of nonbinary support-consistency terminology across sources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonbinary constraint, the labels “generalized arc consistency,” “domain consistency,” and “hyper-arc consistency” are equivalent only when each means that every value of every variable has a full satisfying tuple over the constraint scope. The unqualified term “arc consistency” may instead refer exclusively to binary constraints or to consistency of binary projections. Consequently, an implication or equivalence involving these names is valid across sources only after matching their support quantifiers and the relations on which support is tested.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonbinary consistency names are interchangeable only when they require the same full-tuple supports; unqualified arc consistency may instead mean binary or projection consistency.
assumptions_latex: A finite-domain constraint network is under consideration.
Terminology may originate from different constraint-programming conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Terminological equivalence requires equality of the underlying support predicates, not merely similarity of names.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounds(D) Strictly Implies Bounds(Z)
Bounds(D) Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain-witness form of bounds consistency for one finite-domain constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a constraint with scope \(S\), and let each \(D(x)\) be a nonempty finite ordered domain. The constraint \(C\) is bounds(D) consistent with respect to \(D\) if, for every \(x\in S\) and every \(a\in\{\min D(x),\max D(x)\}\), there exists a tuple \(t\in C\) such that \(t_x=a\) and \(t_y\in D(y)\) for every \(y\in S\setminus\{x\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every current lower and upper bound must occur in a satisfying tuple whose other coordinates are actual current domain values.
assumptions_latex: Each \(D(x)\) is nonempty, finite, and ordered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every bound value has a full domain-valued support in \(C\).

coordinate of tuple t assigned to x

knowledge_statements.title: Bounds(Z) Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-interval witness form of bounds consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb Z^S\) be an integer constraint and let each \(D(x)\subseteq\mathbb Z\) be nonempty and finite. The constraint \(C\) is bounds(Z) consistent with respect to \(D\) if, for every \(x\in S\) and every \(a\in\{\min D(x),\max D(x)\}\), there exists \(t\in C\) such that \(t_x=a\) and \(\min D(y)\le t_y\le\max D(y)\) for every \(y\in S\setminus\{x\}\). The supporting coordinates need not belong to their possibly nonconvex domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every domain bound has an integer satisfying support inside the other variables’ current integer intervals, including values absent from their domains.
assumptions_latex: The constraint and all supporting tuples are integer-valued.
Each current domain is nonempty and finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every bound value has an integer-interval support in \(C\).

notation.meaning: integer hull of the current domain of y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strength comparison under a fixed real extension of an integer relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C_{\mathbb Z}\subseteq C_{\mathbb R}\) and the current domains are integral, bounds(Z) consistency of \(C_{\mathbb Z}\) implies bounds(R) consistency of \(C_{\mathbb R}\). The converse fails when \(D(x)=D(y)=\{0,1\}\), \(C_{\mathbb R}=\{(0,\tfrac12),(1,\tfrac12),(\tfrac12,0),(\tfrac12,1)\}\), and \(C_{\mathbb Z}=C_{\mathbb R}\cap\mathbb Z^2=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer-hull support implies real-hull support under a compatible real extension, but real supports may exist without any integer support.

Current domains are nonempty finite subsets of \(\mathbb Z\).

Bounds(R) Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-interval relaxation form of bounds consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^S\) be a real interpretation of a constraint and let each \(D(x)\subseteq\mathbb R\) be nonempty, finite, and bounded. The constraint \(C\) is bounds(R) consistent with respect to \(D\) if, for every \(x\in S\) and every \(a\in\{\min D(x),\max D(x)\}\), there exists \(t\in C\) such that \(t_x=a\) and \(\min D(y)\le t_y\le\max D(y)\) for every \(y\in S\setminus\{x\}\). Supporting coordinates may be arbitrary real points of these intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every domain bound has a real satisfying support within the other variables’ interval hulls, whether or not those coordinates are domain values.
assumptions_latex: A real-valued interpretation \(C\) of the constraint is fixed.
Each current domain is nonempty, finite, and bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every bound value has a real-interval support in \(C\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strength of every-value integer-hull support relative to actual-domain support and bound-only support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integer constraints, domain consistency implies range consistency, which implies bounds(Z) consistency, and both implications are strict. For \(D(x)=D(y)=\{0,2\}\) and \(C=\{(0,1),(2,1),(1,0),(1,2)\}\), range consistency holds but domain consistency fails. For \(D(x)=\{0,1,2\}\), \(D(y)=\{0,2\}\), and \(C=\{(0,0),(2,2)\}\), bounds(Z) consistency holds but range consistency fails because \(x=1\) has no support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Range consistency lies strictly between domain consistency and bounds(Z) consistency.
assumptions_latex: The constraint and current domains are integer-valued.
All current domains are nonempty and finite.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Range-Consistency Hierarchy
Range Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer range consistency for a single finite-domain constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb Z^S\) and let each \(D(x)\subseteq\mathbb Z\) be nonempty and finite. The constraint \(C\) is range consistent with respect to \(D\) if, for every \(x\in S\) and every value \(a\in D(x)\), there exists \(t\in C\) satisfying \(t_x=a\) and \(\min D(y)\le t_y\le\max D(y)\) for every \(y\in S\setminus\{x\}\). Thus every domain value, rather than only each bound, must possess an integer-interval support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every current domain value must extend to a satisfying integer tuple inside the interval hulls of all other domains.
assumptions_latex: The constraint and supporting tuples are integer-valued.
Every current domain is nonempty and finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(a\in D(x)\) has an integer-range support for each \(x\in S\).

An empty relation proves unsatisfiability.

The binary network is normalized.

Path Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical path consistency for a normalized binary constraint network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) have domains \(D_i\), and let \(R_{ij}\subseteq D_i\times D_j\) denote the binary relation between every distinct pair, with absent constraints represented by universal relations. The network is path consistent if, for every distinct \(i,j,k\) and every \((a,b)\in R_{ij}\), there exists \(c\in D_k\) such that \((a,c)\in R_{ik}\) and \((b,c)\in R_{jk}\). Hence every permitted assignment to two variables extends consistently to each third variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every permitted assignment to two variables can be extended to any third variable while satisfying both incident binary relations.
assumptions_latex: The binary network is normalized with one relation for every variable pair.
Absent binary constraints are interpreted as universal relations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \((a,b)\in R_{ij}\) extends through every third variable \(X_k\).

notation.meaning: binary compatibility relation between Xi and Xj

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X_1\prec\cdots\prec X_n\), process \(k=n,n-1,\ldots,3\) and every \(i<j<k\), setting \(R_{ij}\leftarrow R_{ij}\cap(R_{ik}\circ R_{kj})\). The result preserves all complete solutions and is directionally path consistent; an empty relation proves inconsistency.

The finite binary network is normalized, with reversed relations represented by converses.

Directional Path Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path consistency restricted by a fixed variable ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an ordering \(X_1\prec\cdots\prec X_n\) in a normalized binary network with relations \(R_{ij}\). The network is directional path consistent relative to this ordering if, whenever \(i<j<k\) and \((a,b)\in R_{ij}\), there exists \(c\in D_k\) such that \((a,c)\in R_{ik}\) and \((b,c)\in R_{jk}\). Only extensions from an earlier pair toward a later variable are required; changing the ordering may therefore change whether the property holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a fixed ordering, every permitted pair of earlier assignments must extend consistently to each later variable.
assumptions_latex: A total ordering of the variables is fixed.
The binary network is normalized; absent constraints are universal.
