notation.meaning: binary compatibility relation between Xi and Xj

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf, but directional path-consistency conventions depend on the orientation of the variable ordering; a specific authoritative source is required.

children.title: Restricted Path Consistency
children.top_down_role: The restricted member of the path-consistency family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value deletion triggered by unique supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain arc consistency. Whenever \(a\in D_i\) has a unique support \(b\in D_j\), delete \(a\) if \((a,b)\) fails to extend through some third variable, then propagate arc- and RPC-induced deletions. The finite process preserves all solutions and reaches RPC or an empty domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete a value when its unique support fails a path-consistency test, iterating with arc consistency.
assumptions_latex: The binary network and domains are finite.
Arc consistency is maintained after every deletion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}(N')=\operatorname{Sol}(N),\quad N'\text{ is RPC or has an empty domain}.\)

notation.meaning: A value and its unique support.

knowledge_statements.title: RPC Fixed-Point Enforcement
Restricted Path Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc consistency augmented only at unique supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary constraint network is restricted path consistent if it is arc consistent and satisfies the following condition. For every ordered pair of constrained variables \(X_i,X_j\) and every \(a\in D_i\), if \(a\) has exactly one support \(b\in D_j\) in \(R_{ij}\), then for every third variable \(X_k\) there exists \(c\in D_k\) such that \((a,c)\in R_{ik}\) and \((b,c)\in R_{jk}\). Thus path consistency is imposed only on support pairs forced by uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc-consistent network is restricted path consistent when every unique arc support is compatible through every third variable.
assumptions_latex: The network is finite, binary, and normalized.
Arc consistency is imposed before the restricted test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every unique support pair is path consistent with respect to every third variable.

notation.meaning: binary compatibility relation between Xi and Xj
the unique support of value a in the neighboring domain

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and unique-support condition plausibly describe Restricted Path Consistency, but no relevant source verifies the exact quantifiers and normalized-network convention.

children.title: Max-Restricted Path Consistency
children.top_down_role: The maximal restricted member of the path-consistency family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value deletion under the Max-RPC support condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain arc consistency and repeatedly delete \(a\in D_i\) whenever some neighbor \(X_j\) has no support \(b\in D_j\) for which \((a,b)\) extends through every third variable. Propagating these deletions reaches either an empty domain or a solution-preserving Max-RPC fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete values lacking a path-consistent support on a neighboring constraint until Max-RPC holds.
assumptions_latex: The binary network and domains are finite.
Arc consistency is maintained throughout.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}(N')=\operatorname{Sol}(N),\quad N'\text{ is Max-RPC or has an empty domain}.\)

notation.meaning: Network at the deletion fixed point.

knowledge_statements.title: Max-RPC Fixed-Point Enforcement
Max-Restricted Path Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc consistency requiring a path-consistent support on every constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary constraint network is max-restricted path consistent if it is arc consistent and, for every ordered pair of constrained variables \(X_i,X_j\) and every \(a\in D_i\), there exists a support \(b\in D_j\) with \((a,b)\in R_{ij}\) such that, for every third variable \(X_k\), some \(c\in D_k\) satisfies \((a,c)\in R_{ik}\) and \((b,c)\in R_{jk}\). The same chosen support \(b\) must be extendable through every third variable, although the witness \(c\) may depend on \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every value must have, on each neighboring constraint, at least one support that extends consistently through every third variable.
assumptions_latex: The network is finite, binary, and normalized.
Arc consistency is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each value has a path-consistent support on every incident binary constraint.

notation.meaning: extension witness, possibly depending on the third variable

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and path-consistent-support formulation fit Max-Restricted Path Consistency, but the exact support quantifiers require a cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Restricted-Variant Strength Relations
children.top_down_role: Relative pruning strength across restricted path-consistency variants.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational consequence of the strength hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_C(N)\) be the componentwise domains remaining after a standard monotone enforcement of consistency \(C\) reaches its greatest deletion fixed point on the same finite normalized binary network. Then \(D_{SPC}(N)\subseteq D_{MaxRPC}(N)\subseteq D_{RPC}(N)\subseteq D_{AC}(N)\). Equalities may occur on a particular instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stronger member of the hierarchy cannot retain a domain value deleted by a weaker member, although an instance may show equal pruning.
assumptions_latex: All procedures start from the same network.
Each standard monotone propagator is iterated to its greatest deletion fixed point.

notation.meaning: Remaining domains after enforcing consistency C.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Pruning Order Across Restricted Variants
Restricted-Variant Strength Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative pruning strength for standard binary-network definitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite normalized binary networks, strong path consistency implies max-restricted path consistency; max-restricted path consistency implies restricted path consistency; and restricted path consistency implies arc consistency. In symbols, \(\mathrm{SPC}\Rightarrow\mathrm{MaxRPC}\Rightarrow\mathrm{RPC}\Rightarrow\mathrm{AC}\). Here strong path consistency means the conjunction of arc consistency and path consistency. None of the reverse implications holds in general, so the inclusions between the corresponding classes of consistent networks are strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard strict hierarchy is strong path consistency, Max-RPC, RPC, then arc consistency, from strongest to weakest.
assumptions_latex: All notions use the same finite normalized binary network semantics.
Strong path consistency means arc consistency together with path consistency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{SPC}\Rightarrow\mathrm{MaxRPC}\Rightarrow\mathrm{RPC}\Rightarrow\mathrm{AC}\), with strict reverse separations in general.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the strength-relations leaf, and the stated hierarchy is plausible, but both the implications and strict reverse separations require authoritative support.

children.title: Restricted-Variant Separation Cases
children.top_down_role: Constraint-network regimes that distinguish the restricted variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Variant Separation Cases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit binary networks separating AC, RPC, and Max-RPC.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(D_X=D_Y=D_Z=\{0,1\}\), take \(R_{XY}=R_{XZ}=\{(0,0),(1,1)\}\) and \(R_{YZ}=\{(0,1),(1,0)\}\). This network is arc consistent but not RPC, since the unique pair \((X=0,Y=0)\) cannot extend to \(Z\). For RPC without Max-RPC, add \(W\) with the same binary domains, let \(R_{XY}\) and \(R_{ZW}\) be universal, \(R_{XZ}=R_{XW}\) be equality, \(R_{YZ}=\{(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)\}\), and \(R_{YW}=\{(0,0),(0,1),(1,1)\}\). The network is RPC, but neither support of \(X=0\) on \(Y\) extends through both \(Z\) and \(W\), so it is not Max-RPC.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One explicit triangle separates AC from RPC; a four-variable binary network separates RPC from Max-RPC.
assumptions_latex: Unlisted binary constraints are universal.
Each displayed relation is interpreted symmetrically under reversal of its variables.

notation.meaning: allowed pairs for variables U and V in the displayed order

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits the separation-cases leaf, but the bespoke networks and their claimed RPC and Max-RPC classifications need an inspectable source or independently registered verification evidence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating ordinary k-consistency from strong k-consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Ordinary \(k\)-consistency asserts only extension from locally consistent assignments on \(k-1\) variables to a chosen kth variable; it does not include every lower consistency level. For example, with three singleton-domain variables and an empty binary relation on every pair, 3-consistency holds vacuously because no pair assignment is locally consistent, while 2-consistency fails because a singleton assignment cannot extend to another variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary k-consistency is not shorthand for consistency at all lower orders; the conjunction is strong k-consistency.
assumptions_latex: Partial assignments are tested only against constraints whose scopes they contain.
knowledge_statements.title: k-Consistency Is a Single-Level Property

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-network interpretation of orders one, two, and n.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the classical extension definition, 1-consistency means that for each variable the empty assignment extends to at least one value satisfying its unary constraints. After unary-inconsistent values have been removed, 2-consistency is equivalent to arc consistency for binary networks. If \(n=|V|\), n-consistency means that every locally consistent assignment to any \(n-1\) variables extends to the remaining variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order one gives unary feasibility, order two gives binary arc consistency after unary normalization, and order n gives final-variable extendability.
assumptions_latex: The immutable seed's partial-assignment convention is used.
The arc-consistency equivalence is restricted to unary-normalized binary networks.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Cases of k-Consistency
k-Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical extension definition for finite constraint networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a constraint network on variables \(V\), and let \(1\le k\le |V|\). The network is \(k\)-consistent if, for every set \(U\subseteq V\) of \(k-1\) distinct variables, every assignment to \(U\) satisfying all constraints whose scopes lie within \(U\), and every variable \(x\in V\setminus U\), there exists a value \(a\in D(x)\) such that the extended assignment on \(U\cup\{x\}\) satisfies every constraint whose scope lies within that enlarged set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every consistent assignment to any k−1 variables can be extended consistently to any chosen kth variable.
assumptions_latex: The constraint network and all domains are finite.
Consistency of a partial assignment is evaluated on constraints fully contained in its variable set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every consistent assignment on \(k-1\) variables extends to any additional variable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and extension formulation fit classical k-consistency, but no constraint-network source with a specific section, definition, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Strong Consistency Does Not Ensure Satisfiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of strong consistency below the full variable count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_{2m+1}\) have domain \(\{0,1\}\), with constraints \(X_i\ne X_{i+1}\) around an odd cycle. The network is strongly \(2\)-consistent but has no solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Boolean odd cycle is strongly 2-consistent yet unsatisfiable.
assumptions_latex: Indices are modulo \(2m+1\).

notation.meaning: Variable at vertex i of the odd cycle.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Strong Consistency Does Not Ensure Satisfiability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full Strong Consistency Gives Global Extension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global-extension consequence at the number of variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a finite network on \(n\) variables is strongly \(n\)-consistent, every locally consistent assignment to fewer than \(n\) variables can be extended, in any variable ordering, to a complete solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong n-consistency makes every variable ordering backtrack-free.
assumptions_latex: The network has \(n<\infty\) variables.
The network is strongly \(n\)-consistent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall\theta,\ |\operatorname{vars}(\theta)|<n\land\theta\text{ locally consistent}\Rightarrow\theta\text{ extends to a solution}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Full Strong Consistency Gives Global Extension
Strong k-Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain CSP definition using extension of locally consistent partial assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite constraint network have variables \(X\), domains \((D_x)_{x\in X}\), and constraints \(C\). A partial assignment is locally consistent when it satisfies every constraint whose scope lies within its assigned variables. For an integer \(k\ge 1\), the network is strongly \(k\)-consistent if, for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), every locally consistent assignment to any \(j-1\) distinct variables can be extended to any additional variable \(y\) by some value \(a\in D_y\), with the resulting assignment remaining locally consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network is strongly k-consistent when it is j-consistent at every level from one through k.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and every domain \(D_x\) are finite.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the Strong k-Consistency leaf, but no inspectable authoritative source is cited.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary equality network separating directional from ordinary 2-consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D(x)=\{0\}\), \(D(y)=\{0,1\}\), and impose \(x=y\). Under the convention requiring extension from earlier to later variables, the order \(x\prec y\) is directionally 2-consistent. Ordinary 2-consistency fails because \(y=1\) has no support in \(D(x)\), and directional 2-consistency fails for the reversed order \(y\prec x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional consistency can depend on the ordering and can be strictly weaker than ordinary consistency.
assumptions_latex: Directional extension is required from earlier variables to later variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Order Dependence of Directional 2-Consistency

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional consistency retains only order-compatible extension obligations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any fixed total ordering \(\prec\), ordinary \(k\)-consistency implies directional \(k\)-consistency relative to \(\prec\), provided both notions use the same partial-assignment convention. The converse need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unrestricted extension consistency implies its order-restricted form, which can be strictly weaker.
assumptions_latex: The same local-consistency convention is used in both notions.
\(\prec\) is a fixed total variable ordering.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary k-Consistency Implies Directional k-Consistency
Directional k-Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering-relative version of finite-domain \(k\)-consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a total ordering \(\prec\) of the variables of a finite constraint network. For \(k\ge 2\), the network is directionally \(k\)-consistent relative to \(\prec\) if, whenever distinct variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1},y\) satisfy \(x_i\prec y\) for every \(i\), every locally consistent assignment to \(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1}\) has an extension assigning some \(a\in D_y\) to \(y\) that remains locally consistent. Only extensions from earlier variables to a later variable are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional k-consistency requires k-consistent extensions only when the new variable follows every already assigned variable in a fixed ordering.
assumptions_latex: \(\prec\) is a total ordering of the finite variable set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1}\prec y,\quad s\text{ locally consistent}\Longrightarrow\exists a\in D_y:\ s\cup\{y\mapsto a\}\text{ locally consistent}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ordering-relative definition is plausible and fits the leaf, but directional k-consistency conventions vary and require a specific authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tuple-deletion closure under the seed’s pairwise convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Repeatedly replace \(R_i\) by \(R_i\ltimes R_j\) for ordered pairs \(i\ne j\) until stable. For finite extensional relations, the process terminates, preserves the full natural join, and reaches relational arc consistency. An empty relation proves inconsistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated semijoins delete unsupported tuples while preserving all global solutions.
assumptions_latex: All relations are finite and extensional.
The seed's all-ordered-pairs convention is used.
knowledge_statements.title: Relational Arc-Consistency Semijoin Closure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cyclic Pairwise Support Is Not Global Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of RAC on a cyclic scope hypergraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Boolean \(X,Y,Z\), let \(R_{XY}\) and \(R_{YZ}\) be equality and \(R_{ZX}\) be disequality. Every tuple has compatible tuples in each other relation, but the full natural join is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two equality relations and one disequality relation form a relationally arc-consistent unsatisfiable cycle.
assumptions_latex: All variables are Boolean.
Relations use their displayed ordered scopes.
knowledge_statements.title: Cyclic Pairwise Support Is Not Global Consistency

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent tuple-support form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(R_i\ltimes R_j=\{t\in R_i:\exists u\in R_j,\ t|_{S_i\cap S_j}=u|_{S_i\cap S_j}\}\). Then \((R_i,R_j)\) is relationally arc consistent exactly when \(R_i\ltimes R_j=R_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: RAC means that semijoining with the other relation deletes no tuple.
assumptions_latex: Coordinates bearing the same variable are identified.
knowledge_statements.title: Semijoin Characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global completion on acyclic scopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the constraint scopes admit a join tree with the running-intersection property, every adjacent pair of relations is semijoin-consistent in both directions, and no relation is empty, then every remaining tuple extends to the full natural join. Hence the network is satisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bidirectional relational arc consistency is globally complete on a join tree.
assumptions_latex: The scope hypergraph has a join tree.
Adjacent relations are semijoin-consistent in both directions.
Every relation is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.title: Join-Tree Sufficiency
Relational Arc Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Join–projection definition for arbitrary-arity extensional constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let constraints \(c_i\) and \(c_j\) have scopes \(S_i,S_j\) and current relations \(R_i\subseteq\prod_{x\in S_i}D_x\) and \(R_j\subseteq\prod_{x\in S_j}D_x\). The ordered pair \((c_i,c_j)\) is relationally arc consistent if every tuple of \(R_i\) has a compatible tuple in \(R_j\), equivalently \(\pi_{S_i}(R_i\Join R_j)=R_i\). A network is relationally arc consistent when this condition holds for every ordered pair of distinct constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every allowed tuple of each constraint must be compatible on shared variables with some allowed tuple of every other constraint.
assumptions_latex: All constraint relations are finite.
Natural join identifies coordinates belonging to the same variable.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: join-projection formulation of pairwise relational support

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The join–projection formulation is internally coherent, but it is not established that this exact all-ordered-pairs convention is the standard meaning of relational arc consistency.

children.title: Relational Path Consistency
children.top_down_role: Path-level consistency formulated over relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Relational Path Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tuple-support formulation over a path of three arbitrary-arity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c_0,c_1,c_2\) have relations \(R_0,R_1,R_2\) on scopes \(S_0,S_1,S_2\). The ordered triple is relationally path consistent if every tuple \(t_0\in R_0\) has tuples \(t_1\in R_1\) and \(t_2\in R_2\) that agree pairwise on all shared variables. Equivalently, \(\pi_{S_0}(R_0\Join R_1\Join R_2)=R_0\). A network is relationally path consistent if this equality holds for every ordered triple of distinct constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every tuple of one constraint must have simultaneous compatible support in each pair of constraints completing a three-constraint path.
assumptions_latex: Constraint relations are finite.
Compatibility means equality on every shared variable.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: natural higher-order extension of relational arc support

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact meaning of relational path consistency is convention-dependent. No source supports identifying it with simultaneous support over every ordered triple of distinct constraints.

children.title: Relational k-Consistency
children.top_down_role: Parameterized higher-order consistency formulated over relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Relational k-Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous tuple-support hierarchy indexed by the number of constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k\ge 2\), select distinct constraints \(c_0,c_1,\ldots,c_{k-1}\), with respective scopes \(S_i\) and relations \(R_i\). This ordered selection is relationally \(k\)-consistent if each tuple of \(R_0\) extends to a tuple of the natural join \(R_0\Join\cdots\Join R_{k-1}\). Thus \(\pi_{S_0}(\Join_{i=0}^{k-1}R_i)=R_0\). The network is relationally \(k\)-consistent when the equality holds for every such ordered selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each tuple of a designated constraint must have simultaneous compatible support across any k−1 other selected constraints.
assumptions_latex: All relations are finite and use common variable identities.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed join hierarchy is coherent, but an authoritative source is required to verify that relational k-consistency counts selected constraints and uses this designated-relation support condition.

children.title: Arity-Parameterized Strength
children.top_down_role: Variation in relational-consistency strength across arity parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Arity-Parameterized Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity of simultaneous relational support with respect to the number of constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the simultaneous-support definition of relational consistency, let a finite network contain at least \(k+1\) constraints and be relationally \((k+1)\)-consistent. For any ordered selection of \(k\) distinct constraints, append any further distinct constraint. Support in the resulting \((k+1)\)-fold join projects to support in the original \(k\)-fold join. Consequently, relational \((k+1)\)-consistency implies relational \(k\)-consistency. The converse need not hold because supports available separately for smaller selections may be mutually incompatible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing the number of relations requiring simultaneous support strengthens consistency; level k+1 implies level k, generally not conversely.
assumptions_latex: The network has at least \(k+1\) constraints.
Relational levels use simultaneous natural-join support.

notation.meaning: Relational k-consistency under the local convention.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: monotonicity follows from the stated join-support hierarchy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Monotonicity follows under the candidate's local hierarchy, but that hierarchy is unverified and the claimed failure of the converse requires sourced support or a cited counterexample.

children.title: Path–k Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Regimes connecting relational path consistency to members of the relational k-family.

knowledge_statements.title: Path–k Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Index correspondence within the simultaneous relational-support hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the convention that relational \(k\)-consistency requires support across an ordered selection of \(k\) constraints, relational arc consistency is level \(2\), and relational path consistency is level \(3\). Hence relational path consistency is exactly relational \(3\)-consistency in this hierarchy. This indexing correspondence does not by itself identify relational path consistency with variable-based path consistency for arbitrary nonbinary networks; such an identification requires additional assumptions on scopes and network representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the chosen relational hierarchy, arc consistency is level two and path consistency is level three; equivalence with variable-based notions needs extra assumptions.
assumptions_latex: All relational notions use the same simultaneous-support convention.
The hierarchy parameter counts selected constraints.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: indexing correspondence induced by the local definitions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The correspondence is true by the candidate's chosen indexing, but no evidence establishes that RAC, RPC, and relational k-consistency conventionally use these exact levels.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Baseline singleton-test enforcement without incremental reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Enforce AC, then for each current value \(a\in D_x\), copy the current store, restrict \(x\) to \(a\), and enforce AC. If the temporary closure wipes out a domain, delete \(a\) from the main store and reschedule affected singleton tests. Stop when a complete pass deletes nothing or the main store wipes out.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Temporarily assign each value, run AC, permanently delete failed values, and repeat until stable.
assumptions_latex: Domains are finite.
AC closure is sound and complete for the selected arc-consistency convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure terminates at an SAC store or detects an empty domain.}
knowledge_statements.title: SAC-1 Fixed-Point Enforcement

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coarse bound in terms of AC closure cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\sum_x|D_x^0|\), and let \(T_{AC}\) bound one AC closure on any encountered substore. A complete singleton pass performs at most \(M\) AC tests. Since every changing pass deletes at least one of the initially present values, a restart-after-deletion implementation uses \(O(M^2T_{AC})\) time. Sequential reuse of temporary stores requires \(O(M+S_{AC})\) domain workspace, excluding immutable constraint storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple restarting SAC implementation needs at most quadratically many singleton AC tests; incremental variants can reuse work.
assumptions_latex: Every changing pass deletes at least one value.
Temporary stores are reused sequentially.
Immutable constraint storage is excluded from the workspace bound.

notation.meaning: Total number of values in the initial domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Baseline Restarting SAC Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonempty SAC Does Not Certify Satisfiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singleton arc consistency remains incomplete for global feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the disequality network for 3-coloring \(K_4\), with every vertex domain equal to \(\{1,2,3\}\). The network is unsatisfiable. After fixing any vertex to any color, AC removes that color from the other three domains but leaves the remaining triangle with two nonempty colors at every vertex and no unsupported value. Thus every singleton test avoids wipeout, so the network is SAC despite having no solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The three-coloring model of K4 is singleton arc consistent but unsatisfiable, so nonempty SAC is not a global feasibility certificate.
assumptions_latex: Each edge of \(K_4\) imposes binary disequality.
Every vertex initially has domain \(\{1,2,3\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonempty SAC Does Not Certify Satisfiability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singleton Arc Consistency Strictly Strengthens Arc Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic hierarchy relation with a strict separating instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every singleton arc-consistent finite network is arc consistent. The converse fails: the Boolean disequality triangle is arc consistent, but assigning either value to any vertex and enforcing AC produces a domain wipeout. Hence the triangle is not SAC.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SAC implies AC, and the Boolean disequality triangle shows that the implication is strict.
assumptions_latex: Both conditions use the same constraint representation and arc-consistency convention.
All domains are finite.
knowledge_statements.title: Singleton Arc Consistency Strictly Strengthens Arc Consistency
Singleton Arc Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain singleton testing followed by arc-consistency closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite-domain constraint network. For a variable \(x\) and value \(a\in D_x\), write \(P[x=a]\) for the network obtained by restricting \(D_x\) to \(\{a\}\). The network \(P\) is singleton arc consistent if, for every pair \((x,a)\), enforcing arc consistency to a fixed point on \(P[x=a]\) leaves every variable domain nonempty. A value failing this test is singleton-inconsistent and may be deleted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every value must survive the test that assigns it alone and then enforces arc consistency without causing any domain wipeout.
assumptions_latex: The network and all domains are finite.
Arc-consistency propagation is run to a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall x\in X\ \forall a\in D_x,\quad \operatorname{AC}(P[x=a])\text{ has no empty domain}.\)

notation.meaning: Network with x restricted to the singleton value a.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is the standard form of singleton arc consistency and the definition kind fits the leaf, but no inspectable authoritative citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic deletion-to-fixed-point procedure under the induced-neighborhood convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Repeatedly select \((x,a)\) and decide feasibility of the subproblem induced by \(\{x\}\cup N(x)\) under \(x=a\). Delete \(a\) if that subproblem is infeasible and retest values affected by the deletion. On finite domains, the process terminates at an NIC store or an empty domain; each deletion preserves every global solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve each value's induced neighborhood subproblem, delete values having no extension, and repeat affected tests until stable.
assumptions_latex: Domains are finite.
Each neighborhood feasibility test is complete.
The neighborhood and induced-subproblem conventions are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure terminates at an NIC fixed point or an empty domain.}
knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood-Inverse-Consistency Enforcement

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle Bound for Baseline NIC Enforcement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coarse bound in terms of complete induced-neighborhood feasibility tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\sum_x|D_x^0|\), and let \(T_N\) bound one complete induced-neighborhood feasibility test on an encountered store. A restart-after-deletion implementation performs at most \(M\) tests per pass and at most \(M\) changing passes, hence takes \(O(M^2T_N)\) time. The neighborhood test may itself be computationally hard; no representation-independent polynomial bound follows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Baseline NIC enforcement uses at most quadratically many neighborhood-feasibility calls, whose individual cost may dominate the computation.
assumptions_latex: Every changing pass deletes at least one initially present value.
At most one complete test is charged to each current value per pass.

notation.meaning: Total number of values in the initial domains.
Upper bound for one complete neighborhood-feasibility test.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Bound for Baseline NIC Enforcement

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arc Consistency Does Not Imply Neighborhood Inverse Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict binary separation using a Boolean disequality triangle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x,y,z\) have domains \(\{0,1\}\) and impose pairwise disequality on the triangle. The network is arc consistent. Under \(x=0\), however, both neighbors must equal \(1\), violating \(y\ne z\); therefore \(x=0\) has no induced-neighborhood extension and the network is not NIC.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Boolean disequality triangle is arc consistent but fails NIC because a fixed vertex value cannot extend jointly over its two connected neighbors.
assumptions_latex: The neighborhood subproblem includes the constraint between the two neighbors.
knowledge_statements.title: Arc Consistency Does Not Imply Neighborhood Inverse Consistency

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Neighborhood Inverse Consistency Implies Generalized Arc Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic hierarchy relation under the induced-neighborhood definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every value \(a\in D_x\) extends to a solution of the subproblem induced by \(\{x\}\cup N(x)\), then that extension supplies a supporting tuple for every constraint containing \(x\). Hence NIC implies generalized arc consistency; for binary networks it implies ordinary arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A joint neighborhood extension supplies support on every incident constraint, so NIC is at least as strong as arc consistency.
assumptions_latex: The induced neighborhood subproblem includes every constraint whose scope is contained in \(\{x\}\cup N(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood Inverse Consistency Implies Generalized Arc Consistency
Neighborhood Inverse Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value extendability over the subproblem induced by a variable and its neighbors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite constraint network, let \(N(x)\) be the set of variables sharing a constraint with \(x\), excluding \(x\). The network is neighborhood inverse consistent if, for every variable \(x\) and every value \(a\in D_x\), there exists an assignment to all variables in \(N(x)\) such that the combined assignment with \(x=a\) satisfies every constraint whose scope is contained in \(\{x\}\cup N(x)\). Thus each value extends to a solution of its induced neighborhood subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every value of every variable must extend to a satisfying assignment of all variables in that variable’s constraint neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: The constraint network and its domains are finite.
Neighbors are defined by shared constraint membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall x\in X\ \forall a\in D_x,\quad \exists s:N(x)\to\bigcup_{y\in N(x)}D_y\text{ satisfying the induced neighborhood subproblem with }x=a.\)

notation.meaning: Variables sharing at least one constraint with x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is plausible, but the neighborhood and induced-subproblem conventions for nonbinary constraints require an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: POAC Enforcement by Supporting Singleton Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct finite-domain enforcement following the defining quantifiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: First enforce SAC. For each surviving \((x,a)\) and every \(y\ne x\), test values \(b\in D_y\) by enforcing AC on \(P[x=a,y=b]\) until a non-wipeout support is found. Delete \(a\) if some \(y\) has no such \(b\), reestablish SAC, and repeat affected tests. On finite domains the process terminates at a POAC store or an empty domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After SAC, find an AC-surviving supporting singleton in every other variable for each value; delete unsupported values and repeat.
assumptions_latex: Domains are finite.
AC and SAC subprocedures are run soundly to their required fixed points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The terminal nonfailure store is partition-one arc consistent.}
knowledge_statements.title: POAC Enforcement by Supporting Singleton Tests

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle Bound for Baseline POAC Enforcement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coarse restart bound in terms of AC and SAC subprocedures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\sum_x|D_x^0|\), let \(T_{AC}\) bound one AC closure, and let \(T_{SAC}\) bound one SAC enforcement. In one complete POAC pass, at most \(M^2\) pairwise singleton AC tests are required. A restart-after-deletion implementation has at most \(M\) changing passes, giving \(O(M^3T_{AC}+MT_{SAC})\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A baseline restarting POAC implementation uses at most cubically many pairwise singleton AC tests in the initial number of values, plus repeated SAC enforcement.
assumptions_latex: Every changing pass deletes at least one initially present value.
Tests stop after the first support for each second variable.

notation.meaning: Total number of values in the initial domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Bound for Baseline POAC Enforcement

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier distinction between POAC and a joint extension condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \((x,a)\), POAC requires \(\forall y\ne x\,\exists b_y\in D_y\) such that the corresponding singleton test succeeds. The values \(b_y\) arise from separate tests; the POAC definition does not require the collection \((b_y)_{y\ne x}\) to form one simultaneous satisfying assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: POAC may use a different successful singleton support for each other variable and does not require those supports to be jointly compatible.
assumptions_latex: POAC is interpreted by the seed's per-variable supporting-singleton formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{POAC's witnesses are separately existential, not one required joint extension.}
knowledge_statements.title: Separate Supporting-Singleton Quantifiers
Partition-One Arc Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: POAC defined by singleton support under every second-variable partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-domain network \(P\) is partition-one arc consistent if it is singleton arc consistent and, for every variable-value pair \((x,a)\) and every other variable \(y\ne x\), there exists \(b\in D_y\) such that enforcing arc consistency on \(P[x=a,y=b]\) causes no domain wipeout. Equivalently, each singleton \(x=a\) has at least one arc-consistent supporting singleton in every other variable’s domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Besides singleton arc consistency, each value must have some supporting value in every other variable after both are assigned and arc consistency is enforced.
assumptions_latex: The network and all domains are finite.
Arc consistency is enforced to a fixed point after assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SAC}(P)\ \land\ \forall x,a\ \forall y\ne x\ \exists b\in D_y:\operatorname{AC}(P[x=a,y=b])\text{ has no empty domain}.\)

notation.meaning: Network with x and y restricted to the displayed singleton values.

children.title: Continuous-Domain Consistency Classes
children.top_down_role: Consistency notions for real and interval domains; numerical solution methods remain in their owning chapter.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: 6.6 Arithmetic Constraints on Reals; 6.7 Arithmetic Equations over Reals

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Emptiness under the exact feasible-projection convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the exact operator \(H_c\), \(R_c\cap B=\varnothing\) if and only if any coordinate projection is empty, equivalently if and only if the reduced product box \(H_c(B)\) is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An empty reduced coordinate exactly certifies that the constraint has no satisfying point in the current box.
assumptions_latex: \(H_c\) is the exact projection-hull operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Hull-Inconsistency Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural properties under the immutable seed's exact feasible-projection convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For relation \(R_c\) and box \(B=\prod_i I_i\), define \(H_c(B)=\prod_i\operatorname{hull}(\pi_i(R_c\cap B))\). Then \(H_c(B)\subseteq B\), \(R_c\cap H_c(B)=R_c\cap B\), \(H_c(H_c(B))=H_c(B)\), and \(B\subseteq B'\Rightarrow H_c(B)\subseteq H_c(B')\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact projection-hull reduction is contracting, solution-preserving, idempotent for one constraint, and monotone.
assumptions_latex: Interval hulls exist, with an empty projection mapped to the empty interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H_c\text{ is contracting, solution-preserving, idempotent, and monotone}.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Hull-Reduction Operator
Hull Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact interval-hull consistency for real constraints over a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a real constraint \(c\) have scope \(S\), relation \(R_c\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{S}\), and current interval box \(B=\prod_{x\in S}I_x\). The box is hull consistent for \(c\) if, for every \(x\in S\), its interval equals the interval hull of the feasible projection: \(I_x=\operatorname{hull}(\pi_x(R_c\cap B))\). A continuous-domain network is hull consistent when this condition holds for every constraint using the current domains. An empty feasible projection yields the empty interval and detects inconsistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each variable interval must equal the smallest interval containing that constraint’s feasible values within the current box.
assumptions_latex: Variables range over closed real intervals.
Interval hull means the least closed interval containing a set.

notation.meaning: Exact real relation defined by constraint c.
Current interval box over the constraint scope.
Least closed interval containing the argument set.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact projection-hull formulation of hull consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact projection-hull definition is coherent and fits the leaf, but hull- and bounds-consistency terminology varies across interval-constraint literature and needs a specific source.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Box-consistency tests are relative to interval evaluation rather than solely to the exact zero set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If sound interval extensions \(F\) and \(G\) of the same real function give different enclosures on tested coordinate slices, a box may pass a box-consistency test relative to one extension and fail it relative to the other. Algebraically equivalent expressions therefore need not induce identical box pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval overestimation and expression choice can change box-consistency pruning.
assumptions_latex: Both interval extensions are sound but need not return identical enclosures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\neq G\text{ on tested slices may yield }\mathrm{BC}_F(B)\neq\mathrm{BC}_G(B).

notation.meaning: box-consistency predicate relative to interval extension F

knowledge_statements.title: Dependence on the Interval Extension
Box Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval-evaluation box consistency for a real equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=0\) be a real equation, let \(B=I_1\times\cdots\times I_n\), and let \(F\) be an inclusion-isotonic interval extension of \(f\). For each coordinate \(i\), define \(Q_i=\{t\in I_i:0\in F(I_1,\ldots,I_{i-1},[t,t],I_{i+1},\ldots,I_n)\}\). The box \(B\) is box consistent for the equation relative to \(F\) if \(I_i=\operatorname{hull}(Q_i)\) for every \(i\). For several equations, the condition is imposed equationwise at a common fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each coordinate interval is the hull of singleton coordinate values whose interval evaluation can still contain zero.
assumptions_latex: Each \(I_i\) is a closed real interval.
\(F\) is an inclusion-isotonic interval extension of \(f\).

notation.meaning: Chosen interval extension of the equation function.
Coordinate values not excluded by interval evaluation.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: idealized fixed-point formulation of interval box consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singleton-evaluation hull condition is not reliably identifiable with standard box consistency, which is often formulated using canonical intervals or endpoint tests. A source is needed to determine the correct variant.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine-interval endpoint convention, kept separate from the deferred singleton-slice formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a floating-point interval system. Let \(F\) be an inclusion interval extension of \(f\), let \(B=I_1\times\cdots\times I_n\), and let \(L_i\) and \(R_i\) be the leftmost and rightmost canonical subintervals of \(I_i\). Under the canonical-interval convention, coordinate \(i\) is box consistent for \(f=0\) when \(0\in F(B[i\leftarrow L_i])\) and \(0\in F(B[i\leftarrow R_i])\); the box is box consistent when this holds for every coordinate and equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the canonical machine-interval convention, neither extreme coordinate cell can be excluded by interval evaluation.
assumptions_latex: A floating-point interval system and its canonical intervals are fixed.
\(F\) is an inclusion interval extension.

notation.meaning: extreme canonical subintervals of coordinate interval i

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical-Interval Endpoint Box Consistency

intermediate_metadata.reason: This leaf owns box-consistency tests relative to interval extensions and their representation dependence. Exact projection-hull consistency and numerical solution algorithms are excluded. The topic remains deferred because the singleton and canonical-endpoint conventions are materially different and unresolved.

children.title: Strict Dominance
children.top_down_role: Consistency-strength comparisons with a strict pruning advantage.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Order Structure of Strict Propagation Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic properties for comparisons made on one fixed representation class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a representation class \(\mathcal R\), componentwise store order, and closure convention. If \(C_1\succ C_2\) means \(F_{C_1}(p)\subseteq F_{C_2}(p)\) for every \(p\in\mathcal R\), with strict inclusion for some \(p\), then \(\succ\) is irreflexive and transitive, and hence asymmetric. After identifying notions whose closures agree on every \(p\in\mathcal R\), it induces a strict partial order on the resulting equivalence classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict propagation dominance is irreflexive, transitive, and asymmetric when every comparison uses the same representation class and closure convention.
assumptions_latex: All comparisons use the same \(\mathcal R\), store order, and closure convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \succ\text{ is a strict partial order, including on the quotient by closure equivalence}.

notation.meaning: C1 strictly dominates C2 on the fixed representation class.

knowledge_statements.title: Order Structure of Strict Propagation Dominance
Strict Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines strict propagation strength for two consistency notions on a fixed representation class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\) be a class of represented constraint instances, and let \(F_C(I,D)\) denote the domain store obtained by enforcing consistency notion \(C\) on instance \(I\) from store \(D\). Consistency notion \(C_1\) strictly dominates \(C_2\) on \(\mathcal R\) when \[\forall (I,D)\in\mathcal R,\quad F_{C_1}(I,D)\subseteq F_{C_2}(I,D),\] componentwise, and there exists \((I^\star,D^\star)\in\mathcal R\) such that \[F_{C_1}(I^\star,D^\star)\subsetneq F_{C_2}(I^\star,D^\star).\] Both enforcement operators are required to preserve every solution admitted by the initial store.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One consistency notion strictly dominates another if it always removes at least as many values and removes strictly more on some represented instance.
assumptions_latex: \(F_{C_1}\) and \(F_{C_2}\) are solution-preserving enforcement operators.
Stores are ordered by componentwise domain inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_1\) is strictly stronger than \(C_2\) on \(\mathcal R\).

notation.meaning: Store after enforcing consistency notion C on instance I from store D.
Fixed class of represented constraint instances and initial stores.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard closure-order definition of propagation strength
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the terminal container, but no inspectable constraint-programming source is cited.

children.title: Strength Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Consistency notions yielding equal strength in specified regimes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strength Equivalence Is an Equivalence Relation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic structure of closure equality on a fixed representation class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a fixed representation class \(\mathcal R\), equality of complete enforcement closures is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Moreover, \(C_1\equiv_{\mathcal R}C_2\) exactly when \(C_1\) dominates \(C_2\) and \(C_2\) dominates \(C_1\) on \(\mathcal R\). Strength equivalence therefore partitions consistency notions into equal-pruning classes without equating their implementations or running times.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure equality is an equivalence relation and equals mutual pruning dominance on a fixed representation class.
assumptions_latex: Every notion is compared through its complete solution-preserving closure.
The representation class \(\mathcal R\) and componentwise domain order are fixed.

notation.meaning: strength equivalence on representation class R
pruning-dominance preorder on representation class R

knowledge_statements.title: Strength Equivalence Is an Equivalence Relation
Strength Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines equivalence by equality of pruning closures over a fixed representation class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For consistency notions \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) with solution-preserving enforcement operators \(F_{C_1}\) and \(F_{C_2}\), strength equivalence on a representation class \(\mathcal R\) means \[\forall (I,D)\in\mathcal R,\quad F_{C_1}(I,D)=F_{C_2}(I,D).\] Equality is componentwise equality of the surviving variable domains. Thus equivalence concerns pruning power after complete enforcement, not equality of propagator implementations, execution schedules, or computational cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two consistency notions are strength-equivalent when complete enforcement leaves exactly the same domains on every instance in the chosen representation class.
assumptions_latex: \(F_{C_1}\) and \(F_{C_2}\) are applied to closure.
The same representation class \(\mathcal R\) is used for both notions.

notation.meaning: Strength equivalence on representation class R.
Closure produced by enforcing consistency notion C.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equality of propagation closures defines equal pruning strength
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closure-equality definition is precise and fits Strength Equivalence, but it lacks a source with a specific locator.

children.title: Strength Incomparability
children.top_down_role: Consistency notions lacking a uniform dominance ordering.

knowledge_statements.title: Strength Incomparability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines incomparability as failure of both uniform pruning-dominance directions on one representation class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\) be a class of represented constraint instances with initial stores, and let \(F_{C_1}\) and \(F_{C_2}\) be solution-preserving closure operators whose output stores are ordered by componentwise domain inclusion. The notions \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are strength-incomparable on \(\mathcal R\) when neither uniformly dominates the other; equivalently, there exist \((I_a,D_a),(I_b,D_b)\in\mathcal R\) such that \[F_{C_1}(I_a,D_a)\nsubseteq F_{C_2}(I_a,D_a)\] and \[F_{C_2}(I_b,D_b)\nsubseteq F_{C_1}(I_b,D_b).\] The witnesses may coincide, and their output stores need not be comparable by inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two consistency notions are strength-incomparable when each proposed uniform pruning-dominance direction fails on some instance in the same representation class; the witness stores need not be strictly nested.
assumptions_latex: \(F_{C_1}\) and \(F_{C_2}\) are solution-preserving closure operators on \(\mathcal R\).
Stores are ordered by componentwise domain inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither \(C_1\) nor \(C_2\) uniformly dominates the other on \(\mathcal R\).

notation.meaning: Store obtained after enforcing consistency notion C to closure on instance I from store D.
Fixed representation class of instance-store pairs.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: incomparability is failure of both directions in the componentwise closure order

children.title: Conditional Dominance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Representation or constraint classes under which dominance emerges.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Restriction and Intersection Laws for Conditional Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural laws for transferring dominance statements between explicitly defined regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C_1\) dominates \(C_2\) on \(\mathcal R_P\), it also dominates \(C_2\) on every subclass \(\mathcal R_Q\subseteq\mathcal R_P\). If \(C_1\) dominates \(C_2\) on \(\mathcal R_P\) and \(C_2\) dominates \(C_3\) on \(\mathcal R_Q\), then \(C_1\) dominates \(C_3\) on \(\mathcal R_P\cap\mathcal R_Q\). Strictness survives a restriction or intersection only if a strict witness remains in the resulting regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional dominance is inherited by subclasses and composes on regime intersections; strictness requires a surviving strict witness.
assumptions_latex: All closures are compared under the same componentwise domain-inclusion order.
The regimes use compatible instance representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_1\succeq_{\mathcal R_P}C_2\land C_2\succeq_{\mathcal R_Q}C_3\Rightarrow C_1\succeq_{\mathcal R_P\cap\mathcal R_Q}C_3\).

notation.meaning: C1 has at least the pruning strength of C2 throughout regime R

knowledge_statements.title: Restriction and Intersection Laws for Conditional Dominance
Conditional Dominance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restricts a strength comparison to instances satisfying an explicit structural predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a predicate on represented instances and define \(\mathcal R_P=\{(I,D)\in\mathcal R:P(I,D)\}\). Consistency notion \(C_1\) conditionally dominates \(C_2\) under regime \(P\) precisely when \[\forall (I,D)\in\mathcal R_P,\quad F_{C_1}(I,D)\subseteq F_{C_2}(I,D).\] The dominance is conditionally strict when the inclusion is strict for at least one member of \(\mathcal R_P\). No ordering is asserted outside \(\mathcal R_P\); consequently, the predicate must record all relevant restrictions on representation, constraint language, graph structure, and domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional dominance is uniform pruning dominance only within the subclass selected by a stated structural or representational predicate.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) defines a nonempty subclass \(\mathcal R_P\).
Both notions are enforced to closure on that subclass.

notation.meaning: Subclass of represented instances satisfying P.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: restriction of a uniform strength order to a predicate-defined subclass
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition correctly restricts dominance to a predicate-defined subclass and fits the container, but it has no inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantically equivalent representations with different domain-consistency pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D_x=D_y=\{1,2\}\) and \(D_z=\{1,2,3\}\). The global constraint \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x,y,z)\) and the decomposition \(x
e y\land x
e z\land y
e z\) have the same solutions. Generalized arc consistency on the global constraint deletes \(1\) and \(2\) from \(D_z\), whereas arc consistency on the binary decomposition deletes nothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The global all-different propagator recognizes that x and y occupy values 1 and 2 and fixes z to 3; pairwise disequalities do not.
assumptions_latex: The domains are exactly as displayed.
Each representation is filtered to its corresponding domain-consistency fixed point.
knowledge_statements.title: Global All-Different Versus Pairwise Decomposition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semantic Equivalence Does Not Imply Closure Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates represented solutions from store-by-store propagation behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equality of projected solution relations constrains complete assignments only. Equal projected pruning requires the stronger condition that the projected closure operators agree on every pair of compatible initial stores. Semantic equivalence, channeling constraints, or agreement on one initial store alone does not establish this condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent feasible sets can filter differently; propagation equivalence is a stronger, store-by-store requirement.
assumptions_latex: The compared representations have a declared common-variable projection and compatible initial stores.
knowledge_statements.title: Semantic Equivalence Does Not Imply Closure Equivalence
Representation-Dependent Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States that semantically equivalent formulations can induce different pruning on their shared original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_j\) be a constraint representation over variables \(X\cup Y_j\), where \(X\) is the common set of original variables and \(Y_j\) contains representation-specific auxiliary variables, for \(j\in\{1,2\}\). Let initial stores \(D_1\) and \(D_2\) satisfy \(\pi_X(D_1)=\pi_X(D_2)\), and suppose the encodings have the same projected solutions: \[\pi_X\!\left(\operatorname{Sol}(r_1,D_1)\right)=\pi_X\!\left(\operatorname{Sol}(r_2,D_2)\right).\] For a consistency notion \(C\), propagation strength is representation-dependent if such representations and stores exist for which \[\pi_X\!\left(F_C^{r_1}(D_1)\right)\ne\pi_X\!\left(F_C^{r_2}(D_2)\right).\] Thus equality of the represented solution relation on \(X\) does not imply equality of local-consistency pruning on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semantically equivalent encodings, equipped with representation-specific stores that agree on the original variables, may leave different original-variable domains after enforcing the same consistency notion.
assumptions_latex: \(r_j\) is defined over \(X\cup Y_j\) for each \(j\in\{1,2\}\).
\(D_1\) and \(D_2\) agree after projection onto \(X\).
The projected solution sets of the two represented instances are equal on \(X\).
The same consistency notion \(C\) is enforced to closure in both representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equal projected solution sets need not imply \(\pi_X(F_C^{r_1}(D_1))=\pi_X(F_C^{r_2}(D_2))\).

notation.meaning: Variables shared by the two representations and retained for comparison.
Auxiliary variables specific to representation j.
Closure obtained by enforcing consistency notion C in representation j from its own initial store.
Solutions of representation j admitted by its initial store.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: local-consistency pruning may depend on decomposition and auxiliary variables

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary between solution-preserving local filtering and global satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(P)\) be a sound local-consistency closure represented by domain restriction. Every solution of \(P\) remains admitted by \(F(P)\), and every assignment admitted by \(F(P)\) still satisfies the original constraints exactly when it is a solution of \(P\). Consequently an empty domain in \(F(P)\) certifies unsatisfiability, but \(F(P)\) having only nonempty domains does not generally imply \(\operatorname{Sol}(P)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sound local filtering preserves all solutions, but nonempty locally consistent domains need not contain a globally compatible assignment.
assumptions_latex: The local revision rules are solution-preserving.
The closure changes domains but not the constraint semantics.

notation.meaning: Sound local-consistency closure of network P.
A store containing an empty domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Soundness Without Global Completeness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical structural regime in which local arc support composes globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite binary constraint network whose constraint graph is a tree. If \(P\) is arc consistent and every domain is nonempty, then \(P\) has a solution. Moreover, after selecting any root variable and any value in its domain, compatible values can be selected outward along the tree to obtain a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a binary tree, nonempty arc consistency guarantees satisfiability and supports backtrack-free construction from any root value.
assumptions_latex: All constraints are binary.
The constraint graph is a tree.
The network is arc consistent and every domain is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.title: Arc Consistency on Binary Trees
Local–Global Consistency Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An odd-cycle binary CSP separates arc consistency from global satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X_1,X_2,X_3\) have domains \(D_i=\{0,1\}\), with constraints \(X_1
e X_2\), \(X_2
e X_3\), and \(X_3
e X_1\). Every value of each variable has a supporting unequal value in each neighboring domain, so the instance is arc consistent and arc-consistency enforcement deletes nothing. Nevertheless, \[\operatorname{Sol}(I)=\varnothing,\] because two colors cannot properly color an odd cycle. Hence local support on every constraint does not entail a globally compatible assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Boolean disequality triangle is arc consistent but unsatisfiable, demonstrating that local supports need not combine into a global solution.

Each edge of the three-cycle imposes binary disequality.

children.title: Coarse-Grained Iteration
children.top_down_role: Iteration organized around larger propagation work units.

knowledge_statements.title: Coarse-Grained Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Round-based propagation applies every propagator before testing for another sweep.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite domain store \(D^0\) and contracting, monotone, solution-preserving propagators \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\). For rounds \(k=0,1,\ldots\), set \(E_0=D^k\) and compute \[E_i=f_i(E_{i-1})\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad D^{k+1}=E_m.\] Stop and output \(D^{k+1}\) when \(D^{k+1}=D^k\), or report failure when some domain becomes empty. Otherwise begin another complete sweep. Because stores form a finite descending order and every propagator occurs in every round, the procedure terminates at a common fixpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly sweep through all propagators, stopping when an entire sweep changes no domain or when a domain becomes empty.
assumptions_latex: The domain-store lattice is finite.
Each \(f_i\) is contracting, monotone, and solution-preserving.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a common fixpoint \(D^\star\) satisfying \(f_i(D^\star)=D^\star\) for all \(i\).

notation.meaning: Domain store at the start of round k.
The ith propagator in the fixed sweep order.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite chaotic iteration specialized to complete round-based sweeps
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
