children.title: Last-Support Caching
children.top_down_role: Retention of the most recently successful support location.

knowledge_statements.title: Last-Support Caching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone support search for one directed binary constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed binary constraint \(C_{xy}\), fix an order on \(D_y^0\) and associate a pointer \(L[a]\) with each \(a\in D_x^0\). On a support query for \(a\), return \(L[a]\) when \(L[a]\in D_y\) and \((a,L[a])\in C_{xy}\). If that test fails, scan admissible values strictly after \(L[a]\), or from the first value when \(L[a]\) is undefined, and replace \(L[a]\) by the first support found. Return failure if the suffix contains no support. The suffix rule is sound when earlier scanned values cannot re-enter \(D_y\) during the propagation episode.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A last-support cache reuses a surviving support and, after its deletion, resumes an ordered search without reconsidering permanently rejected earlier values.
assumptions_latex: \(D_y\subseteq D_y^0\) evolves only by deletion.
The cache belongs to a fixed constraint and propagation episode.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each candidate in \(D_y^0\) is passed by a given pointer at most once during the episode.

notation.meaning: Last support or current search position cached for a.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the precise cache invariant.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits Last-Support Caching, and the statement distinguishes monotone ordered search from unrestricted residue reuse. A source is required for the exact suffix-resumption invariant and the claim that each candidate is passed at most once.

children.title: Residue Caching
children.top_down_role: Reusable support witnesses retained across propagation calls.

knowledge_statements.title: Residue Caching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support reuse without an ordered-search invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a constraint \(C\) with scope \(S\), maintain for each literal \((x,a)\) an optional residue \(R[C,x,a]\), namely a previously found satisfying tuple \(t\) with \(t_x=a\). On a support query, first test whether the cached tuple remains valid: \(t_z\in D_z\) for every \(z\in S\). If valid, return it. Otherwise invoke a complete support search over \(C\) for a tuple \(u\) satisfying \(u_x=a\) and \(u_z\in D_z\) for all \(z\in S\); cache and return \(u\), or report failure when none exists. The search need not resume after the residue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residue caching stores a previously found supporting tuple, validates it against current domains, and performs a complete new search only when it has become invalid.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) has finite scope and finite current domains.
The fallback support search is complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure is reported exactly when \((x,a)\) has no current support in \(C\).

notation.meaning: Cached supporting tuple for literal (x,a) in constraint C.

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses residues in constraint propagation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits Residue Caching, and the tuple-validity test plus complete fallback search gives the stated correctness condition. No cited source with a specific locator supports this residue mechanism or its terminology.

children.title: Residue Validity Regimes
children.top_down_role: State changes under which cached support witnesses remain usable.

knowledge_statements.title: Residue Validity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact validity predicate for cached tuple supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) have scope \(S\), current domains \((D_z)_{z\in S}\), and let \(r\) be cached for the literal \((x,a)\). The residue is currently valid precisely when \[r_x=a,\qquad r\in C,\qquad \text{and}\qquad (\forall z\in S)\;r_z\in D_z.\] Under monotone domain deletion, validity persists until some component \(r_z\) is deleted. Across backtracking, domain expansion can make an invalid residue valid again, but a residue may be reused only after evaluating the displayed predicate against the restored domains and the same constraint identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cached tuple is a valid residue exactly when it supports the requested literal, satisfies the same constraint, and all its components remain in current domains.
assumptions_latex: The cached tuple and current constraint use the same variable scope and value representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed predicate is necessary and sufficient for safe reuse of \(r\) as a current support.
review_flags: Mathematical predicate is standard, but supplied sources do not document residue validity.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role is appropriate for Residue Validity Regimes, and the displayed predicate is internally precise. Acceptance still requires an authoritative source with a specific locator supporting residue validity and reuse across domain restoration.

children.title: Support Invalidation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Domain changes that force cached support information to be reconsidered.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Invalidation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Events beyond which cached support cannot be trusted without revalidation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cached support \(r\) for \((C,x,a)\) may be used without a fresh search only while its cache key still denotes the same constraint semantics and \((\forall z\in\operatorname{scope}(C))\,r_z\in D_z\). Deletion of any component \(r_z\), replacement or strengthening of \(C\), rebinding of variables, or reuse under a different scope crosses the validity boundary. After such an event, unconditional reuse is unsound: for example, if \(C=\{(0,0),(0,1)\}\), \(r=(0,0)\), and \(0\) is deleted from the second domain, then \(r\) no longer supports \((x,0)\), although another support may exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support cache becomes unsafe when a tuple component is deleted or the keyed constraint semantics change; the cached object must then be revalidated or replaced.
assumptions_latex: A support is represented by an assignment over the complete constraint scope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Crossing any stated boundary requires validation or a new support search before cache reuse.
review_flags: Concrete boundary statement lacks a relevant supplied source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the terminal container, and the example correctly illustrates invalidation by component deletion. The broader claims about semantic replacement, strengthening, rebinding, and scope reuse lack cited support and therefore require an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic cost expression separating scheduling from constraint-specific support search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If revising literal (x,a) in constraint C costs at most T_{C,x,a} and the schedule invokes that revision q_{C,x,a} times, total support-search time is O(\sum_{C,x,a}q_{C,x,a}T_{C,x,a}) plus queue maintenance. Therefore no representation-independent polynomial bound follows without bounds on support search and invocation counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The schema's cost is the sum of scheduled support-search costs, so the constraint representation controls tractability.
assumptions_latex: Every support-search invocation terminates.
The finite monotone episode performs finitely many scheduled invocations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complete Support Search and Fair Rescheduling Are Necessary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness boundary of the generic support-search schema.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If support search reports failure while a compatible tuple exists, the schema can delete a solution value. If it accepts a tuple incompatible with current domains, or a deletion fails to reschedule a revision whose support may use the deleted value, propagation can terminate with an unsupported literal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: False support failure makes propagation unsound; false support success or missed rescheduling can leave a non-GAC fixpoint.
assumptions_latex: The schema deletes exactly on reported support failure.
Queued revisions are the only mechanism for reconsidering invalidated supports.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{complete current-domain support search and fair dependency scheduling are required}.
knowledge_statements.title: Complete Support Search and Fair Rescheduling Are Necessary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Soundness, Termination, and GAC Fixpoint Contract
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness contract for a finite generic GAC enforcement schema.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume finite domains, sound and complete support search, deletion only after exhaustive support failure, and fair rescheduling after every deletion. Every deletion preserves all solutions, only finitely many literals can be deleted, and termination without an empty domain leaves every remaining literal supported in every incident constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With complete support search and fair rescheduling, the generic schema terminates, preserves solutions, and returns a GAC fixpoint or failure.
assumptions_latex: All domains and scopes are finite.
Support search is sound and complete.
Every deletion-dependent revision is eventually processed.
knowledge_statements.title: Soundness, Termination, and GAC Fixpoint Contract
GAC-Schema Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic generalized-arc-consistency schema for finite constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given finite variables, current domains, and constraints, process each queued pair \((C,x)\). For every \(a\in D_x\), call a complete procedure \(\operatorname{seekSupport}(C,x,a)\) that returns a tuple \(t\in C\) satisfying \(t_x=a\) and \(t_y\in D_y\) for every \(y\in\operatorname{scope}(C)\), or returns failure. Delete \(a\) exactly on failure. Whenever values are deleted from \(D_x\), enqueue every affected pair \((C',y)\) whose available supports may use those values. Stop at an empty domain or when the queue is empty. Implementations may instantiate support search and caching differently while preserving these deletion and scheduling rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: GAC-Schema repeatedly tests every relevant variable-value literal for a compatible constraint tuple, deletes unsupported values, and reschedules constraints affected by each deletion.
assumptions_latex: All scopes and domains are finite.
Every support-search call is sound and complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At a nonfailure fixpoint, every remaining literal has a current support in each constraint containing its variable.

notation.meaning: Complete support oracle for literal (x,a) in C.

This direct incremental access requires space \Theta(M) for the incidence representation, even if only a small fraction of supports is inspected before the fixpoint.

GAC-4 Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Table-based GAC maintained by explicit support sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each extensional constraint \(C\) and literal \((x,a)\), form \(S[C,x,a]=\{t\in C:t_x=a\}\). Mark a tuple active exactly while \((\forall y\in\operatorname{scope}(C))\,t_y\in D_y\), and maintain \(n[C,x,a]\), the number of active tuples in \(S[C,x,a]\). Initially delete every \(a\) having zero count. When a value \(b\) is deleted from \(D_y\), deactivate each still-active tuple with \(t_y=b\), decrement the counts of all literals occurring in that tuple, and enqueue any literal whose count becomes zero. Continue until the queue empties or a domain becomes empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: GAC-4 explicitly records table tuples supporting each literal and propagates deletions by deactivating tuples and removing literals whose active-support count reaches zero.
assumptions_latex: Each constraint is represented by a finite table of allowed tuples.
Each active tuple is deactivated at most once per monotone episode.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At a nonfailure fixpoint, every remaining literal has at least one active supporting tuple in each incident constraint.

children.title: GAC-2001 Family
children.top_down_role: Nonbinary incremental-support filtering variants derived from GAC-2001.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tuple-inspection, time, and cache-space bounds for one deletion-only GAC-2001 propagation episode.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose there are \(e\) constraints, each of arity at most \(k\), and every variable domain has size at most \(d\). If the support-search cursor for each constraint literal \((C,x,a)\) moves monotonically through at most \(d^{k-1}\) candidate tuples, then at most \(ekd^k\) candidates are inspected during one deletion-only episode. With \(O(k)\) validation per candidate, the time is \(O(ek^2d^k)\). Storing one \(k\)-tuple per constraint literal uses \(O(ek^2d)\) scalar components, or \(O(ekd)\) shared tuple references.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Monotone resumption prevents a constraint literal from reconsidering candidate tuples, giving at most e k d^k inspections in one deletion-only episode.
assumptions_latex: Candidate enumeration for each literal is finite and never moves backward during the episode.
Constraint arity is at most \(k\), domain size is at most \(d\), and candidate validation costs \(O(k)\).
review_flags: The operation count depends on whether tuple validation is charged as O(k) or treated as a primitive.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone-Resume Support-Search Bound
GAC-2001 Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental tuple-support search for generalized arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every constraint \(C\) and literal \((x,a)\), store a last support \(L[C,x,a]\) in a fixed enumeration of candidate tuples with component \(x=a\). When revising \((C,x,a)\), retain it if the cached tuple belongs to \(C\) and all its components remain in their current domains. Otherwise resume the constraint-specific enumeration after the cached tuple, testing candidates for membership in the current domain product; cache the first valid support found. Delete \(a\) if the enumeration is exhausted. Schedule revisions affected by each deletion and iterate until quiescence or domain failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: GAC-2001 maintains a last supporting tuple for each constraint literal and resumes an ordered support search when that tuple is invalidated.
assumptions_latex: Domains evolve only by deletion during the propagation episode.
Candidate-support enumeration is finite, complete, and ordered compatibly with the resume rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At a nonfailure fixpoint, all remaining literals are generalized arc consistent.

notation.meaning: Last supporting tuple cached for literal (x,a) in C.
A finite-domain constraint, extensionally or intensionally represented.

review_flags: The exact GAC-2001 enumeration invariant requires an authoritative algorithm source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the GAC-2001 Family container. The exact ordered tuple-enumeration and resume invariant is algorithm-specific and cannot be reliably approved without an authoritative GAC-2001 citation and inspectable locator.

children.title: GAC Residue Families
children.top_down_role: Nonbinary filtering families organized around reusable support residues.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case and cache-hit-sensitive accounting for residue reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q be the number of literal revisions, V the maximum residue-validation cost, T the maximum complete fallback-search cost, and F\le Q the number of absent or invalid residues. Then residue filtering costs O(QV+FT). In the worst case F=Q, so caching alone gives no asymptotic improvement over uncached search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residues help when cache hits are common, but the worst case still performs complete search on every revision.
assumptions_latex: Each revision validates at most one cached residue before fallback.
Fallback support search costs at most T.

notation.meaning: Number of revisions requiring fallback search.

knowledge_statements.title: Hit-Sensitive Residue Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness boundary under domain deletion and restoration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cached tuple ceases to certify (x,a) when any component value is absent from its current domain. Reusing that tuple without validation can retain an unsupported value. Backtracking restoration may make a formerly invalid tuple valid again, but reuse still requires validation or a maintained persistence invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residue certifies support only while it is currently valid; restoration does not remove the validation requirement.
assumptions_latex: The cached object is a full tuple of the constraint.
Domains may shrink and later be restored.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R[C,x,a]\text{ usable}\implies R[C,x,a]\in C\land R_x=a\land\forall y,\ R_y\in D_y.

notation.meaning: Cached residue for literal (x,a) in constraint C.

knowledge_statements.title: Stale Residues Cannot Certify Support

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Validated Residues Preserve the GAC Fixpoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic invariance of caching relative to complete uncached support search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every cached tuple is validated against the constraint and current domains before use, every cache miss invokes sound and complete support search, and scheduling is fair, residue hits only avoid searches. Under the same monotone domain episode, the residue and uncached schemes delete the same values and reach the same GAC closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validated residues are performance hints and do not change the GAC fixpoint.
assumptions_latex: Residues are validated before reuse.
Fallback support search is sound and complete.
Dependency scheduling is fair.
The compared procedures use the same initial monotone domains.

notation.meaning: GAC enforcement using validated cached supports.

knowledge_statements.title: Validated Residues Preserve the GAC Fixpoint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cache-granularity variants within residue-based GAC.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Residues may be stored separately as R[C,x,a] for each literal, or one currently valid tuple may be referenced by several literals that it simultaneously supports. Sharing reduces duplicate tuple storage, but each use must verify that the tuple remains valid and contains the referencing literal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residues may be cached per literal or shared among literals supported by one tuple, subject to current-domain validation.
assumptions_latex: A tuple supports the literals represented by its components.
Shared references identify the same tuple.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t\text{ may support all }(x,t_x),\ x\in\operatorname{scope}(C),\text{ while }\forall y,\ t_y\in D_y.

notation.meaning: Cached tuple potentially shared by several literals.

review_flags: No historical family name is assigned to a particular sharing policy.
knowledge_statements.title: Per-Literal and Shared-Tuple Residues
GAC Residue Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-arc-consistency filtering with cached tuple residues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every constraint \(C\) and literal \((x,a)\), retain an optional residue \(R[C,x,a]\). During revision, accept the residue when it is a tuple of \(C\), has component \(x=a\), and every component lies in its variable's current domain. If validation fails, execute a complete support search for \((x,a)\); cache a returned tuple, or delete \(a\) when no tuple exists. Reschedule incident constraints after deletions and continue to a fixpoint. Variants may share residues among literals of one tuple or discard them on restoration, provided validation precedes every reuse lacking a stronger persistence invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: GAC residue algorithms validate cached supporting tuples and invoke full support search only for literals whose cached tuples are absent or invalid.
assumptions_latex: Domains and constraint scopes are finite.
Fallback support search is sound and complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting fixpoint is generalized arc consistent, independently of cache hits.

notation.meaning: Cached tuple residue supporting literal (x,a) in C.

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses residue-based GAC algorithms.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits GAC Residue Families, and validation followed by complete fallback search is a coherent generic scheme. The family characterization, sharing variants, and restoration behavior require a relevant constraint-programming source with a specific locator.

children.title: Incremental-Support Integration
children.top_down_role: Use of retained support information within GAC-2001-style filtering.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of incremental support integration when a deletion does not awaken every dependent literal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C(x,y)\) be equality on \(D_x=D_y=\{0,1\}\), and cache \((0,0)\) as a support of \((x,0)\). Delete \(0\) from \(D_y\) without scheduling revision of \((C,x,0)\). The worklist can become empty while \(0\in D_x\), although no tuple in \(C\cap(D_x\times D_y)\) supports \((x,0)\). Thus quiescence does not imply GAC when scheduling omits a support dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If deleting y=0 does not awaken the cached support of x=0 in equality, propagation can stop with an unsupported value.
assumptions_latex: Cached support validity is not rechecked spontaneously.
Scheduling omits the dependence of \((x,0)\) on deletion of \((y,0)\).

notation.meaning: Current domains of x and y.

knowledge_statements.title: Missed-Invalidation Counterexample
Incremental-Support Integration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correct integration contract between support caches and a GAC worklist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(C,x,a,D)\) return either a tuple supporting \((x,a)\) in the current domain state \(D\), or failure exactly when none exists. A propagator may retain internal search positions or residues across calls. Integrate \(P\) with a deletion worklist by invoking it for every literal whose known support may have been invalidated, deleting the literal precisely on failure, and scheduling all constraint-variable pairs that can lose support because of that deletion. Cached state may suppress a search call only when its associated support is certified valid in \(D\). Quiescence of this worklist is then equivalent to the GAC support predicate holding everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incremental support state yields correct GAC only when invalidations trigger complete support queries and every deletion schedules all potentially affected literals.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is sound and complete for every current domain state.
The scheduling relation covers every support dependence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If propagation terminates without an empty domain, its domains satisfy generalized arc consistency.

notation.meaning: Incremental support procedure in domain state D.

review_flags: Integration contract is standard but unsupported by the supplied locators.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle role fits Incremental-Support Integration, and the statement explicitly identifies support completeness and scheduling coverage as assumptions. No cited source supports the claimed equivalence between worklist quiescence and global GAC under this integration contract.

children.title: Residue Effectiveness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Constraint representations where residue reuse materially changes filtering cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Residue Effectiveness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: When residue validation reduces repeated GAC support searches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(q\) support queries for one literal and let \(h\) queries find its residue valid. If validating a residue over a constraint of arity \(k\) costs at most \(V(k)\), while a fresh complete support search costs at most \(S\), residue caching costs at most \[qV(k)+(q-h)S\] in support-processing work, apart from cache maintenance. Thus it improves this bound over always searching, whose cost is at most \(qS\), whenever \(hS>qV(k)\). The regime is favored by stable domains and repeated queries; frequent invalidation or cheap native support search can eliminate the benefit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residues are effective when cache hits are frequent enough that avoided support searches outweigh validation and maintenance costs.
assumptions_latex: Validation and search costs are measured in the same deterministic work model.
Cache maintenance is either negligible or accounted for separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequality \(hS>qV(k)\) is sufficient for a strict reduction in the stated upper-bound accounting.

notation.meaning: Number of valid-residue hits among q queries.
Maximum validation cost at arity k.
Maximum cost of a fresh support search.

review_flags: Cost model is explicit but no supplied source supports this effectiveness characterization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role is suitable for Residue Effectiveness Regimes, and the inequality follows within the stated deterministic upper-bound accounting. A relevant complexity or empirical source is required to support this cost characterization and its claimed practical regimes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between generalized arc consistency and coverage by current short supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) have finite nonempty current domains and let \(\mathcal S\) be a set of current short supports. A literal \((x,a)\) is covered when some \(s\in\mathcal S\) explicitly contains \(x=a\), or some \(s\in\mathcal S\) omits \(x\). If every current literal is covered, then \(C\) is generalized arc consistent. Conversely, if \(C\) is generalized arc consistent, choosing one full supporting tuple for each current literal produces a covering set of short supports. Hence a short-support cover exists exactly when \(C\) is GAC.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint with nonempty current domains is GAC exactly when current short supports explicitly or implicitly cover every domain literal.
assumptions_latex: Every member of \(\mathcal S\) satisfies the short-support condition in the current domains.
All current domains are finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{GAC}(C,D)\iff \exists\mathcal S\;\forall x\;\forall a\in D_x:\ (x,a)\text{ is covered by }\mathcal S.
review_flags: Nonempty domains are required so that implicit support yields an actual total completion.
knowledge_statements.title: Short-Support Cover Characterization of GAC

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical example in which omission compresses many full supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Boolean clause \(C=(\ell_1\lor\cdots\lor\ell_m)\) whose literals concern \(m\) distinct variables, the singleton assignment making any \(\ell_i\) true is a short support. It explicitly supports that assignment and implicitly supports every current value of the other \(m-1\) variables. On full Boolean domains, these singleton supports avoid enumerating the clause's \(2^m-1\) satisfying total assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a clause over distinct Boolean variables, one true literal is a short support and implicitly supports every value of the other variables.
assumptions_latex: The clause contains one literal on each of \(m\) distinct Boolean variables.
The singleton assignment is consistent with the current domains.
knowledge_statements.title: Clause Short-Support Compression
Short-Support Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Short supports for finite-domain constraints and their propagation meaning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) have scope \(S\) and current domains \((D_x)_{x\in S}\). A short support is a consistent partial assignment \(s\) on \(T\subseteq S\) such that \[s\subseteq t\ \text{and}\ (\forall x\in S)\,t_x\in D_x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t\in C\] for every total assignment \(t\) on \(S\). A literal explicitly occurring in \(s\) is explicitly supported; any domain literal of an omitted variable is implicitly supported by \(s\). Short-support propagation maintains active short supports and deletes a literal only when it has neither an active explicit support nor an active support omitting its variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A short support is a partial assignment whose every domain-consistent completion satisfies the constraint; omitted variables thereby receive implicit support for all current values.
assumptions_latex: All current domains are finite and the partial assignment is domain consistent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every active short support represents one or more full supports and may support all values of each omitted variable.

notation.meaning: Variables explicitly assigned by the short support.

review_flags: No supplied locator concerns short supports or their propagation semantics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits Short-Support Propagation, and the definition clearly distinguishes explicit and implicit support. No authoritative short-support source with a definition, section, theorem, or page locator is supplied, so the terminology and propagation semantics remain unsupported.

children.title: PC-1 Family
children.top_down_role: Path-consistency filtering variants derived from PC-1.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable outcomes for explicit relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Stability is certified by R_{ij}\subseteq R_{ik}\circ R_{kj} for every required ordered triple, with an intermediate value witnessing each retained pair. If a revised required relation is empty, solution preservation certifies that the input network is unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extension witnesses certify path-consistency stability; an empty revised relation certifies unsatisfiability.
assumptions_latex: All required triples are checked using exact relational composition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_{ij}=\varnothing\Rightarrow\mathrm{Sol}=\varnothing;\qquad\forall i,j,k,\ R_{ij}\subseteq R_{ik}\circ R_{kj}\Rightarrow\text{stable PC closure}.
knowledge_statements.title: PC-1 Stability and Failure Certificates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coarse bound for dense exhaustive sweeps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: One dense sweep performs O(n^3) revisions at O(d^3) time each. At most O(n^2d^2) pairs can be deleted, and every nonterminal sweep deletes at least one pair. Thus naive exhaustive PC-1 uses O(n^5d^5) time and O(n^2d^2) relation space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without incremental scheduling, repeated dense sweeps have the coarse bound O(n⁵d⁵) time and O(n²d²) space.
assumptions_latex: Relations are dense Boolean tables.
Every sweep revises every ordered triple.
No incremental affected-triple scheduling is used.
knowledge_statements.title: Naive PC-1 Sweep Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonempty PC-1 Closure Need Not Certify Satisfiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete global-completeness boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent 3-coloring of K_4 as a binary network: every vertex has domain \{1,2,3\}, and every edge carries disequality. For any allowed pair of colors and any third vertex, the remaining color supports the pair, so the network is path consistent and PC-1 deletes nothing. Yet K_4 is not 3-colorable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The 3-coloring network of K4 is path consistent with all relations nonempty but has no solution.
assumptions_latex: Every pair of distinct vertices is constrained by disequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonempty PC-1 Closure Need Not Certify Satisfiability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic and fixed-point characterization of exhaustive sweeps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Each revision R_{ij}\leftarrow R_{ij}\cap(R_{ik}\circ R_{kj}) is contracting, monotone, and solution preserving. On finite relations, repeated complete sweeps terminate at the greatest common fixed point below the input relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PC-1 preserves all solutions and returns the greatest path-revision fixed point contained in the input network.
assumptions_latex: Variables and domains are finite.
Every ordered triple is revised in every nonterminal sweep.
knowledge_statements.title: PC-1 Closure Correctness
PC-1 Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive fixed-point path-consistency filtering for finite binary constraint networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite binary constraint network have variables \(V\), domains \(D_i\), and relations \(R_{ij}\subseteq D_i\times D_j\). Initialize the current relations from the network. During each sweep, for every ordered triple of distinct variables \((i,k,j)\), perform the revision \[R_{ij}\leftarrow R_{ij}\cap(R_{ik}\circ R_{kj}),\qquad R_{ik}\circ R_{kj}=\{(a,b):\exists c\in D_k,\ (a,c)\in R_{ik},\ (c,b)\in R_{kj}\}.\] Repeat complete sweeps until no relation changes. Return the resulting network, or report inconsistency if some required relation becomes empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PC-1 repeatedly revises every binary relation through every third variable until an entire sweep makes no deletion or an empty relation proves inconsistency.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) and every \(D_i\) are finite.
Converse relations are maintained consistently: \(R_{ji}=R_{ij}^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the common fixed point of all path-revision operators reached from the input network.

notation.meaning: current allowed pairs for variables i and j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and fixed-point sweep description fit the PC-1 leaf, but no citation identifies the historical PC-1 variant or supports its precise revision and termination conventions.

children.title: PC-2 Family
children.top_down_role: Path-consistency filtering variants derived from PC-2.

knowledge_statements.title: PC-2 Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependency-driven worklist implementation of path-consistency closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite binary network, associate with every ordered triple \((i,k,j)\) the operator \(T_{ikj}(R)_{ij}=R_{ij}\cap(R_{ik}\circ R_{kj})\). Initialize a worklist \(Q\) with all applicable triples. Remove a triple, apply its operator, and, whenever \(R_{ij}\) strictly decreases, insert every triple whose composition test uses \(R_{ij}\) or \(R_{ji}\), suppressing duplicate queued entries. Continue until \(Q=\varnothing\). Return the remaining relations, or report inconsistency immediately when a required relation is empty. Every revision invalidated by a deletion must eventually be processed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PC-2 schedules only path revisions potentially affected by recent deletions, terminating when its worklist is empty or an empty relation is detected.
assumptions_latex: The network and all domains are finite.
The dependency worklist is fair: every invalidated revision is eventually processed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \(R_{ij}\subseteq R_{ik}\circ R_{kj}\) for every applicable ordered triple \((i,k,j)\).

notation.meaning: revision of relation ij using paths through k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the PC-2 leaf, but the exact dependency-reactivation schedule and its identification as PC-2 require a specific authoritative locator.

children.title: Revision-Schedule Differences
children.top_down_role: Contrasts in how the two families organize repeated path revisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Revision-Schedule Differences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point comparison of exhaustive and dependency-driven path-revision schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal T\) be the finite family of contracting, monotone path-revision operators on the product lattice of binary relations ordered by componentwise inclusion. Starting from the same network, an exhaustive-sweep schedule and any fair dependency-driven schedule apply operators from \(\mathcal T\) in different orders. Because every strict update deletes at least one tuple, both executions terminate. Their terminal networks equal the greatest common fixed point of \(\mathcal T\) contained in the initial network, although their numbers and ordering of operator applications may differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fair PC-1-style sweeps and PC-2-style worklists reach the same path-consistency closure, but perform revisions in different orders and quantities.
assumptions_latex: All relation tables are finite.
Both schedules use the same revision operators, and the dependency-driven schedule is fair.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits this comparison leaf, but the claimed equality with the greatest common fixed point depends on schedule and operator conditions that have no cited support.

children.title: Redundant-Revision Profiles
children.top_down_role: Differences in repeated work across PC-1-style versus PC-2-style filtering.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant-Revision Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of revisions that cannot delete tuples under PC-1 and PC-2 schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Call an application of \(T_{ikj}\) redundant at state \(R\) when \(T_{ikj}(R)=R\). In PC-1, every complete sweep applies every member of \(\mathcal T\), so a sweep may contain revisions unrelated to all deletions since their preceding applications; the final confirming sweep is entirely redundant. In PC-2, after \(R_{ij}\) decreases, only operators whose tests depend on \(R_{ij}\) or its converse need be reactivated. Such dependency filtering removes schedule-induced revisions, but an activated revision may still be redundant because surviving alternative supports make its result unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PC-1 performs broad redundant sweeps; PC-2 avoids revisions unaffected by deletions, although queued revisions can still find all relevant pairs supported.
assumptions_latex: PC-1 uses full sweeps and PC-2 uses sound dependency reactivation.
Both algorithms apply the same path-revision operators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dependency scheduling reduces avoidable operator applications but does not guarantee that every processed revision deletes a tuple.

notation.meaning: set of all applicable path revisions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the leaf and the comparison is plausible, but the precise PC-1/PC-2 redundancy characterization lacks a source establishing the relevant schedules and dependencies.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-sensitive episode bound for explicit counted path supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let I be the stored multiset of links from relation-pair deletions to affected path-support counters, and let P count represented relation pairs and counters. If construction enumerates each stored support incidence once and each later deletion traverses each affected incidence at most once, initialization and one monotone propagation episode use O(|I|+P) time and O(|I|+P) space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit counted-support propagation is linear in its stored pair-and-incidence representation during one monotone episode.
assumptions_latex: All relations and support incidences are finite and explicit.
Each relation pair is deleted at most once during the episode.
Every stored incidence is initialized and processed at most once.

notation.meaning: Number of represented relation pairs and support counters.

review_flags: This is a representation-sensitive accounting bound, not a historical dense PC-4 bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Incidence-Size Bound for Counted-Support Propagation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness invariant for explicit counted-support implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A zero counter for (a,b)\in R_{ij} through k justifies deletion exactly when the counter initially includes every c with (a,c)\in R_{ik} and (c,b)\in R_{kj}, and every subsequent loss of such a support is reflected exactly once. Omitting an initial support can cause an unsound deletion; omitting a decrement can retain a path-inconsistent pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Counted-support filtering is correct only when support incidences are complete and every lost support updates its counter exactly once.
assumptions_latex: Relations are interpreted extensionally.
Pair deletions are permanent during the propagation episode.

notation.meaning: Maintained current-support count for pair (a,b) through k.

knowledge_statements.title: Completeness Boundary for Support Counters
PC-4 Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-maintaining path-consistency filtering for explicit finite binary relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every allowed pair \((a,b)\in R_{ij}\) and intermediate variable \(k\), maintain the support set \(S_{ikj}(a,b)=\{c\in D_k:(a,c)\in R_{ik},\ (c,b)\in R_{kj}\}\), represented by a count and incidence links from supporting pairs. Initialize all counts and enqueue each pair having a zero count for some \(k\). Repeatedly delete an enqueued pair and its converse, decrement every count containing either deleted pair as a support, and enqueue newly unsupported pairs. Stop at an empty queue; report inconsistency if a required relation becomes empty, otherwise return the remaining relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PC-4 stores path-support counts and propagates pair deletions through incidence links until every surviving pair has support through every intermediate variable.
assumptions_latex: Domains and binary relations are finite and explicitly represented.
All support incidences and converse deletions are maintained consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, every surviving \((a,b)\in R_{ij}\) has \(S_{ikj}(a,b)\ne\varnothing\) for every applicable \(k\).

notation.meaning: values of k supporting pair (a,b) along the two-step path
current allowed pairs for i and j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the PC-4 leaf, but PC-4 has variant-sensitive data structures and update rules; the stated count-and-incidence implementation needs an authoritative algorithm locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct-table bound for the ordered algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dense implementation on n variables with domains of size at most d performs O(n^3) triple revisions. Direct Boolean relational composition costs O(d^3), giving O(n^3d^3) time and O(n^2d^2) relation storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense direct directional path consistency takes O(n³d³) time and O(n²d²) space.
assumptions_latex: Relations are dense Boolean tables.
Each ordered triple required by the reverse schedule is processed once.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense Binary DPC Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Closure Need Not Be Full Path Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete strictness of the ordering-restricted condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Order Boolean variables x\prec y\prec z. Let R_{xy}=\{(0,0)\}, R_{yz}=\{(0,0)\}, and R_{xz}=\{(0,0),(1,1)\}. The sole directional requirement on R_{xy} through z holds, but (1,1)\in R_{xz} has no extension through y. Thus the network is directionally path consistent for this order but not fully path consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordering can certify the earlier pair through the later variable while another orientation of the same triple remains unsupported.
assumptions_latex: Only ordering-directed path tests are required.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Closure Need Not Be Full Path Closure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering-relative consistency condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given v_1\prec\cdots\prec v_n, a binary network is directionally path consistent when R_{ij}\subseteq R_{ik}\circ R_{kj} for every required i<j<k. Missing earlier-neighbor relations must either be represented initially as universal relations or created as fill relations under the declared graph convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every allowed pair of earlier variables must extend through each relevant later variable in the fixed ordering.
assumptions_latex: A total variable ordering is fixed.
The universal-completion or fill-edge convention is declared.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Path Consistency

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural effect of reverse-order processing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When a processed variable v_k has two earlier neighbors v_i,v_j, directional closure may create or strengthen R_{ij}. These fill relations and the number of scheduled triples depend on the ordering, although every revision preserves the network's solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ordering determines which earlier-neighbor fill relations are materialized and therefore affects sparse storage and work.
assumptions_latex: Reverse-order processing uses universal relations for absent earlier-neighbor constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Different orderings may produce different fill graphs and costs while preserving solutions.}
knowledge_statements.title: Ordering Dependence and Fill Relations
Directional Path-Consistency Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering-restricted path-consistency filtering for finite binary networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an ordering \(v_1\prec\cdots\prec v_n\). Process intermediates in decreasing order. For each \(k\) and every pair \(i<j<k\) adjacent to \(k\), revise \[R_{ij}\leftarrow R_{ij}\cap(R_{ik}\circ R_{kj}),\] updating the converse relation simultaneously. Return the contracted network, or report inconsistency if a revised relation becomes empty. The output is directionally path consistent with respect to the ordering: every allowed assignment to \(v_i,v_j\) with \(i<j<k\) extends to a value of the later variable \(v_k\) whenever the corresponding two constraints are present.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional path consistency processes variables backward and requires compatible assignments on earlier variables to extend through each relevant later variable.
assumptions_latex: The binary network and domains are finite.
A total variable ordering is fixed before filtering.

notation.meaning: current binary relation between ordered variables i and j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and ordering-restricted formulation fit the leaf, but directional path-consistency conventions differ, so the decreasing-order schedule and quantified conclusion require a source.

children.title: k-Consistency Algorithms
children.top_down_role: Filtering families enforcing parameterized higher-order consistency.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order dependence of explicit partial-relation processing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For n variables of domain size at most d, explicitly storing assignments on every scope of size at most k-1 requires O(n^{k-1}d^{k-1}) entries for fixed k. Enumerating every candidate extension by an additional variable and value yields O(n^kd^k) candidates per exhaustive direct pass, excluding repeated closure passes and constraint-query costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Direct extensional processing is polynomial for fixed k but exponential in k; the bound is per exhaustive enumeration pass, not a universal closure-runtime bound.
assumptions_latex: Partial relations are represented extensionally.
k is treated as fixed for the polynomial-time statement.
knowledge_statements.title: Direct Extensional Enumeration Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Fixed-Order Consistency Does Not Ensure Satisfiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete incompleteness family for every fixed order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For k\ge2, give every vertex of K_{k+1} the domain \{1,\ldots,k\} and impose disequality on every edge. Every consistent assignment to at most k-1 vertices uses distinct colors and extends to any additional vertex, so the network is strongly k-consistent. It is nevertheless unsatisfiable because K_{k+1} is not k-colorable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The k-coloring network of a (k+1)-clique is strongly k-consistent but unsatisfiable.
assumptions_latex: k\ge2.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Fixed-Order Consistency Does Not Ensure Satisfiability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency properties targeted by this algorithm family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A network is k-consistent if every consistent assignment to any k-1 distinct variables extends consistently to any additional variable. It is strongly k-consistent if it is j-consistent for every 1\le j\le k.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: k-consistency extends every consistent (k−1)-variable assignment to any kth variable; strong k-consistency also requires every lower order.
assumptions_latex: A partial assignment is consistent when it satisfies every constraint whose scope is contained in its assigned variables.
knowledge_statements.title: k-Consistency and Strong k-Consistency

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global endpoint of the hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite network on n variables that is strongly n-consistent and has no inconsistent nullary constraint permits every consistent partial assignment to be extended one variable at a time to a complete solution, along any variable ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong n-consistency makes sequential assignment backtrack-free from every consistent partial assignment.
assumptions_latex: The network has n finite-domain variables.
The network is strongly n-consistent.
No empty-scope constraint is false.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall t\text{ consistent},\ \exists s\supseteq t\text{ satisfying the network}.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong n-Consistency Gives Backtrack-Free Extension
k-Consistency Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic closure algorithm enforcing finite-network consistency at a fixed order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\ge2\). For every ordered set \(S\) of \(k-1\) distinct variables, enumerate assignments \(t\) satisfying all constraints whose scopes lie in \(S\). For each variable \(x\notin S\), test whether some \(a\in D_x\) makes \(t\cup\{x\mapsto a\}\) satisfy every constraint whose scope is contained in \(S\cup\{x\}\). Delete or forbid \(t\) when no such extension exists, and propagate resulting tuple deletions until a fixed point. To enforce strong \(k\)-consistency, perform the same closure for every order \(j\) with \(2\le j\le k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A k-consistency algorithm removes locally consistent assignments to k−1 variables that cannot extend consistently to an additional variable.
assumptions_latex: The constraint network, its domains, and \(k\) are finite.
Relations needed to represent forbidden partial assignments are available explicitly or intensionally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every surviving consistent assignment on \(k-1\) variables extends consistently to each additional variable; all orders through \(k\) hold in the strong variant.

notation.meaning: locally consistent partial assignment on S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but deleting or forbidding partial assignments requires a specified representation, and no citation supports this generic closure as a concrete k-consistency algorithm.

children.title: Relational-Consistency Algorithms
children.top_down_role: Filtering families operating over relation-based information.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pairwise Relational Consistency Is Not Global Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness boundary on cyclic relation networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Boolean x,y,z, let R_{xy}=R_{yz}=\{(0,0),(1,1)\} and R_{xz}=\{(0,1),(1,0)\}. Every tuple has support in each overlapping relation, but R_{xy}\Join R_{yz}\Join R_{xz}=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two equality relations and one disequality relation form a pairwise-consistent but globally inconsistent triangle.
knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Relational Consistency Is Not Global Consistency

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semijoin consistency targeted by the generic relation-revision algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: R_S is directionally consistent with R_T when every t\in R_S agrees on S\cap T with some u\in R_T, equivalently R_S=R_S\ltimes R_T. A family is pairwise relationally consistent when this holds for every ordered pair of overlapping scopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairwise relational consistency requires every tuple to have a compatible tuple in every overlapping relation.
assumptions_latex: Compatibility is equality on all shared variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Relational Consistency

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic and convergence properties of pairwise revision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Each directed semijoin revision is contracting and monotone on the product of relation lattices. It preserves the global solution set exactly. Fair iteration over finite relations terminates at a common semijoin fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semijoin revision preserves all and only the original global solutions while deleting unsupported local tuples, and finite fair closure terminates.
assumptions_latex: All relations are finite.
Every required ordered overlap is revised fairly.

notation.meaning: Revision of R_S by semijoin with R_T.

knowledge_statements.title: Semijoin Closure Correctness
Relational-Consistency Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semijoin-style consistency closure for finite extensional nonbinary constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each constraint be a finite relation \(R_S\subseteq\prod_{x\in S}D_x\) on scope \(S\). Initialize a worklist with ordered pairs of constraints whose scopes overlap. For \((S,T)\), replace \[R_S\leftarrow R_S\ltimes R_T=\{t\in R_S:\exists u\in R_T,\ t|_{S\cap T}=u|_{S\cap T}\}.\] If \(R_S\) decreases, reactivate every revision using \(R_S\) as a supporting relation. Continue until the worklist is empty. Return the remaining relations, or report inconsistency if any required relation becomes empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relational-consistency filtering repeatedly removes constraint tuples lacking a compatible tuple in an overlapping constraint until semijoin closure is reached.
assumptions_latex: All domains and constraint relations are finite.
Constraint relations are represented extensionally, or equivalent support queries are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \(R_S=R_S\ltimes R_T\) for every scheduled ordered pair \((S,T)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the container broadly, but relational consistency names several distinct notions. A source is needed to establish that pairwise semijoin closure is the intended variant.

children.title: Tuple-Extension Filtering
children.top_down_role: Support processing based on extensions of partial tuples.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable positive and negative support evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tuple u\in R_T with u|_{S\cap T}=t|_{S\cap T} certifies support of t against R_T. If a complete overlap-projection index for the current R_T contains no key t|_{S\cap T}, it certifies that t has no support in R_T.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compatible tuple certifies retention; absence of the overlap key from a complete current index certifies deletion against that relation.
assumptions_latex: The relation or projection index is complete and current.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\in\mathrm{Ext}_T(t)\Rightarrow t\text{ supported};\quad t|_{S\cap T}\notin\pi_{S\cap T}(R_T)\Rightarrow t\text{ unsupported}.
knowledge_statements.title: Tuple Support and Deletion Certificates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support relation underlying tuple-extension filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For t\in R_S, define \mathrm{Ext}_T(t)=\{u\in R_T:t|_{S\cap T}=u|_{S\cap T}\}. Tuple t survives directed filtering by R_T exactly when \mathrm{Ext}_T(t)\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tuple is supported by an overlapping relation when some tuple agrees on every shared variable.
assumptions_latex: R_S and R_T are relations on scopes S and T.

notation.meaning: Tuples of R_T compatible with t.

knowledge_statements.title: Tuple Extension and Support

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis for cached-support maintenance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If R'_T\subseteq R_T, then \mathrm{Ext}'_T(t)\subseteq\mathrm{Ext}_T(t). Hence support can disappear but cannot reappear during contraction-only closure, and a cached witness remains valid until that witness is deleted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shrinking a relation can only remove supports; cached support remains valid while its witness remains present.
assumptions_latex: Filtering deletes tuples and does not reinsert them.
knowledge_statements.title: Support Monotonicity Under Deletion
Tuple-Extension Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support deletion for tuples of overlapping finite constraint relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given finite relations \(R_S\) and \(R_T\), inspect each tuple \(t\in R_S\). Retain \(t\) exactly when its projection on the overlap has an extension in \(R_T\): \[t\in R'_S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad t\in R_S\ \text{and}\ \exists u\in R_T:\ t|_{S\cap T}=u|_{S\cap T}.\] Replace \(R_S\) by \(R'_S\), enqueue neighboring relations after any deletion, and iterate directed revisions until no relation changes. An empty required relation certifies inconsistency of the current relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tuple-extension filtering deletes a relation tuple whenever no tuple in an overlapping relation agrees with it on every shared variable.
assumptions_latex: \(R_S\) and \(R_T\) are finite relations.
Compatibility means equality on all variables in \(S\cap T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every surviving tuple has a compatible extension in each relation against which it has been closed.

notation.meaning: projection of tuple t onto variables U
filtered version of relation on scope S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and semijoin-style tuple test fit the leaf, but no source supports the precise iterative neighboring-relation schedule or its intended consistency notion.

children.title: Relational Representation Costs
children.top_down_role: Storage or processing costs induced by relation-level filtering.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbounded Arity Causes Exponential Explicit Storage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding-size boundary for extensional relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An r-ary universal relation over domains of cardinality d contains d^r tuples, so a tuple-list representation requires \Theta(rd^r) stored coordinates. Polynomial time in table size therefore need not be polynomial in the compact parameters r and d.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit relation tables can be exponential in arity even when processing is polynomial in table size.
assumptions_latex: Tuples are stored extensionally with one coordinate per scope variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Arity Causes Exponential Explicit Storage

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary representation for extension queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For U=S\cap T, index R_T by I_T(p)=\{u\in R_T:u|_U=p\}. Then t\in R_S has support in R_T exactly when I_T(t|_U)\ne\varnothing. The index requires O(|U||R_T|) stored key coordinates and supports expected constant-time existence lookup under hashing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Indexing a relation by overlap projections exchanges additional storage for fast tuple-support queries.
assumptions_latex: R_T is extensional.
Expected constant-time hash lookup is available.

notation.meaning: Index from overlap keys to tuples of R_T.

knowledge_statements.title: Overlap Projection Index
Relational Representation Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case explicit-table costs for higher-order constraint relations and semijoins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every domain has size at most \(d\), and a relation has arity at most \(r\). Its explicit table can contain \(d^r\) tuples and therefore requires \(O(r d^r)\) stored values. For scopes \(S,T\), a semijoin \(R_S\ltimes R_T\) can be computed by hashing projections on \(S\cap T\) in expected \(O((|S|+|T|)(|R_S|+|R_T|))\) time and \(O(|S\cap T|\,|R_T|)\) auxiliary space. Materializing a join may instead require \(\Theta(d^{|S\cup T|})\) tuples in the worst case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit higher-order relations cost exponentially in arity; indexed semijoins are linear in table sizes, while materialized joins can grow exponentially in the union scope.
assumptions_latex: Tuples are represented explicitly using one stored value per scope coordinate.
Expected constant-time hashing is available for the semijoin bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Explicit storage is \(O(r d^r)\), whereas a materialized join can have size \(\Theta(d^{|S\cup T|})\).

notation.meaning: number of tuples stored for scope S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the cost leaf, but the storage, expected hashing-time, auxiliary-space, and worst-case join-size bounds need a source specifying the representation and computational model.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-parameterized bound for restarting a complete pass after every deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let L=\sum_x|D_x^0|. If a complete pass is restarted after every permanent deletion and each singleton test, including state copying and propagation, costs at most T_P, then at most L+1 passes test at most L literals each. Thus the algorithm performs at most L(L+1) tests and costs O(L^2T_P), with permanent propagation included in T_P or accounted for separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restart-after-deletion implementation uses at most quadratically many singleton tests in the initial number of literals.
assumptions_latex: Domains are finite.
A complete pass restarts after every permanent deletion.
Each singleton test costs at most T_P.

notation.meaning: Initial total number of variable-value literals.
Maximum cost of one copied singleton propagation.

review_flags: This bound concerns the stated restarting implementation, not optimized singleton algorithms.
knowledge_statements.title: Restarting Singleton-Closure Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singleton Arc Consistency Does Not Imply Satisfiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite binary counterexample to completeness of singleton arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Give each vertex of K_4 the domain \{1,2,3\} and post disequality on every edge. The network is unsatisfiable. After fixing any vertex to any color, arc consistency removes that color from its three neighbors; those neighbors form a triangle with two remaining colors at every vertex, which is arc consistent. Hence every singleton probe survives arc consistency although the original network has no solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The three-coloring CSP of K4 is singleton arc consistent but unsatisfiable.
assumptions_latex: The underlying propagator enforces binary arc consistency.
All six binary constraints are disequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Singleton Arc Consistency Does Not Imply Satisfiability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singleton Consistency Relative to a Propagator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized singleton-consistency condition induced by a fixed propagator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a network N and a sound propagator P, a current literal (x,a) is singleton-P-consistent when P(N\land x=a) does not report inconsistency. The network is singleton-P-consistent exactly when every current literal is singleton-P-consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network is singleton consistent relative to P when temporarily assigning any remaining value and running P never proves inconsistency.
assumptions_latex: P is sound and has a defined inconsistency outcome.
a\in D_x is a current literal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N\text{ is singleton-}P\text{-consistent}\iff \forall x\ \forall a\in D_x,\ P(N\land x=a)\ne\bot.
knowledge_statements.title: Singleton Consistency Relative to a Propagator
Singleton-Consistency Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic singleton testing built around a chosen sound consistency propagator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a sound, contracting consistency propagator. First compute \(P(N)\). For each current value \(a\in D_x\), make a temporary copy, impose \(D_x=\{a\}\), and run \(P\) to a fixed point. If the temporary network becomes inconsistent, delete \(a\) from the permanent domain. After any permanent deletion, propagate again and repeat singleton tests until a complete pass deletes nothing. Return the resulting network, or report inconsistency if a permanent domain becomes empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Singleton consistency tests each value as a temporary assignment, deleting it when ordinary propagation proves that assignment inconsistent, and repeats to closure.
assumptions_latex: The network and all domains are finite.
\(P\) is sound, terminates, and detects inconsistency by an empty domain or relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every surviving \(a\in D_x\), applying \(P\) after imposing \(D_x=\{a\}\) does not derive inconsistency.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the singleton-consistency leaf and the operational claim is coherent relative to P, but a source must establish the parameterized formulation and required properties of the underlying propagator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds contraction for one integer linear inequality over integer interval domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\le b\), with \(x_i\in[\ell_i,u_i]\cap\mathbb Z\), define \(m_i=\sum_{j\ne i}\min\{a_j\ell_j,a_j u_j\}\). If \(a_i>0\), set \(u_i\leftarrow\min\{u_i,\lfloor(b-m_i)/a_i\rfloor\}\); if \(a_i<0\), set \(\ell_i\leftarrow\max\{\ell_i,\lceil(b-m_i)/a_i\rceil\}\). Repeat affected updates until stable. An equality is handled by propagating both opposite inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum residual contributions yield sign-aware rounded bounds for each integer variable.
assumptions_latex: a_i,b,\ell_i,u_i\in\mathbb Z and \ell_i\le u_i.
Domains are represented by their integer interval hulls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Every removed integer value violates the inequality for every assignment of the other variables within their current bounds.}

notation.meaning: minimum contribution of all terms other than i

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Integer-Bounds Propagation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Arithmetic Work per Residual Sweep
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic-operation cost of one complete propagation sweep.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\sum_j\min\{a_j\ell_j,a_j u_j\}\). Since \(m_i=M-\min\{a_i\ell_i,a_i u_i\}\), all single-variable updates in one sweep require \(O(n)\) arithmetic operations after computing \(M\). Repeated sweeps may be needed after bounds change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shared minimum-contribution sum makes one full propagation sweep linear in the number of terms.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic operations are unit cost.
Coefficient bit complexity is not included.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Arithmetic Work per Residual Sweep

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer infeasibility invisible to interval-hull residual propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(2x+2y=1\) with \(x,y\in[0,1]\cap\mathbb Z\), residual bounds propagation on the two opposite inequalities leaves both domains unchanged, although no integer solution exists. More generally, bounds propagation alone need not detect failure when \(\gcd(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\nmid b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval bounds propagation can miss infeasibility detectable by divisibility reasoning.
assumptions_latex: Only residual interval bounds are propagated.
No congruence or gcd reasoning is performed.
knowledge_statements.title: Congruence Blindness
Integer Linear Bounds Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds contraction for one integer linear inequality over interval domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\le b\) with integer bounds \(x_i\in[\ell_i,u_i]\cap\mathbb Z\), define \(m_i=\sum_{j\ne i}\min\{a_j\ell_j,a_j u_j\}\). For each \(a_i>0\), update \[u_i\leftarrow\min\left\{u_i,\left\lfloor\frac{b-m_i}{a_i}\right\rfloor\right\};\] for each \(a_i<0\), update \[\ell_i\leftarrow\max\left\{\ell_i,\left\lceil\frac{b-m_i}{a_i}\right\rceil\right\}.\] Repeat affected updates to a fixed point. An empty interval certifies infeasibility of the current box for this constraint. For an equality, propagate both opposite inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer linear bounds propagation uses the smallest contribution of all other variables to derive rounded upper or lower bounds for each variable.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i,b,\ell_i,u_i\in\mathbb Z\) and \(\ell_i\le u_i\).
Each domain is represented by its integer interval hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every removed integer value violates the inequality for all assignments of the other variables within their current bounds.

notation.meaning: current integer interval domain of variable i
minimum contribution attainable by variables other than i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and rounded bound updates fit the leaf, but the supplied integer-programming locators do not identify this constraint-propagation rule. A specific constraint-programming source is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination of repeated forward–backward sweeps over finite endpoint sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume each variable interval endpoint belongs to a finite ordered set \(E_i\), every complete sweep is contracting, and another sweep is performed only after a strict variable-endpoint change. Each lower endpoint can increase and each upper endpoint can decrease at most \(|E_i|-1\) times. Hence there are at most \(2\sum_i(|E_i|-1)\) strict endpoint changes and at most one more completed sweep to detect a fixpoint. Without finite endpoint sets, exact-real contracting iteration need not attain its limiting fixpoint after finitely many sweeps, so a tolerance or iteration limit may be required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward–backward propagation terminates on finite endpoint grids; exact-real iteration may approach a fixpoint only asymptotically.
assumptions_latex: All produced variable endpoints lie in finite ordered sets \(E_i\).
Every complete sweep is contracting, and rescheduling requires a strict variable-endpoint change.

notation.meaning: Permitted endpoint set for variable i.

review_flags: The bound counts endpoint movements and completed sweeps, not arithmetic operations inside a sweep.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Endpoint Termination Condition
Forward–Backward Interval Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-constraint propagation on an acyclic expression tree using inclusion-isotone interval extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an expression tree represent the constraint \(g(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=0\), and let the current variable box be \(B=I_1\times\cdots\times I_n\). Forward propagation assigns each leaf its interval \(I_i\) and each internal node the interval extension of its operator. Intersect the root interval with \(\{0\}\); an empty intersection certifies infeasibility. Backward propagation applies sound inverse interval operators from the root toward the leaves and intersects every resulting leaf interval with \(I_i\). Repeat forward and backward sweeps until an interval is empty, no endpoint changes, or a prescribed tolerance is reached. The output box \(B'\subseteq B\) contains every point of \(B\) satisfying the constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate intervals from leaves to root, impose the root constraint, propagate inverse images backward, and repeat. The resulting box is contracting and retains every feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a Cartesian product of real intervals.
Every forward and inverse interval operator is inclusion-isotone and sound.
The expression representation is an acyclic tree.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard forward–backward interval-evaluation and inverse-propagation scheme

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and terminal placement fit, and the claimed contraction is standard. No inspectable citation is supplied, however, and “sound inverse interval operators” needs an authoritative specification establishing solution preservation for the backward sweep.

children.title: Hull Contraction
children.top_down_role: Interval filtering organized around hull-based consistency.

knowledge_statements.title: Hull Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ideal interval-hull contractor for one constraint over a real box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a constraint relation \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and a box \(B=I_1\times\cdots\times I_n\), define its hull contraction by \[H_C(B)=\operatorname{hull}(C\cap B)=\prod_{i=1}^n\bigl[\inf \pi_i(C\cap B),\sup \pi_i(C\cap B)\bigr].\] Use \(H_C(B)=\varnothing\) when \(C\cap B=\varnothing\). Thus hull contraction returns the smallest axis-aligned closed box containing all solutions currently admitted by \(B\). It is contracting, sound, monotone under box inclusion, and idempotent whenever the displayed extrema exist in the extended-real sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hull contraction replaces a box by the smallest axis-aligned box containing all feasible points inside it.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
\(B\) is a closed real box.

notation.meaning: ideal hull contractor for relation C

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact Cartesian interval hull of the feasible subset is the canonical ideal hull contractor

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind matches the Hull Contraction leaf and the formula is mathematically coherent for a bounded closed box. An inspectable source is required for the canonical terminology and contractor properties.

children.title: Box Contraction
children.top_down_role: Interval filtering organized around box-based consistency.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical force of empty and nonempty outputs from a sound box contractor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every sound box contractor \(Q_C\), \(Q_C(B)=\varnothing\) implies \(C\cap B=\varnothing\). The converse need not hold: the identity contractor \(Q_C(B)=B\) is sound for every relation \(C\), yet can return a nonempty box when \(C\cap B=\varnothing\). Thus emptiness certifies infeasibility, whereas nonemptiness does not certify feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An empty contracted box certifies infeasibility, but a nonempty contracted box need not contain a solution.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_C\) is contracting and solution preserving.
\(B\) is an interval box.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
Q_C(B)=\varnothing\Rightarrow C\cap B=\varnothing,\qquad Q_C(B)
e\varnothing

e\varnothing.

notation.meaning: Sound box contractor for relation C.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty-Box Certificate and Nonconverse

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of sound box contractors under intersection and sequential composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_C\) and \(R_C\) be box contractors for the same relation \(C\). Then \((Q_C\wedge R_C)(B):=Q_C(B)\cap R_C(B)\) and \((Q_C\circ R_C)(B):=Q_C(R_C(B))\) are box contractors for \(C\). The intersection is contained in both component outputs. Sequential composition is contained in the first-applied output \(R_C(B)\), while comparison with \(Q_C(B)\) additionally requires an order property such as monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersection and sequential composition preserve contractor soundness; intersection is no weaker than either component, while composition is always no weaker than the first-applied contractor.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_C\) and \(R_C\) satisfy contraction and solution preservation for every box.
