knowledge_statements.title: Contractor Intersection and Composition
Box Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract sound contractor whose input and output domains are Cartesian interval boxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a constraint relation and let \(\mathcal B_n\) denote the set of axis-aligned interval boxes in \(\mathbb R^n\), including the empty box. A box contractor for \(C\) is a map \(Q_C:\mathcal B_n\to\mathcal B_n\) satisfying, for every \(B\in\mathcal B_n\), \[Q_C(B)\subseteq B,\qquad C\cap B\subseteq Q_C(B).\] The first inclusion is contraction and the second is solution preservation. A contractor may be required additionally to be monotone, meaning \(B_1\subseteq B_2\) implies \(Q_C(B_1)\subseteq Q_C(B_2)\), and idempotent, meaning \(Q_C(Q_C(B))=Q_C(B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box contractor maps each interval box to a smaller box without deleting any feasible point of the represented constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
Inputs and outputs belong to the box domain \(\mathcal B_n\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: contraction plus solution preservation is the standard abstract contractor specification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and local context fit. Contraction and solution preservation are stated precisely, while monotonicity and idempotence are correctly presented as optional additions, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Hull–Box Strength Relations
children.top_down_role: Relative contraction strength across hull-based versus box-based filtering.

knowledge_statements.title: Hull–Box Strength Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order comparison between the ideal hull and arbitrary sound box contractions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(B\) be a box, and let \(Q_C\) be any sound box contractor. Because \(Q_C(B)\) is itself a box containing \(C\cap B\), minimality of the interval hull gives \[H_C(B)\subseteq Q_C(B)\subseteq B.\] Hence ideal hull contraction is at least as strong as every sound contraction expressible by one output box. Equality holds exactly when \(Q_C(B)\) equals the coordinatewise hull of \(C\cap B\). A strict inclusion measures relaxation or propagation loss, not unsoundness. No sound box contractor can return a proper subbox of \(H_C(B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact feasible hull is contained in every sound contracted box. Equality means hull strength; strict containment records lost pruning precision.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_C(B)\) is an axis-aligned box.
\(C\cap B\subseteq Q_C(B)\subseteq B\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: follows directly from the defining minimality of an axis-aligned hull

children.title: Representation-Sensitive Separation
children.top_down_role: Expression or domain representations that distinguish hull contraction from box contraction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Expressions Can Produce Different Contractions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependency loss in natural interval evaluation of algebraically equivalent constraint representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\in[-1,1]\) and \(x=[1,1]\). The equations \(x=y-y\) and \(x=0\) define the same real relation. Natural interval evaluation without dependency tracking gives \(y-y=[-2,2]\), which intersects \([1,1]\), whereas the normalized expression gives \([0,0]\cap[1,1]=\varnothing\). Thus equivalent representations can yield different one-pass interval separation outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Natural interval evaluation may fail to reject an infeasible box that an algebraically equivalent normalized expression rejects immediately.
assumptions_latex: Repeated occurrences are evaluated independently by natural interval arithmetic.
No algebraic normalization or relational dependency information is used.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Expressions Can Produce Different Contractions
Representation-Sensitive Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependency loss in natural interval evaluation under algebraically equivalent representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\in[-1,1]\) and impose \(x=1\). Consider the algebraically equivalent constraints \(x=y-y\) and \(x=0\). Natural interval evaluation of the first representation treats the two occurrences independently and gives \(y-y=[-1,1]-[-1,1]=[-2,2]\), whose intersection with \(x=[1,1]\) is nonempty. The simplified representation evaluates to \([0,0]\), which is disjoint from \([1,1]\) and immediately proves infeasibility. Thus a one-pass interval contractor based on natural evaluation can separate equivalent representations: shared-variable dependency may prevent pruning that an equivalent normalized representation performs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent formulas can propagate differently: natural interval evaluation loses the dependency between repeated occurrences, while simplification can expose immediate infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: Natural interval arithmetic evaluates repeated occurrences independently.
The contractor uses the displayed expression without algebraic normalization.

children.title: Interval-Newton Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Propagation-facing use of interval-Newton contraction capabilities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar interval-Newton contraction exposed to a propagation engine.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be continuously differentiable on an interval \(B\), choose \(x_0\in B\), and let \(F'(B)\) enclose \(f'(B)\) with \(0\notin F'(B)\). Define \(N(x_0,B)=x_0-f(x_0)/F'(B)\) and return \(B'=B\cap N(x_0,B)\). Every zero of \(f\) in \(B\) lies in \(B'\); hence \(B'=\varnothing\) certifies that \(B\) contains no zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersecting the current interval with its interval-Newton image preserves every zero and can certify exclusion.
assumptions_latex: f is continuously differentiable on B.
F'(B) encloses all derivatives on B.
0\notin F'(B).
Interval operations are inclusion-isotonic and outward rounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Interval-Newton Contraction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Krawczyk-type multivariate zero-preserving interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable on a box \(B\), choose \(x_0\in B\), let \(J(B)\) enclose all Jacobians on \(B\), and choose a real matrix \(Y\). Define \(K(x_0,B)=x_0-YF(x_0)+(I-YJ(B))(B-x_0)\) and return \(B'=B\cap K(x_0,B)\). Every zero of \(F\) in \(B\) belongs to \(B'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A preconditioned Krawczyk enclosure can be imported as a sound multivariate box contraction.
assumptions_latex: F is continuously differentiable on B.
J(B) encloses every Jacobian on B.
Interval operations are inclusion-isotonic and outward rounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Preconditioned Multivariate Interval Contraction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applicability boundary of ordinary connected scalar interval division.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(0\in F'(B)\), ordinary connected interval division in \(x_0-f(x_0)/F'(B)\) is undefined or unbounded and need not contract \(B\). Subdivision, extended interval division, or another contractor is then required. The condition \(0\in F'(B)\) does not imply that \(B\) contains no isolated zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A derivative enclosure containing zero disables the ordinary bounded Newton step but does not rule out roots.
assumptions_latex: The interface uses ordinary connected interval division.
0\in F'(B).
knowledge_statements.title: Derivative-Zero Boundary
Interval-Newton Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar interval-Newton contraction exposed as a sound numerical filtering interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a continuously differentiable function \(f:B\to\mathbb R\), a point \(x_0\in B\), and an interval enclosure \(F'(B)\supseteq\{f'(x):x\in B\}\) with \(0\notin F'(B)\), form \[N_f(x_0,B)=x_0-\frac{f(x_0)}{F'(B)},\qquad B'=B\cap N_f(x_0,B).\] Return failure if \(B'=\varnothing\); otherwise export \(B'\) to the surrounding propagation engine. Every zero of \(f\) in \(B\) lies in \(B'\). Moreover, \(N_f(x_0,B)\subseteq B\) certifies existence of a zero in \(B\), and strict interior inclusion certifies uniqueness under the standard interval-Newton hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface intersects the current interval with an interval-Newton image, preserving all zeros and optionally certifying existence or uniqueness.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuously differentiable on \(B\).
\(F'(B)\) encloses all derivatives on \(B\).
\(0\notin F'(B)\).

notation.meaning: interval enclosure of derivatives over B

children.title: Linear-Relaxation Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Propagation-facing use of linear-relaxation bound information.

assumptions_latex: \(C\cap B\subseteq P(B)\).
Each coordinate optimization is solved with valid bounds.
Declared integer coordinates retain their integrality domains.

notation.meaning: polyhedral relaxation over the current box

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection of a sound linear relaxation back into variable-domain bounds.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 7. Cuts, Lower Bounds and Box Reduction p. 83
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the current box be \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[l_i,u_i]\), and let \(P(B)=\{x:Ax\le b,\ x\in B\}\) be a polyhedral relaxation satisfying \(C\cap B\subseteq P(B)\). For every coordinate solve \[l_i'=\min\{x_i:x\in P(B)\},\qquad u_i'=\max\{x_i:x\in P(B)\}.\] If \(P(B)=\varnothing\), return infeasibility; otherwise return \(B'=\prod_{i=1}^n[l_i',u_i']\). The imported bounds are sound because every feasible point of the original constraint belongs to the relaxation. Integrality-aware rounding may replace \(l_i'\) and \(u_i'\) by \(\lceil l_i'\rceil\) and \(\lfloor u_i'\rfloor\) for integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build a sound polyhedral relaxation, optimize each coordinate over it, and import the resulting extrema as tighter variable bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Relaxation Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 7. Cuts, Lower Bounds and Box Reduction p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Certificates for Imported Coordinate Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP evidence for imported coordinate bounds and relaxation infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\). For \(\min\{c^Tx:x\in P\}\), any \(y\ge0\) with \(A^Ty=-c\) certifies \(c^Tx\ge-b^Ty\) for every \(x\in P\). Taking \(c=e_i\) or \(c=-e_i\) certifies imported coordinate bounds. If \(y\ge0\), \(A^Ty=0\), and \(b^Ty<0\), then \(P=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual multipliers certify imported coordinate bounds, and a Farkas multiplier certifies relaxation infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: All current box bounds are represented in P.
Multipliers and numerical inequalities are validated exactly or with certified error bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^Ty=-c,\ y\ge0\Rightarrow\min_{x\in P}c^Tx\ge-b^Ty;\quad A^Ty=0,\ y\ge0,\ b^Ty<0\Rightarrow P=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Certificates for Imported Coordinate Bounds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of nested sound relaxations on exported coordinate hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\cap B\subseteq P_1\subseteq P_2\subseteq B\), and define \(H(P)=\prod_i[\inf_{x\in P}x_i,\sup_{x\in P}x_i]\). Then \(H(P_1)\subseteq H(P_2)\). Thus strengthening a sound relaxation cannot weaken imported coordinate bounds, although strict relational strengthening may leave the coordinate hull unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stronger nested relaxation gives no weaker coordinate bounds, but may improve only relational information that the interface does not export.
assumptions_latex: Both relaxations contain every feasible point in the current box.
Coordinate extrema are computed validly.

children.title: Interface Coordination Regimes
children.top_down_role: Solver-kernel settings that combine interval contraction with relaxation-derived filtering.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound coordination of multiple contractors over a shared box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the common solution set and let each contractor \(Q_i\) satisfy \(S\cap B\subseteq Q_i(B)\subseteq B\). Sequential or chaotic coordination replaces \(B\) by \(Q_i(B)\). A snapshot batch computes \(Q_i(B)\) from the same input box and merges the results as \(B' = B\cap\bigcap_{i\in I}Q_i(B)\). Every resulting box still contains \(S\cap B\); emptiness therefore certifies infeasibility in the input box.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential updates and intersection of stale-snapshot contractions are sound when every component contractor is sound for the same solution set.
assumptions_latex: All component contractors refer to the same solution relation and current assumptions.
Each component is sound and contracting.
Snapshot results are merged by intersection, not by overwriting one another.

notation.meaning: common solution set under the active assumptions

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential, Chaotic, and Snapshot-Batched Coordination

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unfair Scheduling Can Miss Common Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of fairness for coordinated contractor closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On subintervals of \([0,2]\), let \(Q_1(B)=B\cap[0,1]\) and \(Q_2(B)=B\cap[1,2]\). Starting from \([0,2]\), a schedule that invokes only \(Q_1\) stabilizes at \([0,1]\), although \(Q_2([0,1])=[1,1]\). The stabilized iterate is therefore not a common fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A schedule that permanently neglects an enabled contractor can stabilize before reaching common closure.
assumptions_latex: The activation schedule is not fair.
knowledge_statements.title: Unfair Scheduling Can Miss Common Closure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination and closure for monotone contractors on a finite box domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal B\) be a finite family of boxes ordered by inclusion. If every \(Q_i:\mathcal B\to\mathcal B\) is contracting and monotone, then any fair iteration from \(B^0\), with \(B^{k+1}=Q_{i_k}(B^k)\), terminates at the greatest common fixed point contained in \(B^0\). Fairness means that no contractor that remains capable of changing the current box is postponed forever.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fair chaotic iteration of monotone contracting operators on a finite box domain reaches the common propagation closure.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal B is finite.
Every Q_i is monotone and contracting.
The activation schedule is fair.

notation.meaning: finite box domain ordered by inclusion

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Fair-Iteration Closure
Interface Coordination Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fair fixed-point coordination of multiple sound numerical contractors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_m\) be sound contracting maps on boxes. Initialize \(B^{0}=B\). At iteration \(k\), select an index \(i_k\) and set \[B^{k+1}=Q_{i_k}(B^k).\] Stop on emptiness, a common fixed point, or a declared numerical tolerance. A sequential regime uses a fixed or work-list order; a chaotic regime permits any fair order in which every contractor enabled infinitely often is selected infinitely often; a batched regime computes candidate contractions from one snapshot and safely intersects them. Every finite iterate remains sound. If the box lattice is finite and every contractor is monotone, inflationary in the reverse-inclusion order, and idempotent, fair iteration terminates at the greatest common fixed point below \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinate sound contractors sequentially, fairly, or in batches. Every iterate preserves solutions; finite-domain fair iteration reaches the common propagation closure.
assumptions_latex: Each \(Q_i\) is sound and contracting.
For the fixed-point conclusion, the box domain is finite and every \(Q_i\) is monotone.
The schedule is fair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\cap B\subseteq B^{k+1}\subseteq B^k\subseteq B\), and finite fair iteration reaches a common fixed point.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fair chaotic iteration of monotone contracting propagators on a finite lattice

children.title: Cross-Interface Precision Loss
children.top_down_role: Information losses arising when results pass between interval and relaxation representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precision loss when a relational numerical state is exported only as coordinate bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{(x,y)\in[-1,1]^2:x+y=0\}\). Exporting only coordinate extrema yields \(H(P)=[-1,1]^2\), which contains \((1,1)\notin P\). Coordinate-hull transfer is therefore sound but noninjective: distinct relational sets can have the same exported box, and the receiver cannot reconstruct the discarded correlation without additional relational information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinate-bound exchange preserves feasible points but can discard correlations irrecoverably.
assumptions_latex: The exchange contains only coordinate intervals.
The equality or an equivalent relational constraint is not transmitted.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate-Hull Transfer Loses Correlation
Cross-Interface Precision Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss caused by exchanging only coordinate bounds between relational numerical interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[P=\{(x,y)\in[-1,1]^2:x+y=0\}.\] A linear-relaxation interface retains the equality, but an interface exporting only coordinate bounds sends \(\operatorname{hull}(P)=[-1,1]^2\). The points \((1,1)\) and \((-1,-1)\), absent from \(P\), reappear in the exported box. Consequently, no receiving procedure given only that box can reconstruct the lost correlation without receiving an additional relational constraint. In general, coordinate-hull transfer is sound but noninjective: distinct relational sets can have the same exported box, so alternating sound interfaces need not attain the contraction obtainable in their joint relational representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exporting only variable bounds preserves feasibility but discards correlations. Distinct relational states can therefore become indistinguishable to the receiving interface.
assumptions_latex: The exchange format contains only coordinate intervals.
The sending interface does not transmit the equality separately.

notation.meaning: relational feasible set retained by the sender

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Support Filtering Is Contracting and Idempotent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure properties of exact domain-consistency filtering for one finite global relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F_G(D)_i=\{a\in D_i:\exists v\in\prod_jD_j,\ v_i=a\land G(v)\}\). Then \(F_G(D)\subseteq D\) and \(F_G(F_G(D))=F_G(D)\). Moreover, \(F_G(D)\) is the greatest domain-consistent subdomain contained in \(D\) obtainable solely by deleting unsupported values for this relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact support filtering only deletes values, is idempotent, and returns the greatest domain-consistent subdomain for the relation.
assumptions_latex: G is one finite relation.
All supported-value sets are computed simultaneously from the same input domain state.

assumptions_latex: Each \(D_i\) is finite.
\(G\) denotes the native global relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is domain consistent exactly when every \(a\in D_i\) has a support in \(\prod_j D_j\).

notation.meaning: current finite domain of variable i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized arc consistency for one finite-domain global constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) be a global constraint with finite current domains \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\). The domains are domain consistent for \(G\) if and only if \[\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\;\forall a\in D_i\;\exists (v_1,\ldots,v_n)\in D_1\times\cdots\times D_n:\quad v_i=a\ \land\ G(v_1,\ldots,v_n).\] The witnessing tuple is a support for \(a\). A domain-consistency propagator deletes precisely values lacking support; it reports failure exactly when some resulting domain is empty. The definition concerns the global relation itself, not any chosen decomposition into auxiliary constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every remaining value of every variable must extend to a complete tuple satisfying the global constraint within the current domains.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain Consistency for Global Constraints

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supported Endpoints Need Not Fill an Interior Hole
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of interval-convex supported-value sets for deriving domain consistency from endpoint support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D(x)=\{0,1,2\}\) and \(G(x)\equiv(x=0\lor x=2)\). Both endpoints have support, but the interior value 1 has none. Thus endpoint support does not imply domain consistency when the supported-value set is not an interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relation supporting only the endpoints shows why interval-convex support is necessary.
assumptions_latex: Bounds support means support for the current endpoints.
knowledge_statements.title: Supported Endpoints Need Not Fill an Interior Hole
Interval-Structure Exploitation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: When each coordinate’s supported values form an interval, endpoint support suffices for full domain consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each ordered finite domain be an integer interval \(D_i=[l_i,u_i]\cap\mathbb Z\), and define the supported-value set \[S_i=\{a\in D_i:\exists v\in D_1\times\cdots\times D_n,\ v_i=a\ \land\ G(v)\}.\] Assume every nonempty \(S_i\) is an integer interval. Then support for both endpoints \(l_i\) and \(u_i\) implies \(S_i=D_i\). Therefore, under this interval-support property, bounds consistency and domain consistency coincide. Conversely, without interval support sets, supported endpoints do not exclude unsupported interior holes, so endpoint filtering alone cannot establish domain consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If supported values are contiguous in every ordered domain, supporting both endpoints supports every interior value; bounds and domain consistency then coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(D_i=[l_i,u_i]\cap\mathbb Z\) for every coordinate.
Every supported-value set \(S_i\) is empty or an integer interval.

notation.meaning: values of coordinate i having a global support

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pruning hierarchy for the two common endpoint-support conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let bounds(D) require each current endpoint to have a support in the actual current domains, and let bounds(Z) permit every nonfixed coordinate to range over its integer hull. For one finite ordered global relation, domain consistency implies bounds(D), and bounds(D) implies bounds(Z). Consequently their contracting closures from the same state satisfy \(D^{\mathrm{DC}}\subseteq D^{\mathrm{B(D)}}\subseteq D^{\mathrm{B(Z)}}\subseteq D\). Any inclusion may be strict when unsupported nonendpoint values or domain holes are present. This logical strength ordering alone gives no universal runtime ordering between propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After fixing the endpoint-support convention, domain consistency dominates bounds(D), which dominates hull-based bounds(Z); runtime remains algorithm-dependent.
assumptions_latex: All current domains are finite subsets of an ordered integer universe.
Every closure is computed for the same native relation and initial domains.
Each propagator is sound and reaches its stated consistency closure.

notation.meaning: Closure under endpoint support using actual domains.
Closure under endpoint support using integer hulls.

knowledge_statements.title: Convention-Fixed Domain–Bounds Hierarchy
Bounds Strength–Cost Frontier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal pruning hierarchy and representation-dependent computational tradeoff for global-constraint filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite ordered-domain global constraint, let \(D^{\mathrm{DC}}\) and \(D^{\mathrm{BC}}\) be the closures obtained by domain-consistency and bounds-consistency filtering from the same domains \(D\). Every domain-consistent state is bounds consistent, hence \[D^{\mathrm{DC}}\subseteq D^{\mathrm{BC}}\subseteq D.\] The first inclusion can be strict when an interior value lacks support while both current endpoints have supports. Thus domain consistency never prunes less than bounds consistency, but this ordering alone implies no universal runtime ordering: enforcement cost depends on the global relation’s representation and available algorithm. Bounds filtering occupies a distinct strength–cost point by testing extremal support rather than support for every value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domain consistency dominates bounds consistency in pruning, sometimes strictly; computational cost remains constraint- and representation-dependent.
assumptions_latex: Domains are finite and ordered.
Both closures use the same native global relation and initial domains.
Each filtering procedure is sound and reaches its stated consistency closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^{\mathrm{DC}}\subseteq D^{\mathrm{BC}}\subseteq D\), with possible strict first inclusion.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: support for every value implies support for extremal values

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive witness for retaining a value under native domain-consistency filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A certificate that \(a\in D_i\) is supported for a relation \(C\) is a tuple \(x\in C\cap\prod_jD_j\) with \(x_i=a\). Verification checks current-domain membership, satisfaction of \(C\), and the distinguished equality \(x_i=a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete satisfying tuple containing a candidate value certifies that native filtering must retain it.
assumptions_latex: Satisfaction of C by a supplied tuple is decidable in the chosen representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Tuple Support Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic Properties of Native Domain Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure properties of exact support projection for one finite-domain relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed finite relation \(C\), its native domain-consistency operator \(F_C\) is contracting, monotone under componentwise domain inclusion, and idempotent: \(F_C(D)\subseteq D\), \(D\subseteq E\Rightarrow F_C(D)\subseteq F_C(E)\), and \(F_C(F_C(D))=F_C(D)\). It reports failure exactly when \(C\cap\prod_iD_i=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact native filtering is contracting, monotone, idempotent, and detects failure exactly when no satisfying tuple remains.
assumptions_latex: C is fixed and every current domain is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_C\circ F_C=F_C,\quad F_C(D)\subseteq D,\quad D\subseteq E\Rightarrow F_C(D)\subseteq F_C(E).
knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Properties of Native Domain Filtering
Native Global Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain-consistency filtering applied directly to one finite-domain global constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq \prod_{i=1}^n D_i\) be a constraint relation. Its native domain-consistency filter is the operator \(F_C\) defined componentwise by \[F_C(D)_i=\{a\in D_i:\exists x\in C\text{ with }x_i=a\text{ and }x_j\in D_j\text{ for every }j\}.\] The filter reports failure exactly when some \(F_C(D)_i\) is empty, and otherwise removes precisely the values having no support in a complete tuple of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Native global filtering retains exactly those domain values extendable to a complete satisfying tuple of the global constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(n\geq 1\) and every \(D_i\) is finite.
\(C\) is interpreted over the current Cartesian product of domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_C(D)\) is the strongest sound value-deletion operator determined solely by supports in \(C\).

notation.meaning: Native domain-consistency filtering operator for C.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Native Global Filtering leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no source or inspectable locator supports the domain-consistency definition or strongest-filter conclusion.

children.title: Decomposition-Based Filtering
children.top_down_role: Filtering obtained through a network of simpler component constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why componentwise domain supports need not establish support in the represented global relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a common fixpoint of component domain-consistency filters, a value \(a\in D(X_i)\) may have a supporting tuple in every incident component without any single assignment to shared and auxiliary variables satisfying all components simultaneously. Componentwise support certifies global support only when the local supports can be joined consistently on every shared variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate component supports do not establish global support unless they combine into one consistent assignment.
assumptions_latex: The global relation is the existential projection of the component conjunction.
Every component is domain consistent at the considered store.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\forall k\ni X_i,\ a\text{ has support in }C_k\right)\not\Rightarrow a\text{ has support in }\bigwedge_k C_k.

notation.meaning: Candidate value of an original variable.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Support Compatibility Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of adding sound redundant component filters to a decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F'\supseteq\mathcal F\) be finite families of contracting, monotone, solution-preserving filters, with the added filters enforcing constraints entailed by the represented global relation. On a finite domain-store lattice, their greatest common fixpoints below the same input satisfy \(D^*_{\mathcal F'}\subseteq D^*_{\mathcal F}\). Adding redundant components therefore cannot weaken fixpoint pruning or remove a represented solution, although it may increase propagation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding sound redundant components can only preserve or strengthen common-fixpoint pruning, but may cost more.
assumptions_latex: All component filters are contracting, monotone, and solution preserving.
Every added constraint is entailed by the represented global relation.
The domain-store lattice below the input is finite.

notation.meaning: Greatest common fixpoint below the input for filter family F.

knowledge_statements.title: Strengthening by Redundant Components
Decomposition-Based Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Filtering obtained by propagating a conjunction that represents the global constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a constraint \(C(X)\) is represented by \(\exists Y\,\bigwedge_{k=1}^m C_k(X,Y)\), where \(Y\) are auxiliary variables. Decomposition-based filtering applies a chosen local filter \(F_k\) to each \(C_k\) until a common fixpoint is reached, then projects the surviving domains onto \(X\). The resulting operator is sound for \(C\), but it need not equal native domain-consistency filtering because local supports for different \(C_k\) may be mutually incompatible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decomposition-based filtering repeatedly propagates component constraints and projects the fixpoint onto the original variables; it may retain globally unsupported values.
assumptions_latex: \(C(X)\iff \exists Y\,\bigwedge_{k=1}^m C_k(X,Y)\).
Every component operator \(F_k\) is contracting and sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projected fixpoint contains every solution of \(C\) within the initial domains.

notation.meaning: Auxiliary variables introduced by the decomposition.
Local filtering operator for component constraint k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the decomposition-based filtering leaf, but the fixpoint and projection claims require an authoritative propagation source specifying the iteration semantics and sufficient operator conditions.

children.title: Filtering-Strength Gaps
children.top_down_role: Pruning differences between native versus decomposed representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic comparison of sound filters for the same projected relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For filters \(F\) and \(G\) on comparable domain stores, \(F\) is at least as strong as \(G\) when \(F(D)_i\subseteq G(D)_i\) for every input store \(D\) and variable \(i\). Dominance is strict when the inclusion is strict for some \((D,i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One filter dominates another when it retains no more values on every input; a strict gap occurs when it retains fewer values somewhere.
assumptions_latex: F and G act on comparable stores and are sound for the same projected relation.

notation.meaning: F is at least as strong as G.

knowledge_statements.title: Filtering Dominance and Strict Gap

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semantic Equivalence Does Not Imply Propagation Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between equality of complete solutions and equality of filtering behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The identity \(C(X)\iff\exists Y\,\bigwedge_k C_k(X,Y)\) guarantees equality of complete assignments to \(X\), but does not guarantee equality of native and decomposed filters on partial domain stores. Equality of filters additionally requires the projected component fixpoint to remove every value lacking a complete tuple of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Representations with identical complete solutions may prune differently on partial domains.
assumptions_latex: The decomposition is semantically exact.
Native filtering enforces domain consistency, while the components enforce only their selected local consistencies.
knowledge_statements.title: Semantic Equivalence Does Not Imply Propagation Equivalence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Native Domain Consistency Dominates Sound Decomposition Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General strength relation for an exact decomposition of a finite-domain relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C(X)\iff\exists Y\,\bigwedge_k C_k(X,Y)\), let \(G(D)\) be the projection of any solution-preserving component-propagation result initialized from \(D\), and let \(F_C(D)\) be native domain-consistency filtering. Then \(F_C(D)_i\subseteq G(D)_i\) for every original variable \(X_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact native domain filtering cannot be weaker than a sound projected decomposition filter.
assumptions_latex: The component conjunction existentially projects exactly to C.
Component propagation preserves every solution represented by the input store.
F_C enforces domain consistency for C.
knowledge_statements.title: Native Domain Consistency Dominates Sound Decomposition Filtering
Filtering-Strength Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict propagation gap between AllDifferent and its pairwise disequality decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_1,X_2,X_3\) have identical domains \(D_i=\{1,2\}\). Every binary constraint \(X_i\neq X_j\) is arc consistent: each value of either variable has the other value as a support. Hence propagation of all three binary disequalities deletes nothing. The global constraint \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(X_1,X_2,X_3)\), however, has no satisfying tuple because three variables must take distinct values from a two-element set, so native domain-consistency filtering detects failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three variables over two values defeat AllDifferent immediately, while every pairwise disequality remains arc consistent and performs no pruning.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pairwise arc consistency is strictly weaker than native domain consistency for \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is correct and well matched to Filtering-Strength Gaps, but the record supplies no source or locator for the strict separation between global domain consistency and pairwise arc consistency.

children.title: Propagation Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Constraint classes or decompositions yielding equivalent propagation strength.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient store-wise equality condition for native and exact-decomposition filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(D)\) be the projected common fixpoint of solution-preserving filters for an exact decomposition of \(C\), and let \(F_C(D)\) enforce native domain consistency. Then \(G(D)=F_C(D)\) if and only if every \(a\in G(D)_i\) extends to some \(x\in C\cap\prod_jG(D)_j\) with \(x_i=a\). The filters are equivalent on a class of stores exactly when this condition holds on every store in the class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Native and decomposed filtering coincide exactly when every value surviving decomposition propagation has a complete global support.
assumptions_latex: The decomposition existentially projects exactly to C.
G is solution preserving and F_C enforces domain consistency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G(D)=F_C(D)\iff G(D)\text{ is domain consistent for }C.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Propagation-Equivalence Criterion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching Criterion for Pairwise AllDifferent Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact nonfailure criterion for equality between native AllDifferent filtering and arc consistency on pairwise disequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After arc consistency on all \(X_i\ne X_j\) reaches a nonfailure fixpoint, form the bipartite variable-value graph with edge \((X_i,a)\) for every remaining \(a\in D_i\). Pairwise propagation and native domain-consistency filtering for \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}\) retain the same domains exactly when every remaining edge belongs to a matching saturating all variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a nonfailed pairwise fixpoint, equality with native AllDifferent filtering holds exactly when every remaining variable-value edge extends to a full matching.
assumptions_latex: All domains are finite.
The pairwise disequalities have reached an arc-consistent nonfailure fixpoint.

notation.meaning: Edges of the variable-value graph after pairwise propagation.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching Criterion for Pairwise AllDifferent Equivalence
Propagation Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simple regimes where native AllDifferent filtering and pairwise propagation coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\), native domain-consistency filtering and arc-consistency propagation of all pairwise disequalities have the same fixpoint whenever either \(n\leq 2\) or the current domains are pairwise disjoint. In the first regime the global constraint is itself at most one disequality. In the second, every current value already has a global support formed by independently selecting one value from each disjoint domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Native and pairwise filtering coincide for at most two variables and when all current domains are pairwise disjoint.
assumptions_latex: Every variable has a finite nonempty domain.
Either \(n\leq 2\), or \(D_i\cap D_j=\varnothing\) for all \(i\neq j\).

notation.meaning: Fixpoint of arc consistency on all binary disequalities.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated equivalence regimes are mathematically plausible and fit the property container, but no cited source with a specific locator supports them.

children.title: Decomposition Overhead Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation settings where decomposition introduces material propagation cost.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation-scheduler overhead for a finite explicit decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\delta_v\) be the number of values deleted from variable \(v\). If every component is initially enqueued and a component is subsequently enqueued only after a deletion from a variable in its scope, the number of enqueue events is at most \(m+\sum_v\deg(v)\delta_v\). Since contracting propagation gives \(\delta_v\le |D_v^{(0)}|\), dense incidence can cause substantial scheduling overhead even when component execution itself is inexpensive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each deletion can reactivate every incident component, so dense component-variable incidence creates propagation overhead separate from propagator runtime.
assumptions_latex: All initial domains are finite.
Component filters are contracting.
A deletion triggers at most one enqueue event for each incident component under the accounting convention.

notation.meaning: Number of component constraints incident to variable v.
Number of values deleted from v.

knowledge_statements.title: Deletion-Triggered Reactivation Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation overhead intrinsic to explicitly stored component scopes and auxiliary domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an explicitly represented decomposition \(C(X)\iff\exists Y\,\bigwedge_{k=1}^m C_k\), storing its component records, scope incidences, and explicit auxiliary-domain entries requires \(\Omega\!\left(m+\sum_{k=1}^m|\operatorname{scope}(C_k)|+\operatorname{size}(Y)\right)\) space. Thus superlinear growth of any of these quantities relative to the native input imposes corresponding superlinear representation and initialization overhead, independently of filtering strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit decomposition must store its components, scope incidences, and auxiliary domains, so superlinear growth in these data creates matching representation overhead.
assumptions_latex: The decomposition, component scopes, and auxiliary domains are stored explicitly.
Each component record, scope incidence, and represented domain entry requires constant administrative space.

notation.meaning: Auxiliary variables with explicitly represented domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit-Decomposition Storage Lower Bound
Decomposition Overhead Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-size and naive propagation costs of the complete pairwise decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The explicit binary-disequality decomposition of an \(n\)-variable AllDifferent constraint contains exactly \(\binom{n}{2}\) constraints and therefore requires \(\Theta(n^2)\) propagator records or scheduled constraint incidences. If every domain has size at most \(d\) and binary arc revision tests value pairs without specialized indexing, one complete revision sweep costs \(O(n^2d^2)\) support tests. Thus the decomposition has an unavoidable quadratic representation boundary even when individual disequalities are inexpensive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complete pairwise decomposition has quadratic size; naive full arc revision can require quadratic domain-pair work per constraint sweep.
assumptions_latex: \(n\) variables are connected by one disequality for every unordered pair.
Each domain has cardinality at most \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representation cost is \(\Theta(n^2)\), and a naive sweep uses \(O(n^2d^2)\) support tests.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quadratic constraint count is immediate, but the propagator-record, scheduling-incidence, and support-test bounds depend on a computational model that is neither fully specified nor sourced.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: A Filtering Algorithm for Constraints of Difference in CSPs
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Matching-based generalized arc-consistency filtering
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: A Filtering Algorithm for Constraints of Difference in CSPs

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Consistency levels and filtering families
Conforti, Cornuéjols, and Zambelli, Chapter 4.4: Matchings in Graphs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint count and explicit representation size of the pairwise-disequality encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The decomposition of \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) contains one disequality for every unordered variable pair, hence exactly \(\binom n2\) binary constraints. Its explicit constraint-incidence representation therefore has \(\Theta(n^2)\) constraint entries, excluding storage for the variable domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pairwise encoding uses exactly n choose 2 disequalities and has quadratic explicit size.
assumptions_latex: Each unordered pair is represented by one explicit binary disequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Decomposition Size

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational characterization of arc consistency on the binary-disequality decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a binary disequality \(X_i\ne X_j\), a value \(a\in D_i\) lacks support in \(D_j\) exactly when \(D_j=\{a\}\). Consequently, arc consistency on \(\bigwedge_{i<j}(X_i\ne X_j)\) repeatedly removes a fixed value from every other domain and reports failure if a domain becomes empty. If every domain initially has cardinality at least two, the decomposition is already arc consistent and performs no deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arc consistency on pairwise disequalities is singleton propagation: a value is removed from other domains only after some variable is fixed to it.
assumptions_latex: All domains are finite.
Every binary disequality is enforced to arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a\in D_i\text{ is unsupported by }X_i\ne X_j\Longleftrightarrow D_j=\{a\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Arc-Consistency Closure of Pairwise Disequalities
Binary-Disequality Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solution-equivalent binary representation of the finite-domain AllDifferent constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\), the AllDifferent constraint has the representation \[\operatorname{AllDifferent}(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\bigwedge_{1\leq i<j\leq n}(X_i\neq X_j).\] This equivalence concerns satisfying assignments: a tuple satisfies the global constraint exactly when every pair of components differs. It does not imply propagation equivalence between domain consistency on the global relation and arc consistency on the binary constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AllDifferent is solution-equivalent to all pairwise disequalities, although propagation on the two representations can have different strength.
assumptions_latex: \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) range over arbitrary domains with equality defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two formulations have identical satisfying assignments on \((X_1,\ldots,X_n)\).

notation.meaning: Constraint requiring pairwise distinct variable values.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and its warning about nonequivalent propagation fit the leaf and are mathematically correct, but the candidate contains no inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Solution Equivalence Does Not Preserve Propagation Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed witness comparing the decomposition with global domain filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_1=D_2=\{1,2\}\) and \(D_3=\{1,2,3\}\). Every pairwise disequality is arc consistent, whereas domain-consistent global filtering forces \(D_3=\{3\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hall-set instance separates global domain filtering from binary arc consistency.
assumptions_latex: AllDifferent is imposed on the displayed domains.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution Equivalence Does Not Preserve Propagation Strength

intermediate_metadata.reason: This leaf owns the exact pairwise representation, its quadratic size, and singleton-based arc-consistency behavior. The builder's Hall-set counterexample is deferred because comparison with global filters is primarily owned by AllDifferent Strength–Cost Frontier. Matching, range, bounds, and cross-method cost results are likewise excluded to sibling scopes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision procedure for finite-domain AllDifferent feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute a maximum matching \(M\) in the bipartite value graph \(G=(X\cup V,E)\). The constraint is feasible exactly when \(|M|=|X|\). Hopcroft--Karp computes \(M\) in \(O(|E|\sqrt{|X|+|V|})\) time, and an \(X\)-covering matching directly specifies a satisfying assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximum matching decides AllDifferent feasibility, and a covering matching supplies a satisfying assignment.
assumptions_latex: The variable-value graph is finite.

notation.meaning: Maximum matching in the value graph.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Matching Feasibility Test
Matching-Based Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite-matching characterization of finite-domain AllDifferent feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct the bipartite value graph \(G=(X\cup V,E)\), where \((X_i,v)\in E\) exactly when \(v\in D_i\). The constraint \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) is feasible if and only if \(G\) has a matching covering every vertex of \(X\). Equivalently, feasibility holds if and only if Hall's inequalities \(\lvert N(S)\rvert\geq \lvert S\rvert\) hold for every \(S\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AllDifferent is feasible exactly when its variable-value graph has a matching covering all variables, equivalently when every variable subset satisfies Hall's inequality.
assumptions_latex: Every \(D_i\) is finite.
\(V=\bigcup_{i=1}^n D_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) is feasible if and only if \(G\) admits an \(X\)-covering matching.

notation.meaning: Value vertices adjacent to variables in S.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The matching and Hall characterizations are standard and correctly stated for finite domains, but no specific theorem, section, or page locator is cited.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating Witnesses for Retained Unmatched Edges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable support witnesses underlying alternating-graph edge retention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) cover every variable vertex, and orient unmatched edges from values to variables and matched edges from variables to values. For an unmatched edge \(e=(X_i,v)\), either a directed alternating cycle containing \(e\), or reachability of \(v\) from a value vertex free in \(M\), yields an explicit \(M\)-alternating exchange that produces an \(X\)-covering matching containing \(e\). Thus the cycle or directed reachability path, together with the matched edge incident to \(X_i\), is a checkable support certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating cycle or a directed path from a free value certifies that an unmatched domain edge belongs to a variable-covering matching.
assumptions_latex: M is an X-covering matching in a finite bipartite value graph.
Matched edges are oriented variable-to-value and unmatched edges value-to-variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e\text{ has the stated alternating witness}\Rightarrow\exists M'\text{ covering }X\text{ with }e\in M'.

notation.meaning: Reference matching covering every variable vertex
Covering matching obtained by alternating exchange

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Witnesses for Retained Unmatched Edges

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost of reachability, strongly connected components, and edge deletion once a covering matching is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the value graph have \(N\) vertices and \(E\) edges, and suppose an \(X\)-covering matching is supplied. Constructing the oriented alternating graph, marking vertices reachable from free value vertices, computing strongly connected components, and testing every edge against the resulting labels take \(O(N+E)\) time and \(O(N+E)\) space with adjacency lists. This excludes the cost of finding or repairing the matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After a covering matching is known, the alternating-graph support pass is linear in the value graph size.
assumptions_latex: The finite value graph is represented by adjacency lists.
An X-covering matching is supplied.
Linear-time traversal and strongly connected-component algorithms are used.

notation.meaning: Total number of variable and value vertices

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Postmatching Alternating-Graph Pass
Alternating-Graph Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Régin-style support deletion after obtaining a variable-covering matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an \(X\)-covering matching \(M\) in the value graph, direct each matched edge from its variable to its value and each unmatched edge from its value to its variable. Mark vertices reachable from unmatched value vertices and compute strongly connected components. Retain every edge in \(M\). An unmatched edge \((X_i,v)\) is retained exactly when \(v\) is marked or \(v\) and \(X_i\) lie in the same strongly connected component; otherwise delete \(v\) from \(D_i\). Output the reduced domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A covering matching plus reachability and strongly connected components identifies exactly the value edges belonging to some covering matching.
assumptions_latex: The finite value graph has an \(X\)-covering matching \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The retained edge \((X_i,v)\) exists exactly when some \(X\)-covering matching contains that edge.

notation.meaning: A matching covering all variable vertices.
Current domain represented by edges incident to variable i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm has the appropriate role and broadly matches Régin-style filtering, but its precise directed-graph orientation and edge-retention characterization require an inspectable authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cost of One Decremental Matching Repair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case cost of repairing one invalidated matching edge, excluding support-graph maintenance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If one deleted matching edge exposes one variable, one alternating-path search and at most one augmentation either restore an \(X\)-covering matching or establish that none remains. With adjacency lists, the repair takes \(O(|X|+|V|+|E|)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single matched-edge deletion needs one linear-time alternating-path search and at most one augmentation.
assumptions_latex: Exactly one edge of the maintained matching was deleted.
The current value graph uses adjacency lists.
knowledge_statements.title: Cost of One Decremental Matching Repair

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Update Monotonicity for a Stored Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which graph updates invalidate a stored covering matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every \(X\)-covering matching \(M\) remains valid after domain-edge insertions. After deletions, \(M\) remains valid exactly when no edge of \(M\) was deleted. Insertions cannot destroy feasibility, but insertions and deletions can both change which assignment edges belong to some \(X\)-covering matching and can therefore require support-information refresh.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Insertions preserve the stored matching; deletions require repair only when they remove a matched edge, although either update can change filtering supports.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite variable-value graph.
\(M\) is an \(X\)-covering matching before the update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\subseteq E(G')\iff M\text{ remains an }X\text{-covering matching of }G'.
knowledge_statements.title: Update Monotonicity for a Stored Matching
Incremental Matching Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maintaining AllDifferent feasibility and filtering after domain-edge deletions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an \(X\)-covering matching \(M\) across propagation events. Delete removed domain edges from the value graph. If no deleted edge belongs to \(M\), retain \(M\); otherwise the affected variable becomes exposed, and an alternating-path search attempts to reach an unmatched value. Augment along a found path to restore an \(X\)-covering matching; if none exists, report failure. After restoration, update alternating reachability and component information and delete edges not belonging to any covering matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incremental variants repair a stored matching only when deletions invalidate it, then update alternating-graph support information or report failure.
assumptions_latex: The previous value graph has a stored \(X\)-covering matching.
The update consists only of domain-edge deletions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure either restores a valid covering matching and domain-consistent filtering state or correctly detects infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Noninterval Hall Sets Are Invisible to Hull-Interval Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limitation of Hall-interval reasoning relative to exact-domain Hall-set reasoning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_1=D_2=\{1,3\}\) and \(D_3=\{1,2,3\}\). The noninterval value set \(\{1,3\}\) is reserved for \(x_1,x_2\), so domain consistency forces \(x_3=2\). All three hulls equal \([1,3]\), however, and no proper integer interval contains the hulls of \(x_1,x_2\). Hull-based Hall-interval filtering therefore need not delete 1 or 3 from \(D_3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domain holes can form a Hall set invisible to hull-interval tests, making interval filtering weaker than exact-domain filtering.
assumptions_latex: Hall-interval tests use integer hulls.
knowledge_statements.title: Noninterval Hall Sets Are Invisible to Hull-Interval Tests

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local interval terminology for AllDifferent filtering over domain hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite nonempty integer domains \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\), let \(H_i=[\min D_i,\max D_i]\cap\mathbb Z\) and \(S_I=\{i:H_i\subseteq I\}\) for an integer interval \(I\). The interval is overloaded when \(|S_I|>|I|\) and is a Hall interval when \(|S_I|=|I|\). An overloaded interval certifies infeasibility. For a Hall interval, every distinct assignment of the variables in \(S_I\) uses every value of \(I\), so those values are unavailable to variables outside \(S_I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hall interval contains exactly as many variable hulls as values; an overloaded interval contains too many hulls and certifies failure.
assumptions_latex: Every domain is finite and nonempty.
AllDifferent requires pairwise-distinct assigned values.
Interval tests use each domain's integer hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |S_I|>|I|\Rightarrow\operatorname{AllDifferent}\text{ is infeasible};\quad |S_I|=|I|\Rightarrow I\text{ is reserved for }S_I.

notation.meaning: Integer interval hull of domain i
Variables whose hulls are contained in I

knowledge_statements.title: Hall and Overloaded Integer Intervals
Hall-Interval Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hall-set propagation specialized to integer intervals for AllDifferent bounds filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every integer interval \(I=[a,b]\cap\mathbb Z\), form \(S_I=\{i:D_i\subseteq I\}\). If \(\lvert S_I\rvert>\lvert I\rvert=b-a+1\), report failure. If equality holds, \(I\) is a Hall interval: for every \(j\notin S_I\), remove \(I\) from the lower or upper boundary of \(D_j\) whenever that removal tightens a bound. Repeat these tests and bound updates to a fixpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An overloaded interval proves failure; a saturated Hall interval reserves its values for contained variables and excludes those values from other variables' bounds.
assumptions_latex: Each \(D_i\) is represented by a finite integer interval or its interval hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every reported failure is valid, and every bound deletion preserves all solutions of \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}\).

notation.meaning: Variables whose domains are contained in I.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits Hall-Interval Filtering, but the phrase “interval or its interval hull” blends distinct domain representations, and a source is needed to establish the exact bounds-consistency convention and update rule.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Apply the order-reversing bijection \(v\mapsto -v\) to every domain. Puget Bounds-Filtering Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hall-interval characterization underlying bounds-consistent AllDifferent propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite integer domains represented by their bounds, AllDifferent bounds filtering is characterized by interval Hall tests. Every interval \(I\) must satisfy \(\lvert S_I\rvert\leq\lvert I\rvert\), where \(S_I=\{i:[\min D_i,\max D_i]\subseteq I\}\). Whenever equality holds, the values of \(I\) are reserved for \(S_I\), so any other variable whose lower or upper bound lies in \(I\) must have that bound moved beyond \(I\). Iterating these rules yields the bounds-consistency closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Puget-style bounds filtering detects overloaded intervals and uses saturated Hall intervals to move unsupported lower and upper bounds.
assumptions_latex: Every variable has a finite nonempty integer domain.
Filtering reasons over each domain's interval hull.

Sorting and storing the endpoint list costs \(O(n\log n)\) time and \(O(n)\) auxiliary space and does not increase the cubic pass bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Termination of Repeated Bound Tightening
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination condition for a sorted-bounds procedure iterated after successful integer-bound updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the initial nonempty integer hull of variable \(i\) be \([l_i^0,u_i^0]\). If every continuing round strictly increases some lower bound or strictly decreases some upper bound and no hull is enlarged, then the total hull width decreases by at least one per successful round. Hence there are at most \(\sum_i(u_i^0-l_i^0)\) successful rounds before stability or failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Monotone integer-bound tightening terminates because total hull width decreases after every successful round.
assumptions_latex: All initial bounds are finite integers.
Bounds are only tightened.
Every continuing round performs at least one strict bound change.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Termination of Repeated Bound Tightening
Sorted Bounds Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Batch bounds filtering by sorting interval endpoints before Hall scans.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input finite integer bounds \((l_i,u_i)\) for \(n\) variables. Sort the distinct lower and upper endpoints, and scan candidate intervals \(I=[a,b]\cap\mathbb Z\) whose endpoints occur among these bounds. For each interval compute \(S_I=\{i:l_i\geq a,\ u_i\leq b\}\). Report failure if \(\lvert S_I\rvert>b-a+1\). If equality holds, raise any external lower bound lying in \(I\) to \(b+1\) and lower any external upper bound lying in \(I\) to \(a-1\). Re-sort changed bounds and iterate to a fixpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort bounds, scan endpoint-defined intervals for overload or saturation, apply Hall-interval bound updates, and repeat until stable.
assumptions_latex: Each variable is represented by integer bounds \(l_i\leq u_i\).
Candidate intervals use distinct current bound endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the Hall-interval bounds-filtering fixpoint, or failure if an interval is overloaded.

children.top_down_role: AllDifferent bounds filtering that reuses state across domain changes.

assumptions_latex: The current domains are nonempty integer intervals \(D_i=[\ell_i,u_i]\cap\mathbb Z\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\).
Propagation events only tighten lower or upper bounds.

notation.meaning: Current interval domain of variable i
Set of variables whose domains lie inside interval I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-driven bounds-consistency propagation for interval-domain AllDifferent constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a queue containing every variable whose bound changed. When \(i\) is dequeued, update the endpoint order and reconsider only intervals \(I=[a,b]\cap\mathbb Z\) whose Hall count may have changed. If \(|H(I)|>|I|\), report failure. If \(|H(I)|=|I|\), then for every \(j\notin H(I)\), replace \(D_j\) by its smallest interval obtained by deleting \(I\) from either exposed end; enqueue \(j\) whenever this tightens \(\ell_j\) or \(u_j\). Continue until the queue is empty. The output is the common fixpoint of these Hall-interval bound reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process only changed bounds, update affected Hall intervals, detect overloaded intervals, and trim saturated Hall intervals from other variables until no bound changes remain.
knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Bounds Filtering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the leaf, but no source is cited. The claim that reconsidering only intervals whose Hall count may have changed reaches the common Hall-interval fixpoint requires a precise incremental invariant and an authoritative algorithm locator.

children.title: Incremental Sorting Reuse
children.top_down_role: Retention of ordering information across successive filtering calls.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maintenance of sorted lower- and upper-bound endpoint orders across monotone propagation rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain lower-bound keys \((\ell_i,i)\) and upper-bound keys \((u_i,i)\) in ordered structures, using the variable identifier to break ties. When an endpoint changes, delete its old key and insert its new key. Equivalently, under monotone tightening, move a changed lower bound rightward and a changed upper bound leftward until local order is restored. The resulting orders are exactly those obtained by sorting all current keys from scratch with the same tie rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reposition only changed endpoints while retaining deterministic sorted orders equivalent to fresh sorting.
assumptions_latex: Bounds change monotonically by tightening.
Keys use a stable deterministic tie breaker.
Every changed endpoint is reported to the maintenance mechanism.
knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Endpoint-Order Reuse

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Data-structure cost for exact endpoint-order reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If lower- and upper-bound keys are stored in balanced ordered sets, initial construction costs \(O(n\log n)\). When endpoints of \(k\) variables change, deleting old keys and inserting new keys costs \(O(k\log n)\); enumerating either complete order for a filtering scan costs \(O(n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balanced ordered sets update endpoint orders in logarithmic time per changed variable, with linear time for a full scan.
assumptions_latex: Ordered-set insertion and deletion cost O(\log n) worst-case.
Each changed variable has at most one maintained lower key and one maintained upper key.

notation.meaning: number of variables with changed endpoints

knowledge_statements.title: Balanced-Order Update Cost

assumptions_latex: Bounds are stored in ordered structures keyed by value and a stable variable identifier.
A propagation round changes bounds of exactly \(k\) among \(n\) variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reuse of endpoint orders between monotone bounds-filtering rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(L\) and \(U\) by sorting \((\ell_i,i)\) and \((u_i,i)\), respectively. After a propagation round, remove each changed key from its maintained order and reinsert its new key using the same deterministic tie rule; unchanged keys retain their relative order. Equivalently, a monotone specialized implementation may move a tightened lower bound rightward and a tightened upper bound leftward until local order is restored. Return the updated \(L\) and \(U\) to the bounds-filtering scan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain sorted endpoint orders across propagation rounds by repositioning only changed bounds while preserving a deterministic order among ties.

children.title: Reordering Cost Regimes
children.top_down_role: Domain-update patterns governing the cost of maintaining sorted information.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Comparison Lower Bound for Rebuilding Endpoint Order
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case comparison cost when no endpoint ordering is retained between filtering rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\) pairwise-distinct endpoint keys be arbitrarily permuted at the beginning of a filtering round. Any comparison-based procedure required to reconstruct their complete sorted order uses \(\Omega(m\log m)\) comparisons in the worst case. Thus rebuilding the order of the \(2n\) lower and upper endpoints from no retained ordering information costs \(\Omega(n\log n)\) comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discarding all endpoint-order information forces an n log n worst-case comparison cost to reconstruct the complete order.
assumptions_latex: Endpoint keys are ordered solely through comparisons.
No ordering information from the preceding round is retained.
The required output determines the complete endpoint order.
knowledge_statements.title: Comparison Lower Bound for Rebuilding Endpoint Order

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental endpoint reordering when endpoint records retain handles into a balanced ordered structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Store the \(m=2n\) endpoint records in a balanced comparison-search tree and retain a handle for every record. Deleting and reinserting each of \(k\) endpoints whose key changed takes \(O(k\log m)=O(k\log n)\) time, while the tree and handles use \(O(n)\) space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With retained handles, a balanced ordered tree supports k changed endpoints in k log n time and linear space.
assumptions_latex: A handle identifies the stored record for every endpoint.
Each changed endpoint is deleted and reinserted in a balanced comparison-search tree.
At most k endpoint keys change during the round.
knowledge_statements.title: Handle-Based Balanced-Tree Update Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Changed-Endpoint Count Alone Does Not Determine Reordering Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on adaptive cost claims parameterized only by the number of changed endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Knowing only that \(k\) of \(m\) endpoint keys changed does not imply an \(O(k)\) update. If the old sorted order is retained but changed records have no handles, locating them may require \(\Omega(m)\) work. With handles and an array representation, one changed key can still require \(\Omega(m)\) element moves after its new position is found. If the old order is discarded, the complete rebuilding lower bound applies. Adaptive bounds therefore require an explicit retained-state representation and a parameter controlling displacement or the affected ordered region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Few changed endpoints do not by themselves guarantee cheap reordering; the retained representation and displacement determine the work.
assumptions_latex: Only the count k of changed keys is specified.
Retained handles, storage representation, and key displacement are otherwise unspecified.
knowledge_statements.title: Changed-Endpoint Count Alone Does Not Determine Reordering Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive reordering cost when endpoint records and their current order are retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Retain the endpoint records in a comparison-ordered linked sequence with a handle to every record. After \(k\) keys change, restore sorted order by swapping each affected record with adjacent inverted neighbors until no affected inversion remains. If \(\Delta\) is the total number of adjacent record crossings performed, the repair uses \(O(k+\Delta)\) comparisons and pointer updates and \(O(n)\) storage. Since \(\Delta\) may be \(\Theta(kn)\), the bound is linear only when displacement is correspondingly bounded; in particular, it is \(O(n+k)\) when \(\Delta=O(n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With retained handles and linked order, adjacent repair costs the number of changed endpoints plus their total rank displacement.
assumptions_latex: Endpoint keys use a fixed total comparison order with deterministic tie breaking.
A handle identifies every changed endpoint record in constant time.
Adjacent comparisons, swaps, and linked-sequence updates take constant time.
\(\Delta\) counts all adjacent crossings performed while restoring order.

notation.meaning: total adjacent displacement during order repair

knowledge_statements.title: Displacement-Sensitive Adjacent-Repair Bound

assumptions_latex: Endpoint values are compared in the comparison model.
A round changes \(k\) endpoints among \(2n\) stored endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rebuilding costs \(O(n\log n)\), balanced-tree updates cost \(O(k\log n)\), and order-preserving scans cost \(O(n+k)\) when monotonicity permits them.

notation.meaning: Number of changed endpoints in one round

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison-model costs for rebuilding or incrementally maintaining sorted bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If endpoint orders are discarded after every round, comparison sorting requires \(O(n\log n)\) comparisons. If each order is maintained by a balanced search tree with handles, deleting and reinserting the \(k\) changed endpoints requires \(O(k\log n)\) time and \(O(n)\) storage. If tightening is monotone and an implementation restores order by a linear merge or bucket scan over the affected ordered region, the round costs \(O(n+k)\). Thus incremental reuse is asymptotically preferable when \(k=o(n)\) under tree maintenance, while full rebuilding remains competitive when most endpoints change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full sorting costs n log n; balanced incremental updates cost k log n; monotone scan-based reordering can cost n plus k.
knowledge_statements.title: Reordering Cost Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the leaf. The rebuilding and balanced-tree bounds are standard, but the claimed O(n+k) scan regime needs a precise data structure, affected-region assumption, and authoritative locator; monotonicity alone does not establish that bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval criterion for AllDifferent range consistency under the hull-support convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_i\) be finite nonempty integer domains and \(R_i=[\min D_i,\max D_i]\cap\mathbb Z\). The AllDifferent constraint is range consistent if and only if every integer interval \(I\) satisfies \(|S_I|\le |I|\), where \(S_I=\{i:R_i\subseteq I\}\), and whenever \(|S_I|=|I|\), every external variable \(j\notin S_I\) satisfies \(D_j\cap I=\varnothing\). Thus range filtering detects overload and removes actual domain values in saturated Hall intervals from external variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Range consistency is characterized by nonoverloaded hull intervals and removal of every actual external-domain value in a saturated Hall interval.
assumptions_latex: Every D_i is a finite nonempty subset of the integers.
Support for an untested variable may use any integer in its hull R_i.

notation.meaning: Variables whose hulls are contained in interval I

assumptions_latex: Variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) have finite integer domains \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\).
The constraint is \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraint is range consistent exactly when every \(a\in D_i\) has such a range support for every \(i\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A value \(a\in D_i\) has a range support if there exists an assignment \(s\) satisfying \(s(x_i)=a\), \(s(x_j)\in R_j\) for every \(j
e i\), and \(s(x_p)
e s(x_q)\) whenever \(p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete witnesses for both strict inclusions in the AllDifferent consistency hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(D_1=D_2=\{1,3\}\) and \(D_3=\{1,2,3\}\), domain consistency forces \(D_3=\{2\}\), whereas range supports may use the hull value 2 for either of the first two variables and can leave 1 and 3 in \(D_3\). For \(D_1=\{1\}\), \(D_2=\{2\}\), and \(D_3=\{0,1,2,3\}\), range filtering deletes actual values 1 and 2 from \(D_3\), whereas bounds filtering need only support endpoints 0 and 3. Hence both inclusions in the domain–range–bounds hierarchy are strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hole-domain example separates domain from range consistency, and an interior-value example separates range from bounds consistency.
assumptions_latex: AllDifferent is imposed on each displayed finite-domain instance.
