With no independent activation path, the queue may empty while the execution obligation for \(p\) remains unmet.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A false-negative activation leaves the propagator suspended even though the new store requires another run.
assumptions_latex: A contraction \(D\to D'\) creates a new execution obligation for \(p\).
No independent mechanism schedules \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\text{ remains suspended despite an unmet execution obligation.}

notation.meaning: Store after the missed activating contraction.

knowledge_statements.title: False-Negative Transition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-independent state transition using an activation abstraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\alpha_p(D,D')\in\{0,1\}\) be the activation predicate applied when a suspended propagator \(p\) sees contraction \(D\to D'\subseteq D\). The lifecycle transition is \[S_p\xrightarrow{D\to D'}\begin{cases}Q_p,&\alpha_p(D,D')=1,\\S_p,&\alpha_p(D,D')=0,\end{cases}\] where a watched-event intersection is one possible implementation of \(\alpha_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contraction leaves a propagator suspended or moves it to queued according to its activation predicate; watched events are one implementation.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is validly suspended at \(D\).
\(D'\subseteq D\).
knowledge_statements.title: Abstract Suspension-to-Queue Transition

assumptions_latex: \(p\) is suspended and watches event set \(W_p\).
\(E(D,D')\) is the set of events generated by a domain contraction from \(D\) to \(D'\subseteq D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) transitions to queued precisely when \(E(D,D')\cap W_p\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Events generated by a store transition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-triggered state transition in a duplicate-free scheduler.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a suspended propagator \(p\), the lifecycle transition caused by \(D\to D'\) is represented by \[\operatorname{suspended}(p)\longrightarrow\operatorname{queued}(p)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad E(D,D')\cap W_p\neq\varnothing.\] The transition inserts \(p\) only if it is not already queued. If the intersection is empty, \(p\) remains suspended. A queued or running propagator does not acquire an additional queued instance from the same transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A suspended propagator becomes queued exactly when a store contraction emits at least one event it watches, with duplicate queue entries suppressed.
knowledge_statements.title: Suspension-to-Queue Transitions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind is suitable for the lifecycle transition, but the stated biconditional and duplicate-queue behavior depend on the scheduler's event model and lack supporting evidence.

children.title: Propagator Subsumption
children.top_down_role: Entailment-based completion, subsumption regimes, and residual-state consequences.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational certification when exact entailment testing is unavailable or too costly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A predicate \(T_p(D)\) is a sound subsumption test for propagator \(p\) when \(T_p(D)\Rightarrow D\subseteq C_p\). A positive result is then a valid retirement certificate. Completeness is optional: \(D\subseteq C_p\) may hold while \(T_p(D)\) is false, in which case a redundant propagator is retained without compromising correctness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sound subsumption test may have false negatives: positive results certify retirement, while missed subsumption only causes extra work.
assumptions_latex: \(C_p\) is the relation enforced by \(p\).
Descendant stores are obtained by contraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_p(D)\Rightarrow D\subseteq C_p,\qquad D\subseteq C_p\not\Rightarrow T_p(D)\text{ may hold}.

notation.meaning: Constraint relation enforced by the propagator

knowledge_statements.title: Sound but Incomplete Subsumption Tests

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Propagation Fixpoint Does Not Imply Subsumption
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinction between absence of current pruning and entailment by the store.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D(x)=D(y)=\{0,1\}\), and let \(p\) enforce domain consistency for \(x\le y\). Every individual value has a support, so \(p(D)=D\). Nevertheless \((1,0)\in D(x)\times D(y)\) violates \(x\le y\), hence the constraint is not entailed and \(p\) is not subsumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A propagation fixpoint need not be subsumed: x and y both having domain {0,1} under x ≤ y is an explicit example.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) enforces domain consistency for \(x\le y\).
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Fixpoint Does Not Imply Subsumption

assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a sound propagator for constraint relation \(C_p\).
\(D\) is the current store and descendant stores are obtained only by domain contraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(C_p\cap D=D\), then \(p\) is permanently redundant below \(D\).

notation.meaning: Constraint relation implemented by the propagator
Cartesian product of the current variable domains

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic subsumption under monotone finite-domain contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The propagator \(p\) is subsumed at \(D\) when every tuple admitted by the current store satisfies its constraint: \[D\subseteq C_p.\] Equivalently, \(C_p\cap D=D\). For every descendant store \(D'\subseteq D\), one then has \(D'\subseteq C_p\), so executing \(p\) can neither prune \(D'\) nor detect failure. Consequently its watches and queue membership may be removed permanently on the current search branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A propagator is subsumed when every tuple remaining in the store satisfies its constraint, making all later executions redundant on that branch.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagator Subsumption

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits semantic subsumption and the finite-domain claim is mathematically plausible, but no authoritative source with a specific locator supports the definition or retirement consequence.

children.title: Propagator Deactivation
children.top_down_role: Removal from active propagation, resource release, and deactivation boundaries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restoration requirement for branch-local deactivation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If propagator \(p\) is active in ancestor state \(S_k\) but is deactivated in descendant state \(S_m\) for a justification local to that subtree, restoration to \(S_k\) must restore both its active status and every event registration needed to observe later relevant changes. Otherwise a sibling subtree can omit executions available from \(S_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch-local deactivation must be undone on backtracking, including restoration of relevant event registrations.
assumptions_latex: \(S_m\) is a descendant of \(S_k\).
The deactivation justification need not hold at \(S_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{restore}(S_m,k)\) restores the active status and relevant registrations of \(p\).
knowledge_statements.title: Backtrackable Deactivation State

assumptions_latex: \(p\) is posted in a propagation engine with explicit queue and watch registrations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A deactivated propagator cannot execute or receive events until explicitly reactivated, if reactivation is supported.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational removal independent of whether the constraint is entailed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Deactivation of \(p\) is the lifecycle operation that removes \(p\) from the runnable queue \(Q\), clears or disables its watch set \(W_p\), and marks it ineligible for scheduling. Deactivation alone asserts no semantic relation between the current store and the constraint implemented by \(p\). Thus it is propagation-preserving only when justified externally, for example by subsumption, constraint removal, branch restoration, or replacement by an equivalent active propagator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deactivation makes a propagator unschedulable and removes its watches, but by itself does not establish that its constraint is already satisfied.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagator Deactivation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf, but whether deactivation removes watches, clears queue membership, and permits reactivation is solver-specific and uncited.

children.title: Subsumption–Deactivation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between justified completion and premature operational shutdown.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal witness that deactivation is not a semantic retirement certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D(x)=\{0,1\}\), let \(C_p=\{0\}\), and suppose \(p\) is the only active mechanism enforcing \(x=0\). If \(p\) is deactivated at \(D\), the complete assignment \(x=1\) remains reachable although it violates \(C_p\). Thus deactivation without subsumption or replacement enforcement need not preserve the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the sole propagator for x = 0 is disabled while x has domain {0,1}, the invalid assignment x = 1 can survive.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is the only mechanism enforcing \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\nsubseteq C_p\quad\text{and deactivating }p\text{ may admit }x=1\notin C_p.
knowledge_statements.title: Premature Deactivation Counterexample

assumptions_latex: \(p\) implements relation \(C_p\) at current store \(D\).
Future stores on the branch are descendants \(D'\subseteq D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Subsumption implies safe permanent deactivation, whereas arbitrary deactivation need not imply subsumption or preserve propagation.

notation.meaning: Constraint relation implemented by the propagator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic entailment versus an operational lifecycle action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(D\subseteq C_p\), subsumption justifies permanent deactivation because every descendant \(D'\subseteq D\) also satisfies \(D'\subseteq C_p\). The converse fails: an implementation can deactivate \(p\) while \(D\nsubseteq C_p\). Without another active mechanism enforcing \(C_p\), such deactivation may lose pruning or admit a violating complete assignment. Hence subsumption is a sufficient semantic certificate for retirement, while deactivation is only an operational state change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subsumption certifies safe retirement, but deactivation alone does not: disabling a non-subsumed propagator can lose pruning or permit a violating solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Subsumption–Deactivation Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind correctly distinguishes semantic subsumption from operational deactivation, but the propagation and solution-admissibility consequences need authoritative support.

children.title: Domain Events
children.top_down_role: Events associated with arbitrary domain changes and their propagation relevance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum strict contractions on one restoration-free finite-domain trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\) starts with finite domain \(D_0(x)\) and every counted domain event strictly contracts it, a restoration-free trajectory has at most \(|D_0(x)|-1\) events while domains remain nonempty. If a final emptying event is counted, the bound is \(|D_0(x)|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite domain permits at most one fewer nonempty strict contractions than its initial size, or its initial size when final failure is counted.
assumptions_latex: |D_0(x)|<\infty.
\text{Every counted event removes at least one value}.
\text{No restoration occurs on the trajectory}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{dom}}(x)\le |D_0(x)|-1\text{ for nonempty stores, and }N_{\mathrm{dom}}(x)\le |D_0(x)|\text{ if emptying is counted}.

notation.meaning: domain events for x on the trajectory

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Contraction-Event Bound

assumptions_latex: \(x\) has finite old domain \(D(x)\) and new domain \(D'(x)\subsetneq D(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A domain event records the strict contraction \(D'(x)\subsetneq D(x)\), optionally refined by the deleted values.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General finite-domain change event used for propagator awakening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A domain event for \(x\) is emitted when its domain contracts strictly from \(D(x)\) to \(D'(x)\subsetneq D(x)\). Its most informative finite-domain payload is the deletion set \[\Delta_x=D(x)\setminus D'(x),\qquad \Delta_x\neq\varnothing.\] A propagator subscribed to general domain events for \(x\) is eligible for rescheduling after every such contraction, including bound changes and assignment, unless the solver represents those cases by compatible subtype notifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain event denotes any strict domain contraction and may carry the deleted values; it covers bound changes and assignments as special cases.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain Events

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits domain events, but treating every strict contraction as a general event and using the deletion set as its most informative payload are event-model claims without a source.

children.title: Bounds Events
children.top_down_role: Events associated with lower-bound or upper-bound changes and their filtering uses.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional decomposition of a bounds event.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty finite ordered domains \(D'(x)\subseteq D(x)\), define \(E_{\mathrm{lb}}\iff\min D'(x)>\min D(x)\) and \(E_{\mathrm{ub}}\iff\max D'(x)<\max D(x)\). A bounds event is \(E_{\mathrm{lb}}\lor E_{\mathrm{ub}}\), and both components may occur in one contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounds event consists of a lower-bound increase, an upper-bound decrease, or both.
assumptions_latex: D(x),D'(x)\text{ are nonempty finite ordered domains}.
D'(x)\subseteq D(x).
knowledge_statements.title: Lower- and Upper-Bound Event Components

assumptions_latex: \(D(x)\) and \(D'(x)\) are nonempty finite subsets of a totally ordered value set.
\(D'(x)\subsetneq D(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bounds event occurs exactly when the minimum or maximum changes.

notation.meaning: Lower and upper bounds of a nonempty domain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered finite domains; interior-value deletion alone is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bounds event for \(x\) is emitted precisely when \[\min D'(x)>\min D(x)\quad\text{or}\quad\max D'(x)<\max D(x).\] It is a domain event but need not identify deletions strictly between the new bounds. If \(D'(x)\subsetneq D(x)\) while both extrema remain unchanged, the contraction is not a bounds event, although it remains a general domain event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounds event occurs when a contraction raises a variable's lower bound or lowers its upper bound; deleting only interior values does not qualify.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounds Events

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and extremum-change formula fit bounds events, but the exact notification taxonomy and exclusion of interior-only deletions require a cited solver-independent or implementation-specific source.

children.title: Assignment Events
children.top_down_role: Events associated with variable fixation and assignment-sensitive propagation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone finite-domain contraction without restoration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Along a monotone sequence \(D_0(x)\supseteq D_1(x)\supseteq\cdots\), \(x\) can undergo at most one transition from cardinality greater than one to cardinality one. Backtracking or restoration begins a different trajectory and may permit another assignment event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable becomes newly assigned at most once on one restoration-free contraction trajectory.
assumptions_latex: \text{Domains only contract on the considered trajectory}.
\text{Assignment means a transition from cardinality greater than one to one}.

notation.meaning: assignment events for x on one monotone trajectory

knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness of the Assignment Transition

assumptions_latex: \(D(x)\) is finite with \(|D(x)|>1\).
\(D'(x)\subsetneq D(x)\) is the nonempty domain after contraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An assignment event occurs exactly when \(|D'(x)|=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transition from a non-singleton finite domain to a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An assignment event for \(x\) is emitted when a contraction changes its domain from non-singleton to singleton: \[|D(x)|>1,\qquad D'(x)=\{a\}\ \text{for some value }a.\] The event identifies the newly fixed value \(a\). It is also a general domain event and, on a totally ordered domain, necessarily changes at least one bound unless the old domain was already the same singleton, which is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An assignment event records the transition of a previously non-singleton domain to one value and carries that newly fixed value.
knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Events

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and singleton-transition condition fit assignment events, but emission and payload semantics are implementation-dependent and have no citation.

children.title: Event-Granularity Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Precision, wakeup frequency, and implementation cost across domain, bounds, and assignment events.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness relation between event classifications ordered by information loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_c\) coarsen \(g_f\), so every fine class maps to a coarse class. Fine subscriptions can be simulated soundly by subscribing to all corresponding coarse classes, possibly causing redundant wakeups. Replacing a coarse subscription by only some constituent fine classes is sound exactly when every omitted class is irrelevant to the propagator's required wakeups.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coarsening safely permits extra wakeups; refinement may suppress classes only when they are proved irrelevant.
assumptions_latex: \text{Every fine event is delivered through its mapped coarse class}.
\text{The propagator execution itself is sound}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Coarsening preserves wake-up completeness; refinement requires irrelevance of every omitted class}.
knowledge_statements.title: Sound Coarsening and Refinement Condition

assumptions_latex: Each event class is sound: every store change relevant to a subscribed propagator emits a matching notification.
For event class \(g\), let \(N_g\) be delivered notifications and \(T_g\) total propagation work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Granularity must preserve wake-up completeness; among complete schemes, performance minimizes event-management plus redundant-propagation cost.

notation.meaning: Number of notifications under granularity scheme g

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness constraint and implementation-dependent scheduling cost model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A coarser event scheme may merge several changes and awaken more propagators per notification; a finer scheme may suppress irrelevant awakenings but requires more event classification, registration, and payload handling. Any admissible scheme must satisfy wake-up completeness: if a change can enable additional pruning by \(p\), it must emit an event watched by \(p\). Subject to that condition, an implementation may compare schemes using \[C_g=c_gN_g+T_g,\] where both terms are workload- and solver-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coarse events reduce classification detail but may cause redundant executions; fine events avoid some executions but cost more to maintain. Correctness always requires complete wake-ups.
knowledge_statements.title: Event-Granularity Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits the tradeoff leaf, but the wake-up-completeness requirement and illustrative cost model require authoritative support; the supplied inventory contains no relevant cited source.

children.title: Static Events
children.top_down_role: Fixed event subscriptions, applicable propagator regimes, and expressiveness limits.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correctness condition and monotonicity property for fixed watches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fixed set \(S_p\) is wake-up sound when every reachable contraction satisfies \[p(D')\neq D'\Longrightarrow \exists(x,e)\in S_p:\ e(D(x),D'(x)).\] If \(S_p\) is sound and \(S_p\subseteq S'_p\), then \(S'_p\) is also sound, although it may cause additional activations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A static watch set must catch every change after which the propagator can prune. Adding watches cannot make it unsound but may add redundant wake-ups.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is defined on every reachable store.
No event outside the fixed subscription set is implicitly delivered.
knowledge_statements.title: Soundness and Safe Oversubscription

knowledge_statements.scope_note: False-negative boundary for static subscriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p\) depends on \(y\), but \(S_p\) watches only events on other variables, a reachable transition changing only \(D(y)\) can satisfy \(p(D')\neq D'\) while matching no subscription. Without another activation mechanism, the queue may then become empty at a non-fixpoint of \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Omitting a relevant variable or event can leave a productive propagator unscheduled and permit false quiescence.
assumptions_latex: The omitted-variable transition is reachable.
No independent mechanism schedules \(p\).

notation.meaning: Some subscription in the fixed set matches the transition.

knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete Fixed Watch Set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Framework-neutral definition of static propagation-event subscriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each propagator \(p\), a static event scheme chooses a fixed set \(S_p\) of variable-event predicates before propagation. For every reachable contraction \(D\succeq D'\), the scheduler requests activation of \(p\) whenever \(e(D(x),D'(x))\) holds for some \((x,e)\in S_p\); \(S_p\) does not depend on the current store.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Static events fix each propagator's watched variable-event pairs in advance and use the same watches throughout propagation.
assumptions_latex: Event predicates have defined truth values on consecutive old and new domains.
Store transitions are componentwise contracting.

notation.meaning: Event predicate evaluated on the old and new domain of x.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Event Subscription Scheme
Static Events
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static event subscriptions for finite-domain propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite set of variables, let \(D:X\to 2^{V}\) be a domain store, and let \(p\) be a propagator. A static event scheme assigns before propagation a fixed subscription set \(S_p\subseteq X\times E\), independent of the current store. For consecutive stores \(D\succeq D'\), where \(D'(x)\subseteq D(x)\), the scheduler activates \(p\) whenever some \((x,e)\in S_p\) satisfies the event predicate \(e(D(x),D'(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A static event scheme fixes each propagator’s watched variable-event pairs in advance and activates it when any fixed subscription matches a domain change.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and the event-type set \(E\) are finite.
Store updates are contracting: \(D'(x)\subseteq D(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: The new store D' is componentwise no larger than D.
Fixed event-subscription set of propagator p.
Set of event predicates on old and new domains.

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses constraint-programming propagation events.
Exact event taxonomy and subscription convention require an authoritative propagation reference.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Static Events, but no cited propagation source supports the subscription semantics, and the value universe V is not introduced.

children.title: Dynamic Events
children.top_down_role: State-dependent event subscriptions, adaptation regimes, and lifecycle interactions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local correctness condition for changing subscriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(S_p^-\) is the subscription set effective immediately before a reachable contraction \(D\succeq D'\), dynamic watches are wake-up sound for \(p\) when \[p(D')\neq D'\Longrightarrow \exists(x,e)\in S_p^-:\ e(D(x),D'(x)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every change after which the propagator can prune must match a watch that was effective before that change.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is defined on every reachable store.
Event predicates are evaluated on the old and new domains of a contracting transition.

notation.meaning: Subscriptions effective immediately before the transition.

knowledge_statements.title: Wake-Up Soundness of Dynamic Watches

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Framework-neutral definition of dynamic propagation-event subscriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a propagator \(p\) and reachable store \(D\), let \(S_p(D)\) be the variable-event pairs currently watched by \(p\). The event scheme is dynamic when \(S_p(D_1)\neq S_p(D_2)\) is permitted for reachable stores \(D_1,D_2\); changes to the subscription set affect only transitions occurring after the replacement becomes effective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic events allow a propagator's watched variable-event pairs to change with the current store. A replacement governs subsequent changes, not changes that occurred before it took effect.
assumptions_latex: Each reachable store has a well-defined active subscription set for \(p\).
The implementation defines an effective instant for each subscription replacement.

notation.meaning: Subscription set active for propagator p at store D.

knowledge_statements.title: Store-Dependent Event Subscriptions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifecycle boundary for non-atomic dynamic-watch replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an old watch is disabled before a replacement watch is effective, and a productive transition for \(p\) occurs in that uncovered interval without being buffered or followed by a recheck, then wake-up soundness is not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A non-atomic gap between old and new watches can lose a productive change unless changes are buffered or the propagator rechecks the store.
assumptions_latex: Relevant store changes may occur during replacement.
No independent mechanism schedules \(p\) after every change.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{uncovered replacement interval}\Longrightarrow\text{a lost wake-up is possible}.
review_flags: Concurrent implementations require an appropriate atomic or synchronization protocol.
knowledge_statements.title: Lost Wake-Up During Watch Replacement
Dynamic Events
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Store-dependent event subscriptions for propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) range over finite-domain stores and let \(p\) be a propagator. A dynamic event scheme associates with \(p\) a subscription map \(S_p(D)\subseteq X\times E\) that may change after \(p\) executes. For a contracting transition \(D\succeq D'\), \(p\) is activated when \(e(D(x),D'(x))\) holds for some \((x,e)\in S_p(D)\). After execution at \(D'\), the scheme may replace the subscriptions by \(S_p(D')\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic event scheme lets a propagator revise its watched events as domains evolve, using the pre-change subscriptions to decide activation.
assumptions_latex: The subscription map \(S_p\) is defined for every reachable store.
Each store transition is contracting.

notation.meaning: Subscriptions of p at store D.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports dynamic propagation events.
Whether subscription changes take effect before or after execution is framework-dependent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Dynamic Events, but X and E are not introduced and the pre-change versus post-execution subscription convention requires an authoritative framework-specific source.

children.title: Delta Events
children.top_down_role: Change-specific event payloads, incremental-state uses, and representation boundaries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifetime obligation for unconsumed removals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an incremental propagator may depend on an individual removal, discarding that removal before it is incorporated into every dependent consumer's state destroys any general guarantee of equivalence with full recomputation. A delta may be cleared after all dependent consumers process it or after their state is reinitialized by an equivalent full computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unconsumed relevant removal cannot safely be discarded unless dependent state is updated or fully recomputed.
assumptions_latex: \text{The incremental transition may depend on individual removals}.
\text{No other retained state is assumed to reconstruct a discarded removal}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Premature loss of a relevant delta removes the general incremental/full-equivalence guarantee}.
knowledge_statements.title: Lost-Delta Unsoundness Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition of removals across successive contracting stores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(D^0\succeq D^1\succeq\cdots\succeq D^k\), \[D^0(x)\setminus D^k(x)=\biguplus_{j=1}^{k}\bigl(D^{j-1}(x)\setminus D^j(x)\bigr).\] Thus queued set-valued deltas may be merged by union before the next consumer execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under monotone contraction, the accumulated delta is the disjoint union of intervening removals.
assumptions_latex: D^j(x)\subseteq D^{j-1}(x)\text{ for every }j.
knowledge_statements.title: Delta Accumulation Law
Delta Events
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental propagation using the exact domain information removed since execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a contracting store transition \(D\succeq D'\), the delta of variable \(x\) is \(\Delta_x(D,D')=D(x)\setminus D'(x)\). A delta event delivered to propagator \(p\) contains the family \(\Delta_p=(\Delta_x)_{x\in\operatorname{scope}(p)}\), possibly restricted to subscribed variables. An incremental propagator may compute its next contraction from \(D'\) and \(\Delta_p\), rather than rescanning every old domain, provided the result equals its prescribed propagation result for the accumulated changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A delta event reports the values removed since a propagator’s prior relevant execution, enabling an equivalent incremental update without rescanning all old domains.
assumptions_latex: Domains are represented as sets and updates only remove values.
All removals relevant to \(p\) since its reference execution are accumulated in \(\Delta_p\).

notation.meaning: Values removed from x between the two stores.
Variables inspected or modified by p.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports delta-based propagation.
The required accumulation lifetime is implementation-framework dependent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Delta Events, but no source supports the delivery and accumulation semantics, including the reference execution from which removals are accumulated.

children.title: Event-Variant Selection
children.top_down_role: Workload and propagator characteristics governing event-variant choice.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semantic Admissibility of an Event Variant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness gate applied before performance-based event-variant selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An event variant is admissible for propagator \(p\) if every reachable contraction \(D\succeq D'\) with \(p(D')\neq D'\) eventually makes \(p\) pending, and any incremental invocation receives enough accumulated change information to compute the prescribed operator on \(D'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate event variant is admissible only when it cannot miss a productive propagator and does not omit change data needed by incremental execution.
assumptions_latex: The prescribed propagator operator is fixed across compared variants.
Reachable store transitions are contracting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{admissible}(v,p)\Longrightarrow\text{no productive transition is silently lost for }p.

notation.meaning: Candidate static, dynamic, or delta event variant.

knowledge_statements.title: Semantic Admissibility of an Event Variant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Workload boundary for static, dynamic, and delta-event selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: No static, dynamic, or delta variant is uniformly cheapest over all workloads: stable relevance can make dynamic-watch maintenance wasteful; changing relevance can make a static union generate avoidable wake-ups; and delta construction can cost more than the rescanning it avoids when changes are small or propagator scans are cheap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative cost of static watches, dynamic watches, and deltas reverses across workloads, so no variant is universally fastest.
assumptions_latex: Compared variants are admissible and implement the same propagator operator.
Maintenance and delivery work is included in runtime.

notation.meaning: Total cost of variant v on workload W.

knowledge_statements.title: Absence of Universal Event-Variant Dominance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Performance criterion after semantic admissibility is established.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Among admissible variants, selection should account for delivered activations, propagator executions, subscription maintenance, delta construction and merging, and queue operations. If \(\widehat T_v\) estimates their total cost on the target workload, choose \(v\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{u\in V_{\mathrm{adm}}}\widehat T_u\); admissibility is a hard constraint rather than a cost term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First reject unsound variants; then choose among the remaining variants using workload-specific wake-up, execution, maintenance, payload, and queue costs.
assumptions_latex: Cost estimates compare the same workload and prescribed propagator operators.
\(V_{\mathrm{adm}}\) contains only semantically admissible variants.

notation.meaning: Estimated total work of variant v on the target workload.

review_flags: This is an accounting criterion, not a universal predictive runtime model.
knowledge_statements.title: Workload-Sensitive Variant Choice
Event-Variant Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness criterion for choosing static, dynamic, or delta event delivery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite family of contracting propagators on a finite-height store lattice. An event variant is admissible if every store transition that can make an inactive propagator \(p\) produce a strict contraction eventually activates \(p\), and every delivered delta contains all changes required by its incremental implementation. Under fair processing, any admissible static, dynamic, or delta variant terminates at a common fixpoint whenever the propagators are monotone and the variant preserves their prescribed operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an event variant only if it cannot miss a newly productive propagator and supplies complete deltas; fair scheduling then preserves fixpoint computation.
assumptions_latex: The store lattice has finite height.
Every propagator is monotone and contracting.
The scheduler is fair for activated propagators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall p\in P,\ p(D^*)=D^*\) at termination, independently of the admissible event variant.
review_flags: No supplied locator establishes this event-soundness criterion.
Common-fixpoint invariance needs a source fixing the lattice order and scheduler semantics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits Event-Variant Selection, but its admissibility criterion and common-fixpoint conclusion constitute a substantive chaotic-iteration claim requiring a precise source and scheduler semantics.

children.title: FIFO Queues
children.top_down_role: First-in-first-out propagation queues, scheduling behavior, and workload suitability.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential first-in, first-out processing of pending propagator entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a sequence \(Q\) of pending propagator entries. Remove the head entry, execute its propagator on the current store, and append newly activated entries at the tail according to the separately chosen duplicate policy. Stop on detected inconsistency or when \(Q\) is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: FIFO executes the oldest pending entry and appends newly activated work at the tail until inconsistency or queue exhaustion.
assumptions_latex: Activation detection is sound.
Each extraction and propagator execution completes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q=\varnothing\quad\text{or an inconsistency is detected at termination}.

notation.meaning: FIFO sequence of pending propagator entries.

review_flags: Initialization and duplicate handling are independent scheduling conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: FIFO Propagator Scheduling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arrival-order and per-entry waiting property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an uncancelled entry has \(k\) entries ahead of it, tail insertions cannot increase that number. It is selected after those \(k\) entries have been extracted, provided each earlier extraction completes and no operation inserts at the head.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Later arrivals cannot overtake a pending FIFO entry; an entry with k predecessors is served after those predecessors.
assumptions_latex: Insertion is at the tail and extraction is at the head.
The entry is neither cancelled nor removed and reinserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{predecessors}_Q(a)=k\Longrightarrow a\text{ is selected after }k\text{ earlier extractions}.

notation.meaning: Number of entries ahead of the selected entry.

knowledge_statements.title: FIFO Non-Overtaking Guarantee
FIFO Queues
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-in, first-out scheduling of activated propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a store \(D\), propagators \(P\), and an initial activation sequence. Initialize a queue \(Q\) with that sequence. While \(Q\neq\varnothing\), remove its oldest entry \(p\), replace \(D\) by \(p(D)\), and append at the tail every propagator activated by the resulting store change, subject to the chosen duplicate policy. Stop with failure if some domain becomes empty; otherwise output \(D\) when \(Q=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: FIFO propagation repeatedly executes the oldest queued propagator and appends newly activated propagators at the tail until failure or queue exhaustion.
assumptions_latex: Each propagator maps stores to contracting stores.
Activation detection is sound for the selected event scheme.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q=\varnothing\) on successful termination, and the algorithm outputs the current store \(D\).
review_flags: No supplied locator addresses propagation queue disciplines.
Initialization and duplicate-handling conventions vary among solvers.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the appropriate kind for FIFO Queues, but no propagation-scheduling source supports the initialization, activation, and duplicate-handling conventions.

children.title: LIFO Queues
children.top_down_role: Last-in-first-out propagation queues, locality effects, and workload suitability.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential last-in, first-out processing of pending propagator entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a stack \(Q\) of pending propagator entries. Pop the top entry, execute its propagator on the current store, and push newly activated entries in a specified order according to the separately chosen duplicate policy. Stop on detected inconsistency or when \(Q\) is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LIFO executes the newest pending entry and pushes newly activated work onto the stack until inconsistency or exhaustion.
assumptions_latex: Activation detection is sound.
The push order for a batch of simultaneously activated entries is fixed by the implementation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q=\varnothing\quad\text{or an inconsistency is detected at termination}.
review_flags: Batch push order affects the exact execution trace but not the definition of LIFO extraction.
knowledge_statements.title: LIFO Propagator Scheduling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Starvation boundary of newest-first scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Pure LIFO supplies no finite waiting bound when arbitrarily many entries may be pushed above a pending entry. If only finitely many entries can subsequently be pushed above entry \(a\) and every extraction completes, then \(a\) is eventually selected; without that condition or a fairness override, starvation is possible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An old stack entry is eventually served only if it is overtaken finitely often or another fairness rule intervenes.
assumptions_latex: The entry is not cancelled.
No fairness override is assumed for the negative case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{finite later pushes above }a\Longrightarrow\text{eventual service of }a;\quad\text{unbounded pushes}\Longrightarrow\text{no guarantee}.
review_flags: Finite-height propagation may independently rule out infinite productive arrivals; the statement concerns the queue discipline itself.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Overtaking Under Pure LIFO

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newest-first ordering and locality property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(b\) is pushed after pending entry \(a\), and neither entry is removed before the next extraction, then \(b\) is popped before \(a\). Newly generated propagation can therefore be pursued before older pending work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LIFO selects the newest pending entry, favoring recently generated propagation chains.
assumptions_latex: Insertion and extraction use one stack.
No secondary rule overrides stack order.

notation.meaning: Logical stack insertion and extraction times.

knowledge_statements.title: LIFO Recency Ordering
LIFO Queues
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Last-in, first-out scheduling of activated propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a store \(D\), propagators \(P\), and an initial activation sequence. Initialize a stack \(Q\) with that sequence. While \(Q\neq\varnothing\), remove its newest entry \(p\), replace \(D\) by \(p(D)\), and push every propagator activated by the resulting change, subject to the chosen duplicate policy. Stop with failure if a domain becomes empty; otherwise output \(D\) when \(Q=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LIFO propagation repeatedly executes the most recently queued propagator and pushes newly activated propagators until failure or stack exhaustion.
assumptions_latex: Each propagator is contracting.
Activation detection is sound for the selected event scheme.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q=\varnothing\) on successful termination, and the algorithm outputs the current store \(D\).
review_flags: No supplied locator addresses propagation queue disciplines.
The ordering used when several propagators are pushed simultaneously requires a convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is appropriate for LIFO Queues, but no source is cited and the push order for multiple simultaneously activated propagators is unspecified.

children.title: Priority Queues
children.top_down_role: Priority-ordered propagation queues, ranking regimes, and scheduling overhead.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation scheduling by an explicit ordered key.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain pending entries with keys in a totally ordered set. At each step extract an entry of best key, execute its propagator, and insert newly activated entries. A fixed rule resolves ties; if keys depend on mutable state, the implementation must define whether and when pending keys are recomputed or updated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A priority scheduler repeatedly executes a best-ranked pending propagator, with explicit tie and pending-key update conventions.
assumptions_latex: The priority order and its orientation are specified.
Activation detection is sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\in\operatorname*{arg\,best}_{q\in Q}\pi(q)\quad\text{is selected at each extraction}.

notation.meaning: Priority key of pending entry q.

knowledge_statements.title: Priority-Ordered Propagator Scheduling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic FIFO tie handling inside a priority class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Attach to each entry the lexicographic key \((\pi(q),\tau(q))\), where \(\tau(q)\) is its insertion timestamp and the first component is ordered by priority. Entries whose priority remains equal are then extracted in FIFO insertion order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable priority queue uses insertion time to provide FIFO order among entries with equal unchanged priority.
assumptions_latex: Insertion timestamps are strictly increasing.
Priority keys and timestamps are compared lexicographically.
knowledge_statements.title: Stable Equal-Priority Variant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operation costs for a conventional priority representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For at most \(m\) pending entries in a binary heap, insertion and best-entry extraction take \(O(\log m)\) worst-case time, best-entry inspection takes \(O(1)\), and storage is \(O(m)\). An arbitrary pending-key update takes \(O(\log m)\) when the entry's heap position is maintained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary heap gives logarithmic insertion, extraction, and indexed key updates with linear storage.
assumptions_latex: Key comparisons take constant time.
A position map is available for arbitrary key updates.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary-Heap Priority-Queue Bounds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fairness boundary for fixed best-key extraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an entry remains pending while infinitely many better-ranked entries are selected before it, strict priority need never select that entry. Starvation freedom therefore requires finite better-priority overtaking, aging, or another fairness override.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuing supply of better-ranked work can starve a lower-ranked pending propagator unless aging or another fairness rule intervenes.
assumptions_latex: The priority comparison remains strict.
No aging changes the pending entry's rank in the negative case.
knowledge_statements.title: Starvation Under Strict Priority
Priority Queues
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation scheduling by a numerical or ordered priority key.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a store \(D\), propagators \(P\), and a priority key \(\pi:P\times\mathcal D\to K\), where \(K\) is totally ordered. Insert the initially activated propagators into \(Q\). While \(Q\neq\varnothing\), extract an entry \(p\) having minimal key \(\pi(p,D)\), apply \(p\), and insert or update every propagator activated by the change. Resolve equal keys by a fixed rule. Stop on an empty domain; otherwise output \(D\) when \(Q\) is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A priority scheduler executes an activated propagator with best current key, updates affected entries after each contraction, and stops at failure or queue exhaustion.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is totally ordered.
Propagators are contracting.
Activation detection is sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{q\in Q}\pi(q,D)\) is selected at each iteration.

notation.meaning: Priority key of p at store D; smaller keys are preferred.
Set or heap of activated propagators.

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses priority-based propagation.
Priority orientation and entry-update policy are solver conventions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits Priority Queues, but the priority orientation, tie handling, and pending-key update semantics lack an authoritative propagation reference.

children.title: Queue-Discipline Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Fairness, locality, responsiveness, and overhead across propagation queue disciplines.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fairness comparison for FIFO, LIFO, and strict-priority queues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With completing extractions and no cancellation, FIFO serves an entry after its finite set of predecessors. LIFO serves an entry if only finitely many later entries are pushed above it. Strict priority serves an entry if only finitely many better-ranked selections precede it, or if aging eventually makes it best-ranked.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: FIFO has intrinsic positional service; LIFO and strict priority need finite overtaking or an explicit fairness mechanism.
assumptions_latex: Each extraction completes.
The entry under consideration remains pending until selected.
knowledge_statements.title: Discipline-Specific Service Conditions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Workload-dependent reversal of scheduling advantages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: FIFO, LIFO, and priority scheduling admit no workload-independent runtime ordering. Recency-aligned dependency chains may favor LIFO; workloads needing prompt service of old entries may favor FIFO; informative ranks may favor priority scheduling; and uninformative ranks add maintenance without reducing propagation work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Locality, responsiveness, ranking quality, and maintenance costs vary by workload, so no queue discipline is universally fastest.
assumptions_latex: All compared disciplines use sound activation.
Runtime includes queue maintenance and propagator execution.

notation.meaning: Total cost of discipline d on workload W.

review_flags: The workload families establish non-dominance, not quantitative performance for a particular solver.
knowledge_statements.title: No Universally Best Queue Discipline

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semantic Invariance Under Sound Fair Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which queue order changes execution cost but not the computed closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite family of monotone, contracting propagators act on a finite-height store order. If activation is sound and the scheduler is fair, any FIFO, LIFO, or priority run that reaches quiescence returns a common fixpoint. Under the standard chaotic-iteration closure assumptions, the reachable closure from the same initial store is independent of the fair execution order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With monotone contracting propagators, sound activation, and fairness, queue discipline changes the execution trace and cost but not the common closure reached by fair chaotic iteration.
assumptions_latex: The store order has finite height.
Propagators are monotone and contracting.
Activation is sound and every pending propagator is eventually selected.
review_flags: The order-independent closure clause should receive an authoritative chaotic-iteration locator before citation-sensitive publication.
knowledge_statements.title: Semantic Invariance Under Sound Fair Scheduling
Queue-Discipline Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic invariance and operational differences among fair queue disciplines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be monotone contracting propagators on a finite-height store lattice, and suppose activation is sound. FIFO, LIFO, and priority scheduling may execute different propagator sequences and therefore incur different queue operations and redundant executions. If each discipline is fair—every continuously pending propagator is eventually selected—and each run terminates only with an empty queue, then every output is a common fixpoint of \(P\). Equality of outputs additionally requires uniqueness of the reachable common fixpoint, for example under a specified chaotic-iteration theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Queue disciplines change execution order and cost. Under sound activation and fairness they terminate at common fixpoints, but identical outputs require an additional uniqueness result.
assumptions_latex: The store lattice has finite height.
Every propagator is monotone and contracting.
Activation and scheduling are sound and fair.

notation.meaning: Store returned when the queue becomes empty.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the chaotic-iteration claim.
Identical-result conditions depend on the chosen store order and propagator semantics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits Queue-Discipline Tradeoffs, but the fairness-to-common-fixpoint assertion and conditions for output equality require a specifically located chaotic-iteration result.

children.title: Duplicate Suppression
children.top_down_role: Control of repeated queue entries, coalescing regimes, and associated state costs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential duplicate suppression with a pending indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain \(\operatorname{pending}[p]\in\{0,1\}\) for each propagator. Insert \(p\) only when its flag is zero and set the flag to one atomically with insertion. On extraction, clear the flag before executing \(p\), allowing changes during execution to schedule a later run. The invariant is that the flag equals the number of pending entries for \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pending flag prevents duplicate queued entries and is cleared before execution so later relevant changes can reschedule the propagator.
assumptions_latex: Queue insertion and pending-flag setting are atomic with respect to scheduling.
Each queue entry identifies one propagator.

notation.meaning: Indicator that p currently has a queued entry.

review_flags: Concurrent schedulers require a corresponding atomic state protocol.
knowledge_statements.title: At-Most-One Pending Entry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Space and duplicate-test consequences of at-most-one pending entry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite propagator set \(P\), one pending bit per propagator implies \(|Q|\le |P|\) and \(O(|P|)\) pending-state storage. With indexed bit access, testing and suppressing a duplicate takes \(O(1)\) time, excluding any delta-merge cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At-most-one pending entry bounds the queue by the number of propagators and supports constant-time duplicate tests, apart from payload merging.
assumptions_latex: Pending flags support constant-time indexed access.
Each queue entry represents one propagator.
knowledge_statements.title: Pending-State and Queue-Size Bounds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic condition for merging several activations into one pending entry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Coalescing activations of \(p\) while one entry is pending is safe when the eventual execution recomputes the prescribed operator from the current store. If execution is delta-based, the retained entry must instead accumulate a summary whose merge preserves every change needed to compute that operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicate activations may share one entry when the propagator rescans the current store; incremental propagators must merge all required change information.
assumptions_latex: The retained entry is eventually executed.
Notification multiplicity has no separate semantics unless represented in retained state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{full-store recomputation}\lor\text{sufficient merged delta}\Longrightarrow\text{coalescing preserves the next result}.
knowledge_statements.title: Safe Activation Coalescing

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-loss boundary for incremental propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a second event occurs while \(p\) is pending and its required delta is discarded rather than merged, an incremental execution may receive an incomplete change set and differ from recomputation on the current store. At-most-one queue entry alone therefore does not justify discarding associated payloads.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Suppressing a duplicate entry is unsafe if it also discards change data needed by an incremental propagator.
assumptions_latex: The propagator consumes supplied deltas instead of fully rescanning the store.
The discarded change is not recoverable from retained state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{required delta discarded}\Longrightarrow\text{semantic preservation is not guaranteed}.
knowledge_statements.title: Lost Delta Under Duplicate Suppression
Duplicate Suppression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: At-most-one pending queue entry per propagator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a queue \(Q\) and Boolean flags \(\operatorname{pending}[p]\) for \(p\in P\). To schedule \(p\), insert it only when \(\operatorname{pending}[p]=0\), then set \(\operatorname{pending}[p]=1\). On extracting \(p\), set \(\operatorname{pending}[p]=0\) before applying it, so a change during its execution may schedule it again. The invariant is \(\operatorname{pending}[p]=1\) exactly when \(Q\) contains one entry for \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicate suppression keeps at most one pending entry per propagator, clearing its flag before execution so later relevant changes can reschedule it.
assumptions_latex: Queue insertions and pending-flag updates are atomic with respect to scheduling.
Each queue entry identifies one propagator.

notation.meaning: Indicator that p currently has a queue entry.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports this queue invariant.
Concurrent implementations may require a stronger atomic-state protocol.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits Duplicate Suppression and states a coherent sequential invariant, but no source supports the flag-clearing convention or its scheduling semantics.

children.title: Dynamic Priority
children.top_down_role: Runtime priority adjustment, workload signals, and scheduling consequences.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-independent semantics for store- or history-dependent propagation priorities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For pending set \(Q\), store \(D\), and history \(h\), a dynamic-priority scheduler selects \(p\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{q\in Q}\pi(q,D,h)\). An implementation using cached keys must recompute affected keys eagerly or validate stale keys lazily until the extracted entry is certified minimal for the current \((D,h)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic-priority scheduling chooses a currently minimum-priority pending propagator; cached priorities must be updated or validated before selection.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is finite at each selection step.
\(\pi(q,D,h)\) lies in a totally ordered key set.
Stale cached keys can be detected or safely recomputed.

notation.meaning: Current dynamic priority key; smaller keys are preferred.
Execution history used by the policy.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Priority Selection Semantics

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduling overhead for a standard indexed binary-heap realization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With at most \(n\) pending propagators in an indexed binary heap, extracting a minimum or changing one cached key costs \(O(\log n)\), in addition to the cost of computing or validating the dynamic key. Updating \(r\) affected keys costs \(O(r\log n)\) plus their recomputation costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indexed binary heap gives logarithmic extraction and key-update overhead, separate from the cost of recomputing priorities.
assumptions_latex: The queue is an indexed binary heap with at most \(n\) entries.
Affected entries are identifiable.
review_flags: Bound applies to the stated heap representation, not to every priority-queue implementation.
knowledge_statements.title: Priority-Queue Overhead

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of closure when adaptive priorities are unfair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a dynamic-priority policy can leave a pending propagator \(p\) unselected indefinitely while \(p(D)\subsetneq D\), then the observed store need not be a common fixpoint. Priority adaptation therefore requires fairness, aging, or another starvation-prevention condition whenever queue exhaustion or stabilization is used to certify closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unfair dynamic-priority rule can starve a propagator that still prunes, so apparent stabilization need not be propagation closure.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) remains eligible indefinitely.
\(p(D)\subsetneq D\) at the observed store.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ need not be a common fixpoint.}
knowledge_statements.title: Starvation Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fair Dynamic Ordering Preserves the Common Fixpoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-independence of fair dynamic-priority propagation on finite stores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a finite family of monotone contracting maps on a finite lattice of stores ordered by inclusion. Starting from \(D_0\), every fair iteration that eventually applies each map whenever it remains nonfixpoint terminates at the greatest common fixpoint \(D^*\subseteq D_0\). Thus a fair dynamic-priority policy changes execution order, but not the terminal closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For monotone contracting propagators on finite stores, every fair dynamic-priority order reaches the same greatest common fixpoint below the initial store.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and the store lattice are finite.
\(D'\subseteq D\Rightarrow f(D')\subseteq f(D)\subseteq D\) for every \(f\in F\).
Every propagator that remains nonfixpoint is eventually selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_t\text{ terminates at }D^*=\max\{D\subseteq D_0:\forall f\in F,\ f(D)=D\}.

notation.meaning: Greatest common fixpoint below the initial store.

knowledge_statements.title: Fair Dynamic Ordering Preserves the Common Fixpoint
Dynamic Priority
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Store-dependent reprioritization of pending propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi(p,D,h)\) be a priority key depending on propagator \(p\), current store \(D\), and execution history \(h\). Maintain activated propagators in a priority queue. After each store contraction or history update, recompute or lazily validate every affected pending key. Extract a propagator whose validated key is minimal, apply it, update \(D\) and \(h\), and repeat until failure or queue exhaustion. A stale extracted entry must be rekeyed rather than executed unless it remains minimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic-priority scheduling recalculates affected priorities as domains and execution history change, validating stale heap entries before selecting the current best propagator.
assumptions_latex: Priority keys lie in a totally ordered set.
Affected stale keys can be detected before execution.
Activation detection is sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{q\in Q}\pi(q,D,h)\) is executed after key validation.

notation.meaning: Dynamic priority key; smaller is preferred.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports dynamic propagation priorities.
Eager versus lazy rekeying semantics require a solver-specific source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits Dynamic Priority, but the eager or lazy key-validation protocol and the requirement to rekey stale entries are solver-dependent and uncited.

children.title: Suppression–Priority Interaction
children.top_down_role: Interactions between entry coalescing and adaptive ordering in propagation queues.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-reactivation overhead for an indexed priority queue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the entry for \(p\) is directly addressable, combining a new summary costs the summary-operation time \(T_{\sqcup}\); changing its position in an indexed binary heap costs \(O(\log n)\). Thus one coalesced reactivation costs \(O(T_{\sqcup}+\log n)\), excluding priority recomputation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With direct entry lookup and an indexed heap, coalescing costs the summary operation plus logarithmic key adjustment.
assumptions_latex: There are at most \(n\) pending entries.
Entries are directly indexed by propagator.
The priority queue is an indexed binary heap.
knowledge_statements.title: Coalesced-Key Update Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint event-summary and priority requirements when repeated activations share one entry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose activations of pending propagator \(p\) carry summaries \(s_1,\ldots,s_r\) and priority contributions \(k_1,\ldots,k_r\). Coalescing them into one entry \((p,s,k)\) is semantics-preserving only if \(s\) retains all information required for the contraction and next watch state that the unsuppressed activations would produce, and \(k\) equals the key prescribed by the declared priority-combination policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coalesced entry must preserve both the event information needed by the propagator and the priority required by the scheduling policy.
assumptions_latex: At most one pending entry represents \(p\).
The scheduler declares summary- and key-combination rules.
The propagator executes against the current store.
knowledge_statements.title: Semantics-Preserving Coalescence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Missed pruning or incorrect ordering caused by lossy suppression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p\) is pending after activation summary \(s_x\), and a later activation supplies \(s_y\) or a more urgent key \(k_y\), discarding that activation can be incorrect: when \(\operatorname{run}(p,D,s_x)=D\) but \(\operatorname{run}(p,D,s_x\sqcup s_y)\subsetneq D\), pruning is lost; when the policy requires \(k_y<k_x\), retaining \(k_x\) can select a different next propagator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Suppressing a duplicate while discarding its event summary can miss pruning, and discarding its key change can violate the intended priority order.
assumptions_latex: The later activation changes information used by propagation or priority selection.
knowledge_statements.title: Discarded Reactivation Information
Suppression–Priority Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Priority updates when duplicate queue entries are forbidden.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume at most one pending entry represents each propagator \(p\). If a new activation of pending \(p\) changes its priority from \(k\) to \(k'\), duplicate suppression must combine the activation with the existing entry by updating its key to the policy-prescribed value, such as \(k'\) or \(\min\{k,k'\}\). Silently discarding the activation without performing the required key update preserves queue uniqueness but may violate the intended priority-selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a pending propagator is reactivated, suppression must update its existing priority as prescribed; merely discarding the duplicate can select the wrong next propagator.
assumptions_latex: Each propagator has at most one pending queue entry.
The scheduling policy specifies how reactivation changes priority.

notation.meaning: Pending queue entry or entries representing p.

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses suppression and priority coupling.
The correct key-combination operator is policy-dependent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits Suppression–Priority Interaction, but the combination rule is policy-dependent and uncited; key(Q_p) is also undefined when no pending entry exists.

children.title: Propagator Idempotence
children.top_down_role: Idempotent propagator behavior, recognition regimes, and scheduling consequences.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Individual Idempotence Does Not Prevent Later Reactivation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between immediate idempotence and stability under interaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On subsets of \(\{a,b\}\) ordered by inclusion, let \(q(S)=S\setminus\{b\}\), and let \(p(S)=S\setminus\{a\}\) when \(b\notin S\), with \(p(S)=S\) when \(b\in S\). Both maps are monotone, contracting, and idempotent. Yet for \(S=\{a,b\}\), \(p(S)=S\), \(q(S)=\{a\}\), and \(p(q(S))=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A change by one idempotent propagator can make another idempotent propagator productive again.
knowledge_statements.title: Individual Idempotence Does Not Prevent Later Reactivation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduling consequence of idempotence without an intervening store change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p\) is idempotent and \(D'=p(D)\), then executing \(p\) again before any other store change yields \(p(D')=D'\). A scheduler may therefore omit immediate self-rescheduling but may not permanently disable \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An idempotent propagator need not run twice consecutively, although later changes may make it productive again.
assumptions_latex: For every store \(D\), \(p(p(D))=p(D)\).
No intervening operation changes \(D'\).

notation.meaning: Store produced by one execution of p

knowledge_statements.title: Immediate Self-Rescheduling Is Redundant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic idempotence and its image-fixpoint characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A propagator \(p:\mathcal D\to\mathcal D\) is idempotent when \(p(p(D))=p(D)\) for every store \(D\). Equivalently, every store in the image of \(p\) is a fixpoint of \(p\). The condition concerns consecutive applications with no intervening store change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A propagator is idempotent when one application always leaves an output that the same propagator cannot immediately change again.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a self-map on \(\mathcal D\).
knowledge_statements.title: Idempotent Propagator
Propagator Idempotence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Idempotence of a propagator as a store transformer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal D,\preceq)\) be a store poset and let \(p:\mathcal D\to\mathcal D\) be a propagator. The propagator \(p\) is idempotent if applying it twice has the same effect as applying it once: \(p(p(D))=p(D)\) for every \(D\in\mathcal D\). Equivalently, every image store \(p(D)\) is a fixpoint of \(p\). This property concerns immediate repeated application without intervening changes by other propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A propagator is idempotent when a second immediate application never changes the store produced by the first; every output of the propagator is its fixpoint.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a self-map on the store space \(\mathcal D\).

notation.meaning: Propagator viewed as a store transformer.

review_flags: The algebraic definition is standard, but no supplied locator concerns propagator semantics.
An authoritative constraint-propagation source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is mathematically precise and exactly fits Propagator Idempotence, but the record supplies neither a source nor an explicitly marked standard-field rationale permitted by the evidence contract.

children.title: Propagation Fixpoints
children.top_down_role: Stable propagation states, fixpoint scope, and interactions among propagators.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility interpretation of the bottom store under sound propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every propagator preserves all solutions represented by its input store and propagation from \(D_0\) reaches the bottom store \(\bot\), then \(D_0\) represents no solution. A nonbottom common fixpoint is only propagation-stable and need not contain a feasible complete assignment unless the propagators are complete for the represented constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sound propagation to an empty store proves inconsistency; a nonempty stable store generally does not prove feasibility.
assumptions_latex: Every propagator is solution-preserving.
\(\bot\) represents no assignments.
knowledge_statements.title: Bottom Fixpoint Certifies Inconsistency

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Greatest Common Fixpoint Below the Initial Store
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-independent closure under fair terminating propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite family of monotone, contracting self-maps of a finite store poset. Starting from \(D_0\), suppose iteration terminates only when every member of \(P\) fixes the current store and fairly reconsiders every propagator made relevant by a change. The result \(D^\star\) is the greatest common fixpoint below \(D_0\): every \(E\preceq D_0\) satisfying \(p(E)=E\) for all \(p\in P\) also satisfies \(E\preceq D^\star\). Hence all such iterations return the same store.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fair terminating iteration of monotone contracting propagators reaches the unique greatest common fixpoint below the initial store.
assumptions_latex: The store poset and propagator family are finite.
Every propagator is monotone and contracting.
Termination occurs only at a common fixpoint, with complete reconsideration after relevant changes.

notation.meaning: Propagation closure below the initial store

knowledge_statements.title: Greatest Common Fixpoint Below the Initial Store

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stable store for a family of propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family \(P\) of store transformers, a store \(D^\star\) is a propagation fixpoint when every member fixes it: \(p(D^\star)=D^\star\) for all \(p\in P\). For a singleton family this is the ordinary fixpoint of one propagator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A propagation fixpoint is a store unchanged by every propagator in the active family.
assumptions_latex: Every \(p\in P\) is a self-map on the store space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D^\star\text{ is a propagation fixpoint}\iff\forall p\in P,\ p(D^\star)=D^\star.
knowledge_statements.title: Common Propagation Fixpoint
Propagation Fixpoints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common fixpoints of contracting, monotone propagators on a finite domain-store lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\) be a finite lattice of domain stores ordered by inclusion, and let \(P\) be a finite family of contracting, monotone maps \(p:\mathcal D\to\mathcal D\). A store \(D^\star\) is a propagation fixpoint of \(P\) when \[\forall p\in P,\qquad p(D^\star)=D^\star.\] Starting from \(D_0\), any fair sequence \(D_{k+1}=p_k(D_k)\), in which every persistently applicable propagator is eventually selected, terminates at a common fixpoint because every strict update descends in the finite lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A propagation fixpoint is a store unchanged by every propagator. Fair repeated propagation terminates at such a store when domains form a finite lattice.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal D\) is finite.
\(P\) is finite.
Each \(p\in P\) is contracting and monotone.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The common-fixpoint definition fits the leaf, but the record also asserts a termination theorem. Fairness alone does not ensure operational termination if no-op selections may continue; a terminating work-list policy or equivalent condition is needed. No cited source supports the exact hypotheses or conclusion.

children.title: Non-Idempotent Rescheduling
children.top_down_role: Repeated activation needs and scheduling boundaries for non-idempotent propagators.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound on productive executions over a finite-height store interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every productive execution of a contracting propagator strictly decreases the store and the reachable interval below the initial store has height \(h\), then at most \(h\) productive executions occur before stability. This does not bound no-op queue removals, which depend on the scheduler.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: There is at most one productive execution per strict store descent; scheduler overhead is separate.
assumptions_latex: Every productive execution strictly decreases the store.
The reachable store interval has finite height \(h\).

notation.meaning: Maximum number of strict reachable store descents

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Reexecution Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One Execution Can Stop Before a Fixpoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal witness for reconsidering a non-idempotent propagator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the chain \(0\preceq1\preceq2\), define \(p(0)=0\), \(p(1)=0\), and \(p(2)=1\). The map is monotone and contracting, but \(p(p(2))=0\ne1=p(2)\). Running it once at \(2\) and never reconsidering it therefore stops at a nonfixpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone contracting propagator can require consecutive executions; one-shot scheduling may leave pruning available.
knowledge_statements.title: One Execution Can Stop Before a Fixpoint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-independent work-list protocol that safely handles non-idempotent propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(D\leftarrow D_0\) and \(Q\leftarrow P\). Remove some \(p\in Q\), set \(D'\leftarrow p(D)\), and, if \(D'\prec D\), set \(D\leftarrow D'\) and enqueue every member of \(P\), including \(p\). If \(D'=D\), do not reinsert \(p\) solely for that execution. On a finite store poset with contracting propagators, termination with \(Q=\varnothing\) yields \(p(D)=D\) for every \(p\in P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After every strict store change, reconsider all propagators, including the one that caused it; an empty queue then certifies common stability.
assumptions_latex: The reachable store poset is finite.
Every propagator is contracting.
Every propagator is initially enqueued and every strict change enqueues all propagators.
Queue removals eventually process enqueued entries.
review_flags: Enqueuing all propagators is conservative but avoids an underspecified wake-set dependency relation.
