knowledge_statements.scope_note: Principal implementation variants of solver-state copying.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An eager snapshot duplicates every state component required for independent descendant mutation before exploring the child. A copy-on-write snapshot initially shares components with its ancestor but creates a private descendant copy before any write to a shared mutable component. Either variant satisfies snapshot independence exactly when no descendant write can alter an observation of a retained ancestor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: State copying may be eager or copy-on-write; both are correct only when descendant writes cannot change retained ancestor snapshots.
assumptions_latex: Every shared component is immutable until privately copied.
All search-relevant mutable components participate in the snapshot discipline.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall q,\ q(S_v)\text{ is invariant under mutations of descendant }S_w.
knowledge_statements.title: Eager and Copy-on-Write Snapshots

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time and live-memory bounds for eager complete snapshots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a complete eager snapshot contains \(N\) constant-size cells, creating a child snapshot takes \(\Theta(N)\) time and \(\Theta(N)\) additional space. If depth-first search retains one complete snapshot at each of \(h\) active levels, live snapshot space is \(\Theta(hN)\); retaining only a constant number of complete snapshots requires \(\Theta(N)\) live snapshot space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An eager N-cell snapshot costs linear time and space; retaining one at every active depth costs Θ(hN).
assumptions_latex: Snapshots are eager complete copies of \(N\) constant-size cells.
Snapshot metadata has lower-order size.

notation.meaning: Number of cells in a complete snapshot
Number of simultaneously retained search levels

knowledge_statements.title: Whole-State Copying Bounds

assumptions_latex: A solver state admits an independent snapshot operation.
Search descendants mutate only their own current snapshot.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Selecting the snapshot stored for a node restores that node's solver state without undoing intervening mutations.

notation.meaning: Solver state at search node v

review_flags: The supplied copying-constraints locator concerns decomposition, not solver-state copying.
A constraint-programming implementation reference is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Whole-state copying as a backtracking mechanism in tree search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a search node \(v\) with current state \(S_v\), create each explored child \(w\) with initialization \(S_w:=\operatorname{copy}(S_v)\). Apply the child's branching decision and propagation only to \(S_w\). When exploration of \(w\) stops by failure, completion, or cutoff, discard \(S_w\); to explore another child, start from a fresh copy of \(S_v\). Backtracking to \(v\) outputs the retained snapshot \(S_v\). The copy operation must preserve all semantically relevant domains, propagator states, queues, and auxiliary data while preventing later mutation of a descendant from changing its ancestor's snapshot.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each search child receives an independent solver-state snapshot; discarding it restores the unchanged parent state.
knowledge_statements.title: Copying

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm matches whole-state copying in search, but no cited source supports the snapshot-independence and state-completeness requirements. The inventory's copying-constraints material concerns a different concept.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkpoint-placement variants for checkpoint-and-replay restoration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Root recomputation retains only the root checkpoint and replays the entire decision prefix. Fixed-interval recomputation retains checkpoints at prescribed path-distance intervals. Adaptive recomputation chooses checkpoints using estimated replay cost, checkpoint cost, or observed subtree behavior. Each policy is correct when restoration begins from an ancestor checkpoint and ordered replay produces a state equivalent for all future search outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recomputation may replay from the root, regularly spaced checkpoints, or adaptively selected checkpoints.
assumptions_latex: The chosen checkpoint is an ancestor of the target node.
Recorded decisions are replayed in path order.
Replay is deterministic or confluent with respect to future search.

notation.meaning: Equivalence for all future search outcomes

knowledge_statements.title: Root, Fixed-Interval, and Adaptive Recomputation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restoration and active-path storage bounds under uniform checkpoint spacing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every active target has an ancestor checkpoint at path distance at most \(k\), restoration replays at most \(k\) branch-and-propagate transitions. If each transition costs at most \(R\), replay costs \(O(kR)\), excluding checkpoint initialization. Uniform spacing by \(k\) on a path of depth \(h\) retains \(O(h/k+1)\) checkpoints; if each checkpoint occupies at most \(N\) space, their active-path storage is \(O((h/k+1)N)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximum checkpoint gap k gives O(kR) replay time and, with uniform spacing, O((h/k + 1)N) active-path checkpoint space.
assumptions_latex: The checkpoint gap is at most \(k\).
Each replay transition costs at most \(R\).
Each retained checkpoint occupies at most \(N\) space.
The storage count concerns active-path checkpoints.

notation.meaning: Maximum cost of one replay transition

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Gap Checkpoint Replay

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness boundary for omitted history-dependent or nondeterministic state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replaying the same branching decisions is insufficient when propagation or later search depends on unrecorded history \(H\) and possible histories yield states that are not equivalent for future search. Correct recomputation must reproduce the relevant choices, checkpoint their effects, or guarantee confluence to a future-equivalent state. Byte-for-byte identity is unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decision replay is correct only when omitted history cannot change future search, or its relevant effects are reproduced or checkpointed.
assumptions_latex: Propagation or scheduling may depend on history \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{same decisions}\not\Rightarrow S_{\mathrm{replay}}\equiv_{\mathrm{future}}S_{\mathrm{target}}\text{ without confluence or relevant-history recovery}.
knowledge_statements.title: Replay-Equivalence Boundary

assumptions_latex: Branch decisions on the path from a retained checkpoint are replayable.
Propagation from a fixed checkpoint and fixed decision sequence is deterministic or semantically confluent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replay reconstructs a state semantically equivalent to the state previously reached at the target node.

notation.meaning: Ordered decisions from checkpoint c to target v

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses recomputation in constraint-programming search.
Checkpoint policy and semantic-equivalence conditions need a dedicated source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkpoint-and-replay restoration during constraint-programming search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Retain selected checkpoint states, including \(S_c\), and record the ordered branching decisions \((d_{c+1},\ldots,d_v)\) leading to each active node \(v\). To restore \(v\), initialize \(S:=\operatorname{copy}(S_c)\); for each recorded decision \(d_i\) in order, impose \(d_i\) and replace \(S\) by its propagation closure \(P(S\wedge d_i)\). Stop early and report failure if any closure is inconsistent. Otherwise, after the final decision, output the reconstructed state \(S_v\). Correctness requires that replay preserve the domains and auxiliary propagator information relevant to all future search outcomes, even if internal representations differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restore a search node by copying an earlier checkpoint and replaying its decisions and propagation in order.
knowledge_statements.title: Recomputation

children.title: Persistent Structures
children.top_down_role: Version-preserving solver structures, sharing regimes, and memory consequences.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional cost bound for cell-based path-copying or copy-on-write structures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an update creates or copies exactly \(c\) constant-size representation cells and shares every other reachable cell immutably, then cell creation requires \(\Theta(c)\) work and \(\Theta(c)\) additional space, excluding the cost of locating modified cells. The memory occupied by retained versions is the size of their shared reachable union rather than necessarily the sum of separate full-state sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With immutable structural sharing, update work and extra space are proportional to the copied cells, and retained versions occupy their shared union.
assumptions_latex: Shared cells are immutable.
Each created cell has constant size.
Exactly \(c\) cells are created or copied by the update.

notation.meaning: Number of cells created or copied by one update

knowledge_statements.title: Structural-Sharing Update Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistence variants classified by which retained versions may be updated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A versioned structure is partially persistent when every retained version may be queried but updates are permitted only to the current newest version. It is fully persistent when any retained version may be updated to create a new descendant, allowing the version history to branch. In both regimes, creating descendants leaves observations of existing versions unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial persistence permits queries of all versions but updates only the newest; full persistence lets any retained version spawn a new branch.
assumptions_latex: Versions expose a fixed family of observable queries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{partial: update only the newest version;}\qquad\text{full: update any retained version}.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial and Full Persistence

assumptions_latex: Solver-state versions are indexed by search nodes.
An update may create a new representation while retaining earlier versions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every retained version remains accessible and observationally unchanged after descendant versions are created.

notation.meaning: Version associated with search node v
State update producing a new version

review_flags: No supplied locator covers persistent data structures for backtrackable solver state.
Persistence model and observational semantics require a suitable source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partial persistence of solver data across search-tree versions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A solver-state representation is persistent when an update applied to a version \(S_v\) creates a version \(S_w=U(S_v)\) without destroying \(S_v\). For every retained ancestor version \(S_u\) and every supported observable query \(q\), creating or modifying descendants leaves \(q(S_u)\) unchanged. Backtracking selects the required version reference rather than executing inverse updates. Structural sharing between \(S_u\) and \(S_w\) is permitted only when shared components are immutable or updated by copy-on-write, so that no descendant operation can alter the observable state of an ancestor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A persistent solver representation creates new versions while keeping all retained ancestor versions accessible and unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Structures

children.title: Reversible Structures
children.top_down_role: Restorable solver structures, backtracking integration, and mutation boundaries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by restoring domains but not search-relevant auxiliary state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose backtracking restores domain \(D(x)\) but leaves a propagator cache \(a\) at its descendant value. If later scheduling or pruning depends on \((D(x),a)\), the restored configuration can behave differently from the ancestor although its variable domains agree. Domain restoration alone therefore does not establish reversibility when auxiliary state affects future search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restoring domains is insufficient when a stale propagator cache can alter later scheduling or pruning.
assumptions_latex: Auxiliary datum \(a\) can affect subsequent propagation.
Backtracking restores \(D(x)\) but not \(a\).
knowledge_statements.title: Unrestored Auxiliary-State Failure

assumptions_latex: Search levels are properly nested.
Every update of reversible data has a corresponding restoration action or level-indexed saved value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Restoration to level \(k\) recovers the observable state recorded at entry to level \(k\).

notation.meaning: Observable state of R at level k

review_flags: No supplied locator defines reversible structures in propagation engines.
A dedicated constraint-programming source is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: In-place mutable structures equipped with search-level restoration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mutable solver structure \(R\) is reversible if, for each entered search level \(k\), its observable state \(R_k\) is recoverable by a restoration operation \(\rho_k\) after any finite sequence of deeper, properly recorded updates. Formally, if \(U_{k+1},\ldots,U_m\) are updates performed below level \(k\), then \(\rho_k(U_m(\cdots U_{k+1}(R_k)\cdots))\) is observationally equivalent to \(R_k\). Restoration may use trailed values, timestamps, or inverse actions. It need not preserve object identity or irrelevant internal layout, but it must restore every domain, propagator datum, and queue component that can affect subsequent search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reversible structure mutates in place but can restore every search-relevant observation to its value at an earlier level.
knowledge_statements.title: Reversible Structures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits reversible structures, but the observational restoration contract and inclusion of domains, propagator data, and queues are unsupported by a cited source.

children.title: Persistence–Reversibility Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Sharing, restoration cost, memory use, and search-regime suitability.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Access-pattern distinction between retained versions and a lone nested undo state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A persistent representation may retain versions \(S_{v_1},\ldots,S_{v_r}\) and select any retained version without changing the others. A reversible representation consisting only of one mutable current state and nested undo information directly restores states along its current ancestor chain; access to an unrelated retained branch requires an added snapshot, replay, redo, or equivalent version mechanism. Thus arbitrary retained-version selection is native to persistence but not supplied by a lone LIFO undo state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistence supports selection among retained versions; a lone reversible LIFO state needs an additional mechanism to reach an unrelated retained branch.
assumptions_latex: Persistent versions remain observationally unchanged.
The reversible representation contains one current state and only nested undo information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Arbitrary retained-version selection is not provided by a lone LIFO undo state.}

notation.meaning: Solver-state version associated with search node \(v_i\)

knowledge_statements.title: Version-Access Order Boundary

assumptions_latex: Persistent and reversible representations implement the same observable solver-state interface.
Updates occur along a depth-first search with possible retained branches.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither representation uniformly dominates: cost depends on update volume, sharing, checkpoint retention, and restoration frequency.

notation.meaning: Cost of producing a descendant version
Cost of restoring or selecting an ancestor

review_flags: Tradeoff is model-dependent and lacks a supplied supporting locator.
Complexity claims need a source specifying persistence and trailing cost models.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative cost boundary between persistent versioning and reversible mutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For equivalent solver states, persistence typically pays \(C_{\mathrm{upd}}\) to allocate a new version and may reduce \(C_{\mathrm{back}}\) to selecting an existing version; reversible mutation typically reduces allocation during forward updates but pays to record and execute restoration information. Persistence can share immutable substructure across simultaneously retained branches, while reversibility naturally exploits a single depth-first current path. Consequently, total time and memory \(M\) are functions of the number and locality of updates, the amount of structural sharing, the number of live versions, and backtracking frequency. Without fixing these parameters and the data structure, no general asymptotic dominance follows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistence favors retained versions and sharing; reversibility favors in-place depth-first updates, so neither dominates without a workload and cost model.
knowledge_statements.title: Persistence–Reversibility Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The qualitative property fits the tradeoff leaf, but its allocation, sharing, restoration, and non-dominance claims require a source that states the applicable representation and workload model.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Immediate construction and storage of propagation explanations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the explanation store empty. When a propagator derives a literal \(p\) from the current active literals \(A\), immediately compute a finite reason \(R_p\subseteq A\) such that \(\bigwedge_{r\in R_p}r\Rightarrow p\) is valid for the propagator's constraint. Store \((p,R_p)\) before placing \(p\) on the propagation trail. If no valid reason can be produced, do not expose \(p\) to explanation-based conflict analysis. Stop when propagation reaches a fixpoint or conflict; output the propagated trail together with a stored reason for every explained propagation. Backtracking may discard reasons whose propagated literals are removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eager generation computes and stores a valid explanation at the same time each literal is propagated.
knowledge_statements.title: Eager Reason Generation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits eager reason generation and states a soundness condition, but no cited source supports the reason lifecycle, trail ordering, or behavior when a reason is unavailable.

children.title: Lazy Reason Generation
children.top_down_role: Deferred reason construction, reconstruction requirements, and suitable propagation contexts.

assumptions_latex: A propagator can retain enough witness state to reconstruct a reason later.
Any reconstructed reason uses literals valid at the propagation's recorded context.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On demand, the generator returns \(R_p\) satisfying \(\bigwedge_{r\in R_p}r\Rightarrow p\), or explicitly reports that no reason is available.

Required witness persistence and historical-context semantics need authoritative sourcing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: On-demand reconstruction of explanations for earlier propagations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When a propagator derives \(p\), record a witness \(w_p\) and the propagation context needed for later explanation, but do not necessarily materialize a reason. If conflict analysis requests the reason for \(p\), invoke the propagator's explanation procedure on \(w_p\) and that recorded context to produce a finite set \(R_p\). Accept the output only if its literals held in the relevant context and \(\bigwedge_{r\in R_p}r\Rightarrow p\) is valid for the constraint. Cache \(R_p\) optionally. Stop after returning a valid reason or an explicit unavailable result; the interface must not substitute literals that became true only after \(p\) was propagated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lazy generation stores a witness at propagation time and reconstructs a valid historical reason only when conflict analysis requests it.
knowledge_statements.title: Lazy Reason Generation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits lazy reason generation, but witness retention, historical-context reconstruction, and the unavailable-result behavior require authoritative support.

children.title: Reason-Generation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Latency, memory, reconstruction cost, and explanation availability across generation regimes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic work comparison for the same propagation sequence and requested-reason set; memory and latency require separate measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be the explained propagations and \(Q\subseteq P\) those whose reasons are requested. Let \(e_p\) be eager construction work, \(w_p\) lazy witness-maintenance work, and \(r_p\) lazy reconstruction work. After excluding work common to both regimes, lazy generation uses less total work exactly when \(\sum_{p\in P}w_p+\sum_{p\in Q}r_p<\sum_{p\in P}e_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lazy generation saves total construction work exactly when witness maintenance plus requested reconstructions cost less than eagerly constructing every reason.
assumptions_latex: Both regimes soundly explain the same propagations.
All costs are measured under one additive accounting model.
Repeated requests are included in \(r_p\) or eliminated by caching consistently.

notation.meaning: eager construction, lazy witness, and lazy reconstruction work

review_flags: The inequality is an accounting condition, not an implementation-independent performance prediction.
Peak memory and request latency must be compared separately.
knowledge_statements.title: Work Threshold for Lazy Materialization

assumptions_latex: Eager and lazy regimes produce logically valid reasons for the same propagations.
Conflict analysis requests reasons for only a subset of propagated literals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Eager generation shifts work and storage to propagation; lazy generation avoids unused reasons but incurs reconstruction and witness-retention costs.

notation.meaning: Cost of constructing the reason for p

review_flags: No supplied source covers reason-generation cost regimes.
The comparison needs an explicit implementation and cost model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work, memory, and historical-state tradeoffs between eager and lazy reasons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Ignoring shared overhead, eager generation performs reason construction for all \(N\) explained propagations, with construction work \(\sum_{p}c(p)\), and stores materialized reasons until they can be released. Lazy generation constructs reasons only for the \(Q\) requested propagations, but must retain witnesses or historical state sufficient for sound reconstruction and may increase conflict-analysis latency. Thus \(Q\ll N\) favors laziness when witnesses are compact, whereas frequent reason requests, cheap immediate explanations, or expensive historical reconstruction can favor eagerness. Logical soundness is identical only if both regimes return reasons valid for the propagation context.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eager reasons cost work for every propagation; lazy reasons save unused work but retain witnesses and add on-demand latency.
knowledge_statements.title: Reason-Generation Tradeoffs

children.title: Conflict Interface
children.top_down_role: Propagation-to-conflict-analysis communication, explanation payloads, and interface boundaries.

assumptions_latex: The current assignment or domain state is inconsistent with at least one active constraint.
Conflict analysis consumes finite sets of active literals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A returned conflict set \(C\) certifies inconsistency through \(\bigwedge_{\ell\in C}\ell\Rightarrow\bot\).
review_flags: No supplied locator defines a conflict interface for explanation-producing propagators.
Literal encoding and verification contract require a relevant solver source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagator-to-analysis contract for reporting an explained inconsistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conflict interface accepts a failing propagator and its current active-literal context \(A\), and returns a finite set \(C\subseteq A\) such that the propagator's constraint validates \(\bigwedge_{\ell\in C}\ell\Rightarrow\bot\). The interface must distinguish an explained conflict from an unexplained failure and must preserve the search-level identity of every literal in \(C\). A checker can verify the certificate by confirming membership in the relevant context and validating that the constraint has no solution satisfying all literals of \(C\). The conflict set need not be minimal, but removing literals is permitted only when the implication remains valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conflict interface returns active literals whose conjunction is impossible, providing a checkable explanation of propagator failure.
knowledge_statements.title: Conflict Interface

children.title: Nogood Interface
children.top_down_role: Nogood production, consumption, retention, and propagation-facing integration.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation and conflict outcomes when a valid registered nogood is evaluated under a partial assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N=\{\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_k\}\) be a registered nogood. If every \(\ell\in N\) is true, report conflict. If exactly one literal \(u\in N\) is unassigned and every literal in \(N\setminus\{u\}\) is true, enforce \(\bar u\). If some literal of \(N\) is false, the nogood is already satisfied; otherwise it produces no inference.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nogood conflicts when all its literals are true and propagates the complement of its sole unassigned literal when all the others are true.
assumptions_latex: \(N\) is valid in the current model and assumption scope.
Literal truth, falsity, unassignment, and complementation are defined consistently.

notation.meaning: sole unassigned literal in the unit case

knowledge_statements.title: Nogood Consumption Semantics

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary for retaining conditional nogoods across assumption or constraint changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nogood \(N\) may remain active after a context change only if the constraints \(C'\) active in the new context entail \(\neg\bigwedge_{\ell\in N}\ell\). If its derivation depends on removable assumptions \(H\), sound registration must either deactivate \(N\) when \(H\) is inactive or encode the dependency as \(\left(\bigwedge_{h\in H}h\right)\Rightarrow\neg\bigwedge_{\ell\in N}\ell\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A learned nogood may outlive its original context only while it remains entailed; conditional nogoods must retain or encode their supporting assumptions.
assumptions_latex: The solver may remove assumptions or constraints while retaining learned records.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C'\not\models\neg\bigwedge_{\ell\in N}\ell\quad\Longrightarrow\quad N\text{ cannot be activated unconditionally under }C'.

notation.meaning: constraints active after the context change

knowledge_statements.title: Scope-Safe Nogood Retention

assumptions_latex: Solver literals have a defined complement operation.
A finite reason or conflict set is valid in the relevant propagation context.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface emits a clause or forbidden conjunction logically entailed by the modeled constraints.

notation.meaning: Finite set of literals forbidden jointly

review_flags: No supplied locator covers nogood exchange in constraint or clause-learning solvers.
The required literal and clause representation needs authoritative sourcing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation contract between propagator explanations and nogood learning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nogood interface represents a finite forbidden conjunction by a set \(N=\{\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_k\}\) satisfying \(\neg(\ell_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\ell_k)\). Equivalently, it may emit the clause \(K_N=\bar\ell_1\vee\cdots\vee\bar\ell_k\). The interface must provide canonical solver literals, their complements, and any search-level metadata required by propagation and conflict analysis. It accepts \(N\) only when the modeled constraints entail \(K_N\); duplicate literals may be removed, but contradictory, undefined, or context-invalid encodings must be rejected. The output is the registered nogood or its equivalent clause representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nogood interface encodes a forbidden set of jointly true literals as the equivalent clause of their complements.
knowledge_statements.title: Nogood Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly relates a forbidden conjunction to a clause of complemented literals, but the canonical-literal, metadata, validation, and registration requirements lack a relevant cited source.

children.title: Conflict-to-Nogood Translation
children.top_down_role: Representation transfer between detected conflicts and reusable nogood records.

knowledge_statements.title: Conflict-to-Nogood Translation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation for finite-domain equality literals under an explanation-producing propagator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A=\{x_1=a_1,\ldots,x_m=a_m\}\) be a set of decision or propagated literals whose conjunction is certified inconsistent with the constraint set \(C\). The associated nogood is \(N=A\), interpreted as the forbidden simultaneous assignment \(\neg\bigwedge_{i=1}^m(x_i=a_i)\). Its clausal representation is
\[\bigvee_{i=1}^m(x_i\ne a_i).\]
Every solution of \(C\) satisfies this clause. If the conflict explanation is conditional on additional valid premises, those premises must also occur in \(A\); otherwise the translated nogood need not be globally valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inconsistent conjunction of assignment literals becomes a nogood forbidding that conjunction, equivalently a clause containing the negation of every explained literal.
assumptions_latex: \(C\land\bigwedge_{i=1}^m(x_i=a_i)\) is unsatisfiable.
Every premise used by the conflict explanation is represented in \(A\).

notation.meaning: set of literals explaining the conflict
nogood represented by the forbidden literal set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically coherent and fits the translation-interface leaf, but no citation supports the explanation-to-nogood validity conditions.

Every literal has a semantics-preserving complement.

children.title: Propagation–Search Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Propagation roles at search boundaries without duplicating branching, learning, or optimization algorithms.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Chapter 8: Search; forward checking, partial lookahead, and maintaining arc consistency

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Descent Bound for Root Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound on strict store changes rather than propagator invocations or internal runtime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every root propagator is contracting, every strict store change deletes at least one current value. Thus an execution starting from \(D^0\) has at most \(\sum_x|D^0(x)|\) strict changes before failure or stability. This does not bound no-op invocations or propagator cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite contracting root propagation can make only finitely many strict domain changes, though it may perform additional no-op work.
assumptions_latex: All initial domains are finite.
Every propagator is contracting.
Every strict store change deletes at least one value.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Descent Bound for Root Closure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonempty Root Closure Need Not Prove Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for root closure instantiated by arc-consistency propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For three variables with domains \(\{0,1\}\) and pairwise disequalities on a triangle, every arc-consistency propagator is already at a fixpoint, yet the CSP is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arc-consistency root closure leaves the infeasible two-color triangle unchanged.
assumptions_latex: The root propagator family enforces binary arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonempty Root Closure Need Not Prove Feasibility
Root Consistency Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common fixpoint closure of contracting propagators before search begins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D^0\) be the initial finite-domain store and let \(P=\{p_1,\ldots,p_r\}\) be sound, monotone, contracting propagators ordered by componentwise domain inclusion. A root consistency closure is a store \(D^*\subseteq D^0\) obtained by fair repeated application of propagators such that
\[p_j(D^*)=D^*\qquad(j=1,\ldots,r).\]
When every propagator is monotone, fair iteration from \(D^0\) computes the greatest common fixpoint contained in \(D^0\). If any component domain of \(D^*\) is empty, the original root problem is inconsistent; otherwise search starts from \(D^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Root closure repeatedly applies all propagators before branching until none changes the domains; an empty domain proves root infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(D^0\) is a finite-domain store.
Each \(p_j\) is sound, monotone, and contracting.
The propagation schedule is fair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*\) is the greatest common fixpoint of \(P\) below \(D^0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but the greatest-common-fixpoint claim requires an inspectable propagation or chaotic-iteration source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sound Reduction Is Not Complete Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between solution preservation and removal of every globally unsupported value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The identity reduction \(r(D)=D\) is sound for every CSP but can retain values occurring in no solution. Sound static reduction therefore does not imply domain consistency, maximal reduction, or detection of every infeasible root instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Doing no deletion is sound but can retain globally unsupported values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S(C,r(D))=S(C,D)\centernot\Rightarrow\text{every surviving value extends to a solution}.
knowledge_statements.title: Sound Reduction Is Not Complete Filtering

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of root-preprocessing soundness under sequential composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D^i=r_i(D^{i-1})\). If every step satisfies \(S(C,D^i)=S(C,D^{i-1})\), then \(S(C,D^k)=S(C,D^0)\). Incomplete reductions can nevertheless produce order-dependent final stores when they are not iterated to a common fixpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequentially composing sound root reductions remains sound, although incomplete pipelines can be order dependent.
assumptions_latex: Each reduction is contracting.
Each reduction preserves all solutions in its input store.
knowledge_statements.title: Composition of Sound Static Reductions
Static Domain Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solution-preserving domain deletion performed once at the root node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a constraint satisfaction problem with constraints \(C\), initial store \(D\), and solution set \(S(C,D)\), a static domain reduction replaces \(D\) by \(D'\subseteq D\) before branching. The reduction is sound exactly when
\[S(C,D')=S(C,D).\]
Equivalently, every deleted value \(a\in D(x)\setminus D'(x)\) has no extension to a solution of \(C\) within \(D\). Such reduction may be incomplete: a surviving value need not extend to a solution unless the employed consistency notion guarantees that stronger property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Static reduction deletes values before search while preserving every solution; soundness requires each deleted value to lack any feasible extension.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is fixed during preprocessing.
\(D'\subseteq D\) componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reduction is solution-preserving if and only if \(S(C,D')=S(C,D)\).

notation.meaning: domain stores before and after reduction
solutions of the constraints within the store

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The solution-preservation characterization is plausible, but no relevant preprocessing source is cited. The record also reads more like a definition or condition than a property.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost of checking constraints incident to one newly assigned variable in a normalized binary CSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume at most one explicit binary relation per variable pair and \(O(1)\) compatibility tests. After assigning \(x_k\), a direct forward-checking pass takes \(O(\sum_{x_j\in N^+(x_k)}|D(x_j)|)\) time, at most \(O(\deg^+(x_k)d)\) when residual domains have size at most \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One direct forward-checking pass is linear in the total current domain size of the newly assigned variable's unassigned neighbors.
assumptions_latex: The binary CSP is normalized to one relation per variable pair.
A compatibility test against the assigned value takes constant time.
Residual domain size is at most \(d\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forward Checking Can Miss Residual Inconsistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical separation between forward checking and propagation among unassigned variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x,y,z\in\{0,1\}\) with \(x
e y\), \(x
e z\), and \(y
e z\). After assigning \(x=0\), forward checking reduces \(D(y)=D(z)=\{1\}\) but, because it does not revise the constraint whose endpoints are both unassigned, need not detect the violated constraint \(y
e z\) immediately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward checking can leave nonempty domains even though constraints among unassigned variables are already inconsistent.
assumptions_latex: Forward checking revises only constraints incident to the newly assigned variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D(y)=D(z)=\{1\}\land y\ne z\text{ is inconsistent but need not be rejected immediately.}
knowledge_statements.title: Forward Checking Can Miss Residual Inconsistency

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness of deleting values incompatible with the newest assignment in a binary CSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After assigning \(x_k=a_k\), deleting \(b\in D(x_j)\) whenever \((a_k,b)\notin R_{kj}\) removes no completion of the current partial assignment, because every completion must satisfy \(R_{kj}\). Consequently, an empty revised domain certifies that the current partial assignment has no feasible completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward checking preserves every completion, and an emptied revised neighbor domain certifies failure of the current branch.
assumptions_latex: \(R_{kj}\) exactly represents the binary constraint between \(x_k\) and \(x_j\).
\(x_k=a_k\) is fixed in the current branch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D'(x_j)=\varnothing\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{the current partial assignment has no feasible completion}.

notation.meaning: domain after checking compatibility with the newest assignment

knowledge_statements.title: Solution Preservation of Forward Checking
Forward Checking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical forward checking for a binary finite-domain CSP under a fixed variable order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a binary CSP with variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), a partial assignment to \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\), and current domains for the unassigned variables, forward checking revises every constraint joining the newly assigned variable \(x_k=a_k\) to an unassigned variable \(x_j\). It replaces
\[D(x_j)\leftarrow\{b\in D(x_j):(a_k,b)\in R_{kj}\}.\]
The node fails if some revised domain becomes empty. Otherwise the reduced store is retained and search selects another unassigned variable. Forward checking does not revise constraints whose two endpoints are both unassigned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After each assignment, forward checking removes incompatible values from neighboring unassigned variables and backtracks if a domain becomes empty.
assumptions_latex: The CSP has finitely many variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), binary constraints, and finite domains.
\(x_k=a_k\) is the newest assignment.
Every relevant binary relation \(R_{kj}\) can be tested.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every retained value adjacent to \(x_k=a_k\) is compatible with that assignment.

notation.meaning: current domain of unassigned variable x_j
allowed-pair relation between x_k and x_j

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cost of a Fixed Partial-Lookahead Sweep
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Naive table-scan cost for a prescribed nonrepeating schedule of binary revisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every current domain has size at most \(d\), testing an allowed pair costs \(O(1)\), and no directed arc is rescheduled, one naive revision costs \(O(d^2)\). A sweep over \(Q\) therefore costs \(O(|Q|d^2)\), excluding forward checking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed naive sweep over Q costs O(|Q|d²), excluding forward checking.
assumptions_latex: Binary relation membership is testable in constant time.
Each domain has size at most \(d\).
No directed arc is rescheduled during the measured sweep.
knowledge_statements.title: Cost of a Fixed Partial-Lookahead Sweep

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Witness that partial lookahead need not leave the future store arc consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let future variables \(x,y\) have \(D(x)=D(y)=\{0\}\) and constraint \(x\ne y\). If the schedule processes neither direction of this constraint, both domains remain nonempty although neither value has support and the residual CSP is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Omitting the only inconsistent future constraint can leave nonempty domains that are neither arc consistent nor feasible.
assumptions_latex: The partial-lookahead schedule omits both directed arcs between \(x\) and \(y\).
knowledge_statements.title: Omitted-Arc Counterexample
Partial Lookahead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional partial lookahead for an ordered binary finite-domain CSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an ordered binary finite-domain CSP with variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and an assignment to \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\), first perform forward checking. Then process a prescribed incomplete schedule \(Q\) of directed arcs between future variables \(x_{k+1},\ldots,x_n\), revising each selected arc \((i,j)\) by
\[D(x_i)\leftarrow\{a\in D(x_i):\exists b\in D(x_j),\ (a,b)\in R_{ij}\}.\]
The node fails when a domain becomes empty. Otherwise search continues with the resulting store. Because \(Q\) does not require arc-consistency closure over the entire future subproblem, the resulting future store need not be arc consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial lookahead performs forward checking plus an incomplete schedule of revisions among future variables, without requiring full arc-consistency closure.
assumptions_latex: The CSP has ordered variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), binary constraints, and finite domains.
\(Q\) is a specified schedule of future-variable arcs that does not require full arc-consistency closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each selected revision removes values unsupported on its processed arc, but the final future subproblem need not be arc consistent.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed comparison between nested revision schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The proposed implication \(Q_1\subseteq Q_2\Rightarrow D_{Q_2}\subseteq D_{Q_1}\) is not determined by set inclusion alone when schedules may order each directed revision differently and do not reschedule arcs to a fixpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested sets of arcs do not by themselves order the stores produced by one-pass schedules with different revision orders.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q_1\subseteq Q_2\centernot\Rightarrow D_{Q_2}\subseteq D_{Q_1}\text{ without an execution-prefix or closure condition}.
knowledge_statements.title: Schedule Monotonicity of Partial Lookahead

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case cost under the explicit convention that full lookahead is implemented as AC-3 arc-consistency closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a binary residual CSP with \(e\) directed arcs and maximum domain size \(d\), a standard AC-3 closure takes \(O(ed^3)\) time and \(O(e+nd)\) space with explicit domains and an arc queue. Repeating closure independently at search nodes multiplies this cost by the number of visited nodes; incremental implementations may reuse work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the AC-3 interpretation, one full-lookahead arc-consistency closure takes O(ed^3) worst-case time.
assumptions_latex: The CSP is binary with explicit finite domains.
Full lookahead is explicitly defined as AC-3 arc-consistency closure.
\(e\) counts directed arcs and \(d\) bounds domain size.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arc Consistency Does Not Decide Satisfiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness boundary for full arc-consistency lookahead.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x,y,z\) each have domain \(\{0,1\}\), with \(x
e y\), \(y
e z\), and \(z
e x\). Every value has support across each incident constraint, so the instance is arc consistent, but no assignment satisfies all three disequalities.

assumptions_latex: Full lookahead enforces binary arc consistency, not a stronger global consistency.
knowledge_statements.title: Arc Consistency Does Not Decide Satisfiability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strength comparison under the binary arc-consistency interpretation of full lookahead.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from the same post-decision store, full arc-consistency lookahead performs the revisions required by forward checking and continues fairly revising every residual arc to a common fixpoint. Its final domains are therefore subsets of the forward-checking domains, and it detects every failure detected by forward checking; the converse need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full arc-consistency lookahead is at least as strong as forward checking on the same binary CSP store.
assumptions_latex: Both methods start from the same domains after the same decision.
Full lookahead fairly revises every residual arc to a fixpoint.
Both methods use the standard binary-CSP definitions.
review_flags: Comparison is conditional on the standard binary arc-consistency interpretation.
knowledge_statements.title: Dominance over Forward Checking

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure characterization conditional on defining full lookahead as fair binary arc-consistency enforcement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite binary CSP, fair iteration of standard arc-revision operators from store \(D^0\) terminates at a common fixpoint \(D^*\). This fixpoint is the greatest substore of \(D^0\) closed under every such revision and is independent of fair revision order, although computation cost may depend on scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the binary arc-consistency convention, fair full lookahead reaches the unique greatest arc-consistent subdomain of the starting store.
assumptions_latex: Full lookahead means fair closure under all standard binary arc-revision operators.
All domains are finite.
Each revision deletes exactly values lacking support on the revised arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D^*=\max\{D\subseteq D^0:D\text{ is closed under every standard arc revision}\}.
review_flags: The result applies only under the binary arc-consistency interpretation of full lookahead.
knowledge_statements.title: Greatest Arc-Consistent Subdomain Fixpoint
Full Lookahead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full arc-consistency lookahead on the residual binary CSP after each branching decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a binary finite-domain CSP and a current partial assignment, restrict every assigned variable to its chosen singleton and repeatedly revise every directed arc \((i,j)\) of the residual constraint graph by
\[D(x_i)\leftarrow\{a\in D(x_i):\exists b\in D(x_j),\ (a,b)\in R_{ij}\}\]
until a common fixpoint is reached. Reject the search node if any domain becomes empty; otherwise branch from the resulting store. At termination, every value of every residual domain has support across each incident binary constraint, so the residual CSP is arc consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full lookahead enforces arc consistency throughout the residual binary CSP after each decision and rejects the node if any domain empties.
assumptions_latex: The CSP is binary and finite-domain.
Arc revisions are scheduled fairly until no domain changes.

Maintaining Arc Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: MAC search for binary finite-domain constraint satisfaction problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At each search node of a binary finite-domain CSP, impose the current branching decision on the inherited domain store and enforce arc consistency to a fixpoint. For every directed constraint arc \((i,j)\), delete each \(a\in D(x_i)\) for which
\[\nexists b\in D(x_j)\quad (a,b)\in R_{ij}.\]
If a domain becomes empty, backtrack; if all domains are singleton, return the induced solution; otherwise branch and repeat on each child. Domain changes are trailed or copied so that backtracking restores the parent store.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MAC enforces binary arc consistency after every search decision, backtracking on an empty domain and restoring domains when leaving a branch.
assumptions_latex: The CSP is binary and finite-domain.
Arc revision is sound and scheduled to a fixpoint.

knowledge_statements.title: Maintaining Generalized Arc Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search maintaining generalized arc consistency for arbitrary finite-arity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At each search node, impose the branching decision and propagate every constraint \(c\) to generalized arc consistency. For each variable \(x\in\operatorname{scope}(c)\), retain \(a\in D(x)\) only if there exists a tuple \(t\in c\) satisfying
\[t_x=a\quad\text{and}\quad t_y\in D(y)\ \text{for every }y\in\operatorname{scope}(c).\]
Repeat constraint propagation to a fixpoint. Backtrack if any domain becomes empty; otherwise continue branching from the reduced store, restoring the parent store upon backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MGAC restores tuple support for every value in every constraint after each decision, then backtracks if propagation empties a domain.
assumptions_latex: All variables have finite domains.
Each constraint propagator soundly removes values lacking a supporting tuple.

Maintaining Stronger Consistencies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search maintaining a chosen consistency strictly stronger than generalized arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a sound local-consistency operator on finite-domain stores such that every \(K\)-consistent store is generalized arc consistent. Maintaining \(K\) during search means applying the branching decision at each node and computing \(K(D)\) to a fixpoint before further branching. If \(K(D)\) contains an empty domain or otherwise detects inconsistency, the node is rejected. Otherwise search continues from \(K(D)\). Soundness requires
\[S(C,K(D))=S(C,D),\]
although the stronger deletions may incur greater propagation cost than generalized arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stronger-consistency search restores a sound consistency stronger than GAC after every decision, trading potentially greater pruning for higher propagation cost.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is contracting and solution-preserving.
\(K\)-consistency implies generalized arc consistency.
The finite-domain propagation process terminates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact support formulation for an explicit finite-domain objective relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the relation \(z=f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) and current finite domains, domain consistency holds when every retained value of each variable belongs to a tuple in \(D(z)\times\prod_iD(x_i)\) satisfying \(z=f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\). Enforcing it deletes exactly the values unsupported by this objective relation; support in this relation alone need not satisfy unrelated model constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domain-consistent objective propagation retains exactly values supported by the explicit objective relation within the current domains.
assumptions_latex: The objective is represented by \(z=f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\).
All participating domains are finite.

Thus exact extrema need not establish domain consistency for the objective relation.

Iteration \(D^{t+1}=P(D^t)\) terminates after finitely many strict deletions at a fixpoint \(D^*=P(D^*)\), and every tuple satisfying the objective relation in \(D^0\) remains represented in \(D^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contracting sound objective propagator over finite domains reaches a solution-preserving fixpoint after finitely many deletions.

\(P\) is contracting, monotone, and solution-preserving.

Objective Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound propagation from an explicit objective variable in a minimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Represent the minimization objective by a variable \(z\) constrained by \(z=f(x)\), with current domains or bounds for \(x\) and \(z\). An objective propagator computes a valid lower bound \(L(D)\) on \(f\) over the current store and updates
\[\underline z\leftarrow\max\{\underline z,L(D)\}.\]
It then propagates the constraint \(z=f(x)\) backward, deleting values or tightening variable bounds that cannot attain any objective value remaining in \(D(z)\). Updates repeat to a fixpoint or until infeasibility is detected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective propagation derives objective bounds from decision-variable domains and pushes the remaining objective range back to prune those domains.
assumptions_latex: The problem minimizes \(f(x)\).
\(L(D)\le f(x)\) for every feasible x represented by D.
Backward pruning through \(z=f(x)\) is solution-preserving.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The updated store preserves all feasible points and satisfies \(z\ge L(D)\).

notation.meaning: valid objective lower bound over D

children.title: Incumbent Propagation
children.top_down_role: Propagation driven by incumbent solutions, improving bounds, and dominance consequences.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness boundary for pruning driven by an incumbent or another certified upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A minimization cutoff \(f(x)<U\) is sound for strict-improvement search whenever \(U\) is a valid upper bound on the optimum for the same model and objective. Calling \(U\) an incumbent additionally requires a verified feasible witness \(\hat x\) with \(f(\hat x)=U\). An unsupported value below the true optimum can remove every feasible solution and cause a false infeasibility or optimality conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cutoff needs a valid upper bound; an incumbent value specifically needs a verified feasible witness for the same problem.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem.
A strict cutoff \(f(x)<U\) is proposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U\text{ must be a valid upper bound, and incumbent status requires }\exists\hat x\in F:\ f(\hat x)=U.

notation.meaning: feasible set of the current model

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nesting of strict-improvement regions as minimization incumbents improve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization define \(C(U)=\{x:f(x)<U\}\). If verified incumbent values for the same model and objective satisfy \(U'\le U\), then \(C(U')\subseteq C(U)\). Thus replacing \(U\) by a better incumbent can only preserve or strengthen cutoff pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A better minimization incumbent yields a nested, never weaker strict-improvement region.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(U'\) are verified incumbent values for the same minimization model and objective.

notation.meaning: assignments strictly improving incumbent value U

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity of Incumbent Cutoff Propagation
Incumbent Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict incumbent cutoff propagation for exact minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U=f(\hat x)\) be the objective value of a feasible incumbent \(\hat x\) in a minimization problem. To search only for a strict improvement, add the cutoff
\[f(x)<U,\]
or \(f(x)\le U-1\) when the objective is integer-valued. Propagate this cutoff with all model constraints, deleting any domain value whose every feasible extension has objective at least \(U\). A node is pruned when its valid objective lower bound is at least \(U\); discovery of a better feasible solution replaces \(U\) by its smaller value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incumbent propagation posts a strict-improvement cutoff, prunes nodes unable to beat the incumbent, and tightens the cutoff whenever a better solution appears.
assumptions_latex: \(\hat x\) is feasible and \(U=f(\hat x)\).
The problem is an exact minimization problem.
All propagated objective lower bounds are valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any pruned node contains no feasible solution with objective value strictly below \(U\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strict incumbent-cutoff algorithm is coherent for exact minimization and fits the leaf, but no authoritative branch-and-bound or constraint-optimization source is cited.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Feedback Does Not Certify Global Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between local objective–incumbent closure and exhaustive global certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a search node, monotone increases of a valid local lower bound \(L_N\), monotone decreases of a verified feasible incumbent value \(U\), and local closure with \(L_N\ge U\) certify only that node's inability to improve the incumbent. Global optimality follows only when every feasible solution is represented by the incumbent or lies in a search region closed by a valid infeasibility or bound certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing one node through objective–incumbent feedback does not prove global optimality without exhaustive coverage of unresolved solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(L_N\) is valid for node \(N\).
\(U\) is the value of a verified feasible incumbent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_N\ge U\ \not\Rightarrow\ U=z^*\quad\text{without exhaustive valid coverage}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local fixed-point condition after consequences of the current incumbent and objective bounds have been propagated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local feedback state \((D,U)\) is quiescent when objective propagation and propagation of the cutoff \(f(x)<U\) cannot further contract \(D\). Any subsequent decrease of \(U\), or any newly derived objective deduction that contracts \(D\), invalidates quiescence and requires the affected objective and cutoff propagators to be rescheduled until a new common fixpoint is reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The feedback loop is locally stable only until a better incumbent or stronger objective deduction arrives.
assumptions_latex: Objective and cutoff propagators are solution-preserving.
\(U\) is a verified incumbent value for the same model and objective.
Propagation events are scheduled fairly until quiescence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U'<U\ \Longrightarrow\ (D,U')\text{ is not quiescent before repropagation}.

Objective–Incumbent Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone feedback loop between objective bounds, propagation, and incumbent improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In exact minimization, maintain a valid node lower bound \(L(D)\) and a feasible incumbent upper bound \(U\). Objective propagation may increase \(L(D)\) or reduce \(D\), while a newly found feasible solution may decrease \(U\). After every such change, repropagate the cutoff \(f(x)<U\) and the objective relation until a fixpoint. The interval
\[[L(D),U)\]
therefore shrinks monotonically. A node is closed when \(L(D)\ge U\); if all open nodes are closed, the incumbent is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective bounds and incumbent improvements reinforce each other: tighter bounds prune domains, better incumbents tighten cutoffs, and matching bounds certify optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(L(D)\) is a valid lower bound for every feasible completion of the node.
\(U\) is the value of a feasible incumbent.
Propagation is solution-preserving.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every open node satisfies \(L(D)\ge U\), the incumbent objective value \(U\) is globally optimal.

notation.meaning: valid lower bound at the current node

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global branch-and-bound frontier certificate, not a locally owned objective–incumbent interface claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal N\) be an exhaustive live-node frontier, let each node have a valid lower bound \(L_N\), and let \(U\) be a verified feasible incumbent value. Then \(\min_{N\in\mathcal N}L_N\) bounds unresolved solutions, and exhaustive valid closure of the frontier at bounds at least \(U\) certifies optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exhaustive frontier and a feasible incumbent can certify a global optimality gap or optimality.
assumptions_latex: The frontier and certified closures cover every unresolved feasible solution.
Every node bound is valid in its node scope.
\(U\) is a verified feasible incumbent value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{N\in\mathcal N}L_N\le z^*\le U\text{ while unresolved feasible regions remain.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization interface exchanging relaxation lower bounds with propagation and incumbent information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z^*=\min\{f(x):x\in F\}\) and \(L_R=\inf\{f(x):x\in R\}\), where \(F\subseteq R\). Then \(L_R\leq z^*\). A relaxation-to-propagation message may therefore delete a search state only when its valid lower bound is at least the current incumbent \(U\). Conversely, domain restrictions or valid constraints communicated by propagation may tighten the relaxation from \(R\) to \(R'\) only if \(F\subseteq R'\subseteq R\); the returned bound then satisfies \(L_R\leq L_{R'}\leq z^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation supplies valid lower bounds for pruning, while propagation may tighten the relaxation only without excluding feasible solutions.

Promoting a local or conditional bound beyond its scope can prune improving feasible solutions.

\(L_A\) was derived under assumptions \(A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(L_R\le f(x)\) for every original feasible point and every such \(f(x)\) is integral, then \(\lceil L_R\rceil\) is a valid lower bound. A node may therefore be pruned against incumbent \(U\) when \(\lceil L_R\rceil\ge U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integral-valued objective, rounding a valid real lower bound upward preserves validity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unentailed Explanation Clauses Can Remove Valid Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness boundary for the CP-to-SAT explanation channel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a CP component returns a clause \(C\) with \(E\not\models C\), then some Boolean assignment \(\beta\) satisfies \(E\land\neg C\). Permanently adding \(C\) removes \(\beta\) and may eliminate a valid encoded solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reason or conflict clause not entailed by the shared encoding can make combined search unsound.

\(E\not\models C\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness of CP reason and conflict clauses supplied to SAT search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a satisfiability-preserving Boolean encoding of a finite-domain model. If every CP reason clause and conflict clause added to the SAT database is entailed by \(E\), then adding those clauses does not change the models of \(E\). CDCL learning and backjumping based on them therefore preserve satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CP explanations safely drive SAT learning and backjumping when every exchanged clause is entailed by the shared encoding.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(E\) is a finite, satisfiability-preserving Boolean encoding; CP propagation adds only clauses entailed by \(E\); and the coordinating SAT procedure is complete for finite CNF. If every reported Boolean model is correctly decoded and validated, the combined procedure returns a finite-domain solution exactly when one exists, while an UNSAT result establishes that none exists.

Every CP-generated clause is entailed by \(E\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational cycle connecting SAT decisions, CP propagation, learning, and backjumping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Translate the current SAT assignment into CP domain restrictions and run CP propagation. For each inferred literal, enqueue it in SAT with an entailed reason clause. If CP detects contradiction, return an entailed conflict clause; the SAT engine performs conflict analysis, learns an entailed clause, backjumps, and resumes Boolean and CP propagation. If neither component propagates or conflicts, SAT decides another unassigned literal. A total Boolean model is accepted only after decoding and validation in the finite-domain model.

SAT conflict analysis preserves entailment.
Decoded total models are validated.

A detected contradiction is returned as an entailed clause falsified by \(\alpha\). SAT assignments are translated into the corresponding CP restrictions before propagation.
