knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pairwise All-Different Decomposition Can Miss Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-separation witness between native GAC and a semantically exact decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_1,x_2,x_3\) all have domain \(\{1,2\}\). The conjunction \(x_1
e x_2\land x_1
e x_3\land x_2
e x_3\) is solution-equivalent to \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\). Arc consistency on the binary disequalities deletes nothing, while native domain consistency detects that three variables cannot take distinct values from a two-value set and reports failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three variables over two values show that pairwise disequality propagation can reach a nonempty fixed point while native all-different propagation detects infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: All three variables have domain \(\{1,2\}\).
Each binary disequality is made arc consistent.
knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise All-Different Decomposition Can Miss Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preorder for comparing native and decomposed closures on original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For closures \(F\) and \(G\) on the same original-variable stores, \(F\) is at least as strong as \(G\) when \(F(S)_x\subseteq G(S)_x\) for every store \(S\) and original variable \(x\). For a decomposition \(D\), use the projected operator \(S_X\mapsto(F_D^*(\iota_D(S_X)))|_X\). Dominance is strict when the inclusion is strict for some store and variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One propagator dominates another when it always leaves subsets of the other's domains; one strict inclusion witnesses strict dominance.
assumptions_latex: Both closures are sound for the same projected relation.
The auxiliary lift \(\iota_D\) is fixed.

notation.meaning: F is at least as strong as G
fixed initialization lift for the decomposition

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Propagation Dominance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Posting Both Views Cannot Weaken Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonic effect of retaining native and decomposed representations together.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_C\) and \(F_D\) be sound, monotone, contracting propagators for a native constraint and an exact decomposition. On finite domains, the common fixed point reached by fair iteration of both is componentwise contained in the fixed point reached by iterating either alone from the same lifted store. Retaining both views therefore cannot weaken pruning, although it may increase propagation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Running native and decomposed propagators together can only preserve or strengthen pruning, at additional computational cost.
assumptions_latex: Both propagators are sound, monotone, and contracting.
Iteration is fair and domains are finite.
knowledge_statements.title: Posting Both Views Cannot Weaken Propagation
Native versus Decomposed Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance of native generalized arc consistency over local propagation on an exact decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a finite-domain constraint on original variables \(X\), and let \(D\) be an exact decomposition over \(X\cup Y\), so that the satisfying tuples of \(C\) equal the projection onto \(X\) of the solutions of \(D\). At any domains, every original value surviving generalized arc consistency on \(C\) has a supporting tuple of \(C\). Local generalized arc consistency on the individual constraints of \(D\) may retain values having no common global extension through \(Y\). Therefore native filtering can be strictly stronger than decomposed local filtering after projection onto \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even an exact decomposition can propagate less strongly than a native global propagator because locally compatible supports may not combine into one global support.
assumptions_latex: All domains are finite.
The decomposition is solution-equivalent after existential projection of auxiliary variables.
Each decomposed constraint is filtered only locally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{GAC}(C)\) can delete original-variable values retained by \(\pi_X(\operatorname{GAC}(D))\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: propagation strength is not preserved by arbitrary exact decomposition
precise closure-order convention requires authoritative source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the representation-boundary leaf, but comparison of native and decomposed closures requires a precise auxiliary-domain initialization and projection convention supported by a source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection Equivalence Does Not Control Encoding Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size boundary for auxiliary-variable encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An extended system \(D(X,Y)\) may satisfy \(\pi_X(\operatorname{Sol}(D))=\operatorname{Sol}(C)\) while using exponentially many auxiliary values, variables, or constraints. Therefore exactness after projection does not imply a polynomial-size encoding or polynomial-time propagation in the original input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact auxiliary encoding may still be exponentially large, so projection equivalence alone gives no efficiency guarantee.
assumptions_latex: Encoding size counts auxiliary-domain descriptions and all introduced constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Equivalence Does Not Control Encoding Size
Auxiliary-Variable Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Width–domain tradeoff induced by hidden-variable encodings of global constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a constraint \(C(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\) have relation \(R\subseteq D_1\times\cdots\times D_r\). Introduce an auxiliary variable \(y_C\) with domain \(R\), and for every \(i\) impose the binary compatibility constraint \(x_i=(y_C)_i\). This hidden-variable encoding is solution equivalent to \(C\) after projecting out \(y_C\), and replaces the primal clique on \(x_1,\ldots,x_r\) by a star centered at \(y_C\). However, the auxiliary domain has size \(|R|\), which may be as large as \(\prod_{i=1}^r|D_i|\); reduced graph width can therefore incur exponential domain growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An auxiliary tuple variable can replace an r-variable clique by a star, but its domain may contain every allowed r-tuple and grow exponentially.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is an explicitly represented finite relation.
The auxiliary value records a complete allowed tuple of \(C\).

notation.meaning: auxiliary variable ranging over allowed tuples
the i-th component of the tuple assigned to the auxiliary variable

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: hidden-variable encoding of a finite extensional constraint

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hidden-variable encoding and width–domain tradeoff are precise and fit the leaf, but no authoritative encoding source or locator is provided.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Auxiliary Initialization Is Part of Propagation Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed convention for comparing extended and original-variable propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an extended encoding on original variables \(X\) and auxiliaries \(Y\), projected propagation depends on the initial auxiliary domains. A comparison therefore fixes a canonical lift \(\iota_D\), ordinarily assigning each auxiliary its full static encoding domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagation through auxiliaries can be compared only after fixing how auxiliary domains are initialized.
assumptions_latex: The extended encoding is solution-equivalent after projection.
Propagation starts from a store on \(X\cup Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_X\mapsto\bigl(F_D^*(\iota_D(S_X))\bigr)|_X\text{ is defined only after }\iota_D\text{ is fixed}.
review_flags: deferred_canonical_home: auxiliary initialization is primarily part of native/decomposed comparison and propagation-preservation semantics
knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary Initialization Is Part of Propagation Comparison

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cycles Remove the General Acyclic Preservation Guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limitation of the join-tree sufficient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In cyclic decompositions, local consistency of component relations and their overlaps need not imply that all remaining component tuples have common global extensions. Thus semantic exactness plus local propagation does not generally guarantee propagation preservation without the join-tree condition; particular cyclic decompositions may still preserve propagation for additional reasons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The join-tree guarantee does not extend to arbitrary cyclic decompositions, although some cyclic decompositions may preserve propagation through stronger structure or inference.
assumptions_latex: The decomposition hypergraph is cyclic.
Only local component and overlap consistency is enforced.
knowledge_statements.title: Cycles Remove the General Acyclic Preservation Guarantee

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Acyclic Join Decompositions Preserve Complete Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural sufficient condition for local relational filtering to match the undecomposed relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let finite relations \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) form an exact decomposition \(R=\Join_jR_j\), and suppose their scopes admit a join tree satisfying the running-intersection property. After restricting the relations by the current domains and enforcing semijoin consistency in both directions along every join-tree edge, every remaining tuple of every \(R_j\) extends to a tuple of the full join. Consequently the projected remaining values are exactly those occurring in tuples of \(R\) compatible with the current domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an exact acyclic relational decomposition, two-way semijoin propagation on a join tree removes exactly the component tuples and values lacking a global extension.
assumptions_latex: The decomposition is an exact natural join of finite relations.
The scopes admit a join tree satisfying running intersection.
Relations are restricted by the current domains before semijoin closure.

notation.meaning: component relation after join-tree semijoin closure

review_flags: Terminology also appears as global consistency of acyclic database schemes or acyclic CSPs.
knowledge_statements.title: Acyclic Join Decompositions Preserve Complete Propagation
Propagation-Preserving Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure-level definition relative to original variables, canonical auxiliary initialization, and chosen propagation operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a constraint on variables \(X\), let \(D\) be a solution-equivalent decomposition on \(X\cup Y\), and let \(F_C\) and \(F_D\) be the chosen domain-reduction operators. For each domain store \(S_X\) on \(X\), let \(\iota_D(S_X)\) be the canonical decomposed store that agrees with \(S_X\) on \(X\) and initializes every auxiliary variable in \(Y\) to its full encoding domain. The decomposition is propagation preserving on \(X\) when \[F_C^{*}(S_X)=\bigl(F_D^{*}(\iota_D(S_X))\bigr)|_X\] for every \(S_X\). It is failure preserving when these closures report domain wipeout for exactly the same original-variable stores.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decomposition preserves propagation when, from the canonical auxiliary initialization, its fixed-point pruning projected to the original variables exactly matches native fixed-point pruning for every original-variable domain store.
assumptions_latex: The native constraint and decomposition have the same solutions after projection onto \(X\).
The canonical lift \(\iota_D\) and the auxiliary encoding domains are specified.
Both reduction operators terminate at well-defined fixed points.

notation.meaning: fixed-point closure of a reduction operator
domain store on the original variables
canonical lift of an original-variable store to the decomposed representation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equality of projected propagation closures under canonical auxiliary initialization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Propagation Preservation Is Transitive Under Compatible Replacement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed compositionality of closure-equivalent decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a propagation-preserving decomposition is recursively replaced by component decompositions that preserve each component's projected closure, then the composite decomposition preserves the original closure provided all interfaces and canonical lifts are compatible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagation-equivalent component replacement is proposed to preserve the outer decomposition when interfaces and lifts agree.
assumptions_latex: Each replacement is solution equivalent and propagation preserving on its declared interface.
Canonical lifts compose consistently.
All closures terminate.
review_flags: deferred_unreliable: interface-level projected closure equality is not sufficient as stated to control propagation under every surrounding store and iteration context
requires a stronger context-congruence or commuting-closure hypothesis
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Preservation Is Transitive Under Compatible Replacement

intermediate_metadata.reason: The leaf owns closure-level preservation, acyclic join-tree sufficiency, and the failure of that general guarantee for cyclic decompositions. The proposed replacement-transitivity claim was deferred because its interface assumptions do not ensure contextual closure equivalence. Strict weakness examples and auxiliary-size effects were excluded as sibling scopes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arity Enumeration Gives an XP Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized classification of direct tuple enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When every domain is explicitly listed and has size at most \(|I|\), enumerating assignments to an arity-\(r\) scope takes \(|I|^{O(r)}\) time, assuming polynomial-time tuple membership. This is an XP bound parameterized by \(r\). Because its polynomial exponent depends on \(r\), this bound alone is not an FPT bound; it neither proves nor disproves the existence of another FPT algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Brute-force filtering by scope arity gives an XP bound, not an FPT bound, although another FPT algorithm may exist.
assumptions_latex: Domains are explicitly represented.
Candidate-tuple membership is polynomial-time decidable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(I)=|I|^{O(r)}\in\mathrm{XP}[r],\qquad\text{this bound alone does not establish membership in or exclusion from }\mathrm{FPT}[r].
knowledge_statements.title: Arity Enumeration Gives an XP Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parameterized Hardness Transfers from Support to Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional lower-bound transfer under the same parameterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If designated-value support is \(\mathrm W[1]\)-hard for parameter \(\kappa\) under a parameter-preserving reduction, then complete filtering is \(\mathrm W[1]\)-hard for \(\kappa\), because complete filtering decides whether the designated value survives. Hence an FPT complete filter would imply \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm W[1]\). Unparameterized NP-hardness alone does not establish this conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: W[1]-hard support rules out an FPT complete filter under the usual assumption, but only for the same preserved parameterization.
assumptions_latex: The hardness reduction preserves \(\kappa\) up to a computable function.
Complete filtering reports whether the designated value survives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Support}\text{ is W[1]-hard in }\kappa\Longrightarrow\operatorname{Filter}\text{ is W[1]-hard in }\kappa.
review_flags: Concrete hardness requires a family-specific parameter-preserving reduction.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized Hardness Transfers from Support to Filtering
Parameterized Global Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-parameter and bounded-arity boundaries for global-constraint filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) encode a global-constraint filtering instance of length \(L\), let \(\kappa(I)\) be a structural parameter, and let support checking determine whether each variable-value pair extends to a permitted tuple. Filtering is fixed-parameter tractable in \(\kappa\) when all unsupported values can be removed in time \(f(\kappa(I))L^c\), where \(c\) is independent of \(\kappa\). If the only method enumerates assignments to an arity-\(r\) scope with domain bound \(d\), its time is \(O(r d^r\operatorname{poly}(L))\): polynomial for fixed \(r\), but not by itself an FPT bound parameterized solely by \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global filtering is fixed-parameter tractable only when parameter dependence separates from a fixed polynomial input factor; brute-force bounded arity gives merely fixed-arity polynomiality.
assumptions_latex: The constraint and domains have a finite encoding of length \(L\).
Filtering is based on deciding support for each variable-value pair.
Enumeration tests a candidate tuple in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(I)=f(\kappa(I))L^c\) is FPT, whereas \(O(r d^r\operatorname{poly}(L))\) is only a fixed-arity polynomial bound without further parameterization.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: parameterized-complexity definition combined with tuple-enumeration filtering bound
exact parameter and representation are constraint-family dependent

knowledge_statements.statement_title: FPT Support Testing Lifts to FPT Complete Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed parameter-preserving support-to-filter reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an instance has polynomially many explicitly represented variable-value pairs and designated-value support is FPT, testing every pair yields an FPT complete filter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An FPT support test yields an FPT complete filter when the number of represented domain values is polynomial.
assumptions_latex: Current domains are explicitly represented.
Designating a variable-value pair does not increase the parameter beyond a computable function.

knowledge_statements.title: FPT Support Testing Lifts to FPT Complete Filtering

knowledge_statements.title: Locally Consistent Unsatisfiable Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd-cycle family separating arc consistency from global satisfiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(m\ge1\), take variables \(x_0,\ldots,x_{2m}\), each with domain \(\{0,1\}\), and impose \(x_i\ne x_{i+1}\) for indices interpreted modulo \(2m+1\). Every value of every variable has the opposite value as a support in each incident constraint, so the network is arc consistent and propagation deletes nothing. Nevertheless, following the disequalities around the odd cycle forces \(x_0\ne x_0\), which is impossible. Thus the network is unsatisfiable despite being nonempty and arc consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary disequality on an odd cycle remains arc consistent with two-value domains, yet no global two-coloring exists.
assumptions_latex: Every variable domain is \(\{0,1\}\).
The constraints are disequalities on one odd cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N_m\text{ is arc consistent and }\operatorname{Sol}(\mathcal N_m)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: the disequality network on a cycle of length 2m+1

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The odd-cycle counterexample is correct, explicit, and appropriately classified, but no inspectable source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Global Conflicts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pigeonhole conflict invisible to pairwise arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge 2\), let \(x_1,\ldots,x_{n+1}\) all have domain \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and impose every binary disequality \(x_i\ne x_j\). Each value has a distinct supporting value in every neighboring domain, so the binary network is arc consistent and no value is removed. Globally, however, \(n+1\) variables cannot take pairwise distinct values from an \(n\)-element set. The conflict is therefore detectable by the global all-different constraint but remains hidden from arc consistency on its binary decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairwise disequalities among n+1 variables over n values are arc consistent, although the pigeonhole principle makes the complete network unsatisfiable.
assumptions_latex: All \(n+1\) variables have the common \(n\)-value domain.
Every pair of variables is constrained to differ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N_n\text{ is arc consistent but unsatisfiable}\).

notation.meaning: complete binary disequality network with n+1 variables and n values

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pigeonhole counterexample for binary decomposition of all-different

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parity Infeasibility Invisible to Interval Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infeasibility caused by interior holes that interval-hull reasoning fills.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D(x)=D(y)=D(z)=\{1,3\}\) and impose \(x+y+z=6\). Every admissible sum is odd, so the finite-domain constraint is infeasible. Replacing each domain by its integer hull \([1,3]\) creates supports for every endpoint, such as \((1,2,3)\) and \((3,1,2)\). Hence bounds reasoning over the hulls need not detect failure, whereas complete domain filtering does.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three odd-only domains cannot sum to six, but filling their holes creates endpoint supports and hides the contradiction from hull-based bounds reasoning.
assumptions_latex: Bounds reasoning uses the integer interval hull of each domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{(x,y,z)\in D(x)\times D(y)\times D(z):x+y+z=6\}=\varnothing,\text{ while the hull instance is bounds-consistent}.
knowledge_statements.title: Parity Infeasibility Invisible to Interval Hulls
Bounds Hole-Blindness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of propagation based only on minimum and maximum domain values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_1=\{1,3\}\) and \(D_2=\{1,2,3\}\), and define the bounds abstraction by \(\beta(D)=[\min D,\max D]\). Then \(\beta(D_1)=\beta(D_2)=[1,3]\), although \(2\notin D_1\) and \(2\in D_2\). Consequently, every propagator whose output depends only on \(\beta(D)\) must behave identically on these two domains and cannot exploit the hole at \(2\). Thus bounds-based consistency can be strictly weaker than domain-based consistency whenever interior membership affects support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domains with identical extrema but different interior holes are indistinguishable to bounds-only propagation, so pruning that depends on those holes is necessarily lost.
assumptions_latex: \(D_1,D_2\) are finite nonempty integer domains.
The propagator accesses each domain only through its interval hull \(\beta(D)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\beta(D_1)=\beta(D_2)\) while \(D_1\ne D_2\), so bounds-only propagation cannot detect the missing value \(2\).

notation.meaning: Interval hull of a finite domain.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary example is mathematically precise and fits Bounds Hole-Blindness, but no source is supplied for the general comparison between bounds-based and domain-based consistency.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global GAC Dominates Local Consistency on an Exact Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation-strength ordering for an exact finite-domain decomposition of one relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the finite-domain relation \(G\) be represented exactly by constraints \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\), possibly with auxiliary variables, so every tuple of \(G\) compatible with the current original-variable domains has an extension satisfying all \(C_j\), and every satisfying decomposition tuple projects into \(G\). Starting with unrestricted compatible auxiliary domains, enforce GAC on \(G\), or enforce sound local consistency to closure on all \(C_j\). No decomposition propagator can delete an original-variable value retained by GAC on \(G\). Therefore \(D_{\mathrm{GAC}(G)}(v)\subseteq D_{\mathrm{decomp}}(v)\) for every original variable \(v\), and the inclusion may be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an exact decomposition with compatible auxiliary domains, GAC on the original relation prunes at least as strongly on original variables as sound local propagation of the decomposition.
assumptions_latex: All domains and relations are finite.
The decomposition is extensionally exact under projection.
Initial auxiliary domains admit every extension required by exactness.
Local decomposition propagators are sound and are run to closure.

notation.meaning: Domain after GAC on the global relation.
Projected domain after propagation closure of the decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Global GAC Dominates Local Consistency on an Exact Decomposition
Decomposition Pruning Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict pruning loss from decomposing a global constraint into weaker primitive constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D(x)=D(y)=\{1,2\}\) and \(D(z)=\{1,2,3\}\). Generalized arc consistency on \(\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x,y,z)\) removes \(1\) and \(2\) from \(D(z)\), because \(x\) and \(y\) must occupy those two values, and therefore yields \(D(z)=\{3\}\). The logically equivalent decomposition \(x
e y\), \(x
e z\), \(y
e z\) is already arc-consistent on the original domains and removes no value from \(D(z)\). Hence equivalence of solution sets does not imply equivalence of propagation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decomposing AllDifferent into pairwise disequalities preserves solutions but loses Hall-set pruning: the global propagator fixes z to 3 while the decomposition prunes nothing.
assumptions_latex: Arc consistency is enforced separately on each binary disequality.
Generalized arc consistency is enforced on the global constraint.

notation.meaning: Current finite domain of variable v.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The AllDifferent counterexample is correct and the counterexample kind fits the leaf, but the propagation-strength claim lacks a cited global-constraint source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonic Strengthening by a Redundant Propagator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General interaction between semantic redundancy and propagation closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a finite-domain model and let \(G\) be satisfied by every solution of \(C\). Suppose the original propagators remain active and the greatest common fixed-point closures below the same store \(D\) exist for both propagator families. Then
\[\operatorname{cl}_{C\cup\{G\}}(D)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_C(D).\]
If all propagators are sound, both closures retain every solution of \(C\) contained in \(D\); the inclusion may nevertheless be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keeping the original propagators and adding a sound redundant propagator preserves solutions and cannot weaken the greatest common propagation closure, but it may strengthen pruning.
assumptions_latex: Every solution of \(C\) satisfies \(G\).
The original propagators remain active after adding \(G\).
All propagators are sound and contracting.
Both displayed greatest common fixed-point closures exist.

notation.meaning: Greatest common fixed point below D for the propagators associated with C.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonic Strengthening by a Redundant Propagator
Redundant-Constraint Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation strengthening by a constraint redundant at the solution-set level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(D(x)=D(y)=\{1,2\}\) and \(D(z)=\{1,2,3\}\), let \(C=\{x
e y,x
e z,y
e z\}\). Adding \(G=\operatorname{AllDifferent}(x,y,z)\) does not change the solution set because \(G\) is logically equivalent to the conjunction of \(C\). Nevertheless, separate arc consistency on \(C\) leaves every domain unchanged, whereas generalized arc consistency on \(C\cup\{G\}\) yields \(D(z)=\{3\}\). A logically redundant constraint may therefore strengthen a propagation closure when its propagator reasons over a richer representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A logically redundant global constraint can strengthen propagation because its propagator detects interactions that separate propagators for an equivalent decomposition miss.
assumptions_latex: The constraints are interpreted over finite domains.
Each constraint is propagated using the stated local consistency.

notation.meaning: Assignments satisfying every constraint in C.

knowledge_statements.title: Floating-Point Interval Soundness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outward-rounding condition for sound floating-point interval evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=[\underline{x},\overline{x}]\) and \(Y=[\underline{y},\overline{y}]\) be floating-point intervals, and let \(\circ\in\{+,-,\times,/\}\), with \(0\notin Y\) for division. An implemented interval operation is sound if its lower endpoint is rounded toward \(-\infty\), its upper endpoint is rounded toward \(+\infty\), and the resulting interval \(X\mathbin{\circ_I}Y\) contains every real result \(x\circ y\) for \(x\in X\) and \(y\in Y\). Round-to-nearest evaluation without a compensating enclosure is not sufficient for this guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Floating-point interval operations are sound when directed outward rounding makes every computed interval contain all corresponding real results.
assumptions_latex: All finite endpoints are representable floating-point numbers.
Exceptional values and overflow are handled by enclosing infinities.
\(0\notin Y\) when division is used.

notation.meaning: Outward-rounded interval extension of a real operation.

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete enclosure failure when an inexact endpoint is not rounded outward.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In radix-two floating-point arithmetic, \(1/10\) is not representable. If \([1,1]/[10,10]\) is evaluated by rounding both endpoints to \(r=\operatorname{RN}(1/10)\), the returned interval is \([r,r]\). Since \(r\ne1/10\), this singleton excludes the exact real quotient and is unsound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using the nearest floating-point approximation to 1/10 as both interval endpoints produces a singleton that excludes the exact quotient.
assumptions_latex: The floating-point radix is two.
Both quotient endpoints use round-to-nearest without a compensating enclosure.
knowledge_statements.title: Round-to-Nearest Unsoundness Witness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Range-enclosure guarantee for expressions composed from sound outward-rounded interval primitives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e\) be an arithmetic expression whose primitive operations have sound outward-rounded interval extensions. If every real intermediate operation is defined for every input in a box \(X\), and exceptional floating-point results are conservatively enclosed, then recursive interval evaluation \(E(X)\) satisfies \(\{e(x):x\in X\}\subseteq E(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing sound outward-rounded interval primitives preserves enclosure of the real expression range when all admitted real operations are defined.
assumptions_latex: Every primitive interval operation encloses its corresponding real operation.
Every real intermediate operation is defined throughout \(X\).
Overflow and exceptional floating-point results are conservatively enclosed.

notation.meaning: Recursive floating-point interval evaluation of e over X.

knowledge_statements.title: Compositional Inclusion Soundness

children.title: Dependency Effects
children.top_down_role: Loss of relational information caused by repeated or correlated quantities in numerical propagation.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependency Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of variable identity in natural interval evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=[a,b]\) with \(a<b\), and evaluate \(f(x)=x-x\) by replacing both occurrences of \(x\) independently with \(X\). Ordinary interval subtraction gives \(F(X)=X-X=[a-b,b-a]\), while the exact range is \(f(X)=\{0\}\). The excess width \(2(b-a)\) arises solely because interval arithmetic does not preserve the equality of repeated occurrences. Thus inclusion remains sound, but repeated dependent occurrences can destroy exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treating repeated occurrences of one variable as independent enlarges interval results; x minus itself becomes a nondegenerate interval instead of exactly zero.
assumptions_latex: \(X=[a,b]\) is a nondegenerate real interval.
The natural interval extension evaluates repeated occurrences independently.

notation.meaning: Natural interval evaluation of f over X.

children.title: Overestimation Effects
children.top_down_role: Excess enclosure growth, weakened pruning, and scale-sensitive numerical consequences.

knowledge_statements.title: Overestimation Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of interval exclusion caused by a sound but excessively wide enclosure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty box, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(F(X)\) be an interval satisfying \(f(X)\subseteq F(X)\). Suppose feasibility requires \(f(x)=0\), and consider the exclusion test that rejects \(X\) when \(0\notin F(X)\). If \(0\in F(X)\) while \(0\notin f(X)\), then \(X\) contains no feasible point, but this sound interval exclusion test cannot reject it. Thus overestimation can cause missed infeasibility detection without compromising soundness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sound but overestimated interval containing zero can prevent the interval exclusion test from rejecting a box whose exact function range excludes zero.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty box and \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\).
\(f(X)\subseteq F(X)\).
Feasibility requires \(f(x)=0\), and the exclusion test rejects a box when \(0\notin F(X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in F(X)\setminus f(X)\) implies that this interval exclusion test fails to detect the infeasibility of \(X\).

notation.meaning: Exact range of f on X.
Sound interval enclosure of the exact range.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 7. Cuts, Lower Bounds and Box Reduction p. 83

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization-bound consequence of an excessively wide interval range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(X)\subseteq F(X)=[\underline F,\overline F]\subseteq G(X)=[\underline G,\overline G]\), with \(X\ne\varnothing\). For minimization over \(X\), \(\underline G\leq\underline F\leq\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\). Both lower endpoints are valid lower bounds, but the wider enclosure can give a strictly weaker bound and thereby lose incumbent-based pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Widening a sound interval range preserves lower-bound validity but can weaken the bound and prevent pruning.
assumptions_latex: \(X\ne\varnothing\).
\(f(X)\subseteq F(X)\subseteq G(X)\).
The problem minimizes \(f\) over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.title: Overestimation Weakens Objective Lower Bounds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of enclosure width on range-disjointness exclusion, independent of the source of overestimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(X)\subseteq F_1(X)\subseteq F_2(X)\), and suppose feasibility requires \(f(x)\in T\). Then \(F_2(X)\cap T=\varnothing\) implies \(F_1(X)\cap T=\varnothing\), while the converse can fail. Thus widening a sound enclosure cannot create an exclusion certificate and may destroy one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A wider sound range enclosure cannot strengthen a range-disjointness exclusion test and may prevent exclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(f(X)\subseteq F_1(X)\subseteq F_2(X)\).
A box is excluded when its enclosure is disjoint from the feasible target set \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_2(X)\cap T=\varnothing\Rightarrow F_1(X)\cap T=\varnothing,\text{ but not conversely}.

notation.meaning: Target set of feasible function values.

knowledge_statements.title: Enclosure Inclusion Monotonicity of Exclusion

children.title: Dependency-Driven Overestimation
children.top_down_role: Cases where dependency loss directly amplifies enclosure overestimation.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependency-Driven Overestimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete overestimation caused only by repeated dependence on one variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X=[1,2]\), consider \(f(x)=x/x\). Since \(0\notin X\), the exact range is \(f(X)=\{1\}\). Natural interval division treats the numerator and denominator occurrences independently and returns \(F(X)=X/X=[1/2,2]\). Hence the enclosure is sound but has positive width and contains values unattainable by any common choice of \(x\). This is dependency-driven overestimation rather than floating-point rounding error; it occurs even with exact endpoint arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On [1,2], natural interval evaluation of x/x gives [1/2,2] although the exact range is {1}, purely because repeated occurrences lose dependence.
assumptions_latex: Natural interval division is used with exact endpoint arithmetic.

children.title: Missed Wakeups
children.top_down_role: Lost or absent propagator activations, affected event regimes, and correctness consequences.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient event-subscription condition under which queue quiescence certifies a common propagation fixpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite family of propagators. If every store transition \(D\to D'\subseteq D\) for which an inactive \(p\in P\) satisfies \(p(D')\subsetneq D'\) schedules \(p\), and every scheduled propagator is eventually executed unless failure occurs, then an empty queue at \(D^*\) implies \(p(D^*)=D^*\) for all \(p\in P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Queue emptiness certifies a common fixpoint if every domain change that enables new pruning wakes the affected propagator.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is finite.
Every \(p\in P\) is contracting.
Every enabled inactive propagator is scheduled.
Every scheduled propagator is eventually executed unless failure is detected.

notation.meaning: Propagation queue at the quiescent store.

knowledge_statements.title: Wakeup Completeness Condition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete bounds-propagation witness for an omitted wakeup event.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initially let \(D(x)=D(y)=\{0,1\}\), a fixpoint of the bounds propagator \(p\) for \(x\le y\). After another operation contracts \(D(y)\) to \(\{0\}\), suppose the decrease of \(\max(y)\) is omitted from \(p\)'s wakeup events. If no propagator remains queued, the queue is empty at \(D'(x)=\{0,1\}\), \(D'(y)=\{0\}\), although executing \(p\) would remove \(1\) from \(D'(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Omitting the wakeup caused by a decrease in y's upper bound can leave an x≤y propagator able to prune after the queue becomes empty.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) performs sound bounds filtering for \(x\le y\).
A separate operation contracts \(D(y)\) to \(\{0\}\).
The decrease of \(\max(y)\) does not schedule \(p\).

notation.meaning: Queue after the contraction of y's domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty Queue with Residual Pruning
Missed Wakeups
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of propagation closure when a relevant domain event is not scheduled.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\) be a contracting propagator and let domain store \(D'\subsetneq D\) result from another propagator. A missed wakeup occurs when \(p(D')\subsetneq D'\) but the event transforming \(D\) into \(D'\) does not schedule \(p\). If the queue then becomes empty, the solver reports quiescence at \(D'\), although \(D'\) is not a common propagation fixpoint. The retained values may lack support, so the operational fixpoint is weaker than the specified propagation closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a domain change could make a propagator prune but does not wake it, an empty queue may falsely signal a propagation fixpoint.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is sound, monotone, and contracting.
The scheduler invokes propagators only for subscribed events.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(D')\subsetneq D'\) while \(p\) is unscheduled implies that reported quiescence need not be a propagation fixpoint.

notation.meaning: A domain store ordered by componentwise inclusion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary formulation is coherent and appropriately distinguishes queue quiescence from a common propagation fixpoint, but no propagation-kernel source is supplied.

children.title: Stale Supports
children.top_down_role: Invalid retained supports, cache-validity failures, and unsound filtering consequences.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal concrete witness showing unsound retention through a stale cached tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be \(x=y\) with \(D(x)=D(y)=\{0,1\}\), and cache \(s=(0,0)\) as a support for \(x=0\). After contracting \(D(y)\) to \(\{1\}\), the tuple \(s\) is stale. No tuple in \(C\cap(D(x)\times D(y))\) supports \(x=0\); therefore a propagator that accepts \(s\) without revalidation incorrectly retains \(0\) in \(D(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For x=y, a cached support (0,0) becomes invalid when y loses 0; trusting it retains the now-unsupported value x=0.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is the equality relation on \(\{0,1\}\).
The cached tuple \((0,0)\) is reused without checking the current domain of \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s\notin D'(x)\times D'(y)\quad\text{and}\quad \nexists t\in C\cap(D'(x)\times D'(y)):t_x=0.

notation.meaning: Cached tuple supporting x=0 before the domain contraction.

knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Equality Support Retained
Stale Supports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unsound reuse of a support invalidated by domain reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a constraint \(C\), value \(a\in D(x)\), and stored support tuple \(s\), validity requires \(s\in C\), \(s_x=a\), and \(s_y\in D(y)\) for every variable \(y\) of \(C\). The support is stale after a reduction to \(D'\subseteq D\) if some \(s_y\notin D'(y)\). If the propagator accepts this cached tuple without revalidation and no alternative support exists in \(D'\), it incorrectly retains \(a\), violating generalized arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cached support becomes stale when one of its tuple values leaves the domain; trusting it can retain a value with no current support.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a finite-domain constraint.
The domain store only contracts between support creation and reuse.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\notin\prod_y D'(y)\) and absence of another support imply that retaining \(a\) is incorrect.

notation.meaning: Cached satisfying tuple supporting a variable-value pair.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stale-support condition is precise and fits the leaf, but the cached-support validity and generalized-arc-consistency claim require an authoritative source.

children.title: Wakeup–Support Coupling
children.top_down_role: Failure chains linking missed notifications to unrefreshed support state.

knowledge_statements.title: Wakeup–Support Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduler invariant connecting domain events to cached-support validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_p\) be the supports cached by propagator \(p\), and let a domain event change \(D\) to \(D'\subseteq D\). Correct wakeup–support coupling requires that whenever the event can invalidate some \(s\in S_p\), the kernel either schedules \(p\) or atomically revalidates and replaces every affected support before quiescence. Formally, if \(s\in\prod_x D(x)\) but \(s\notin\prod_x D'(x)\), then quiescence is permitted only after the affected supported value has a valid replacement or has been removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every event capable of invalidating a cached support must trigger propagation or immediate revalidation before the solver may declare quiescence.
assumptions_latex: Domains contract monotonically during one propagation phase.
Cached supports identify the domain values on which they depend.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\notin\prod_x D'(x)\) forces rescheduling or successful support revalidation before quiescence.

notation.meaning: Set of supports cached by propagator p.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This proposes a strong kernel invariant connecting invalidated cached tuples to scheduling or immediate revalidation. No source is supplied to confirm that this is the necessary invariant rather than one sufficient implementation discipline.

children.title: Incorrect Subsumption
children.top_down_role: Premature entailment decisions, propagator removal errors, and lost future pruning.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition permitting permanent omission of a propagator below the current store.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a constraint over variables \(V\), and let \(D\) be the current domain store. A correct propagator whose sole obligation is enforcing \(C\) is semantically subsumed at \(D\) when \[\prod_{v\in V}D(v)\subseteq C.\] Every descendant store \(D'\subseteq D\) then also satisfies \(\prod_vD'(v)\subseteq C\), so permanent deactivation below \(D\) is sound. Merely having \(p(D)=D\) is a propagator fixpoint and does not imply subsumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint is subsumed only when every tuple in the current domain product satisfies it; a no-change propagator call is insufficient.
assumptions_latex: p\text{ is responsible only for enforcing }C.
D'\subseteq D\text{ denotes componentwise domain contraction along descendants}.
review_flags: Implementation-specific subsumption tests must imply semantic entailment over the represented store.
knowledge_statements.title: Semantic Subsumption of a Propagator
Incorrect Subsumption
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixpoint incorrectly treated as permanent entailment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(C:(x\le y)\) with \(D(x)=D(y)=\{1,2\}\). Arc-consistency propagation makes no deletion, so its propagator is at a fixpoint, but \(C\) is not entailed because \((x,y)=(2,1)\) violates it. If the kernel interprets the absence of pruning as subsumption and permanently deactivates the propagator, a later branch fixing \(x=2\) and \(y=1\) may retain an inconsistent store. Subsumption therefore requires entailment over every assignment in the current domain product, not merely idempotence at the current store.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A propagator doing no current pruning is not necessarily subsumed; deactivating x≤y on {1,2}² can miss the later inconsistent branch (2,1).
assumptions_latex: Subsumed propagators are permanently removed from scheduling.
Branching may contract domains to any subdomain of the current store.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(D)=D\) does not imply \(\prod_v D(v)\subseteq C\), so fixpoint-based subsumption is unsound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly separates a current propagator fixpoint from entailment under all assignments in the domain product, but the subsumption semantics and permanent-deactivation claim lack a kernel source.

children.title: Incorrect Reversibility
children.top_down_role: State-restoration failures across backtracking, copying, or persistent-state regimes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trace showing that restoring domains without restoring a propagator cache changes propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C:x+y=2\) with \(D_0(x)=D_0(y)=\{0,1,2\}\). Suppose a bounds propagator caches \(m=\min D(x)\) and uses it to enforce \(y\le2-m\). In a child branch set \(x=2\), so \(m=2\) and propagation gives \(y=0\). Backtrack and restore both domains to \(\{0,1,2\}\), but retain \(m=2\). The stale cache again derives \(y\le0\), deleting the supported values \(1\) and \(2\); with the restored cache \(m=0\), no such deletion occurs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stale cached lower bound retained after backtracking causes false pruning even when all variable domains are restored.
assumptions_latex: The cached value is used without recomputation after restoration.
The ancestor store gives both variables domain \(\{0,1,2\}\).

notation.meaning: cached minimum of the current domain of x

knowledge_statements.title: Stale Incremental-Sum Cache After Backtracking
Incorrect Reversibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backtracking failure caused by incomplete restoration of mutable propagation state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a search node have domain store \(D_0\) and propagation state \(m_0\). Suppose a child branch changes them to \((D_1,m_1)\). Correct reversibility requires backtracking to restore an observationally equivalent state \((D_0,m_0)\): for every subsequent domain event sequence \(E\), propagation from the restored state must produce the same domains and failure result as propagation from the original state. If restoration yields \((D_0,\widehat m_0)\) violating this equivalence, cached supports, queue flags, or subsumption marks may cause missed pruning or false failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backtracking is correct only when restored propagation state behaves exactly like the original ancestor state under every subsequent event sequence.
assumptions_latex: Mutable propagation state can affect scheduling or pruning.
Backtracking restores the ancestor domain store \(D_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat m_0\not\equiv_{D_0}m_0\) constitutes an incorrect-reversibility failure even when the domains themselves are restored.

notation.meaning: Mutable propagation-kernel state at the ancestor node.
Observational equivalence under all future event sequences from D₀.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The observational-equivalence condition appropriately captures restoration of mutable propagation state, but its universal event-sequence formulation and stated failure consequences require an authoritative backtracking-kernel source.

children.title: Subsumption State Restoration
children.top_down_role: Interactions between propagator completion state and restoration across search.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic criterion for retaining or reversing a descendant deactivation after restoring a wider store.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_v\subseteq D_u\) be descendant and ancestor stores for constraint \(C\). After restoration to \(D_u\), a descendant subsumption mark may remain effective only if \(\prod_xD_u(x)\subseteq C\) is established at the restored store. Otherwise the propagator must regain an active state capable of responding to relevant future domain events. The weaker condition \(p(D_u)=D_u\) is insufficient because a current fixpoint need not remain a fixpoint after later contractions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After backtracking, retain a subsumption mark only if the constraint is entailed at the restored store; otherwise reactivate the propagator.
assumptions_latex: D_v\subseteq D_u\text{ componentwise}.
p\text{ is a sound propagator for }C.
Search descendants are formed by domain contraction.

knowledge_statements.title: Sound Restoration of Subsumption State

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Descendant Subsumption Mark Retained at an Ancestor
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branch in which valid descendant subsumption becomes invalid after backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C:x\le y\) and let \(D_u(x)=D_u(y)=\{1,2\}\). In a child branch impose \(x=1\). Every tuple in \(\{1\}\times\{1,2\}\) satisfies \(C\), so child subsumption is valid. After backtracking, restore both domains to \(\{1,2\}\) but retain the child subsumption mark. In the subsequent branch \(x=2,y=1\), the inactive propagator fails to reject the violating tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A propagator can be validly subsumed in a child yet require reactivation after backtracking to a wider ancestor store.
assumptions_latex: A subsumed propagator is not scheduled.
Backtracking restores the ancestor domains before the subsequent branch.
knowledge_statements.title: Descendant Subsumption Mark Retained at an Ancestor
Subsumption State Restoration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reversibility boundary for a propagator discarded as subsumed at a descendant search node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\) be an ancestor of search node \(v\), let \(D_v\subseteq D_u\) be their domain stores, and let \(p\) be a contracting propagator. Suppose \(p\) is marked subsumed at \(v\), so its state there is \(\sigma_v=\mathrm{subsumed}\). Backtracking from \(v\) to \(u\) must restore the state recorded at \(u\). A subsumption-state restoration failure occurs precisely when the restored state remains \(\mathrm{subsumed}\) although \(p(D_u)\subsetneq D_u\). The resulting kernel state is unsound because omitting \(p\) leaves values in the restored store that propagation by \(p\) would remove.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After backtracking, a propagator must be reactivated whenever it can prune the restored domains; retaining its descendant subsumed status is an unsound restoration failure.
assumptions_latex: \(D_v\subseteq D_u\) and backtracking restores \(D_u\).
\(p(D)\subseteq D\) for every store in the domain of \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_u=\mathrm{subsumed}\ \wedge\ p(D_u)\subsetneq D_u\) characterizes the restoration failure.

children.title: Propagation Thrashing
children.top_down_role: Excessive reactivation, low-yield propagation cycles, and workload-sensitive degradation.

knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Thrashing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic boundary where repeated propagator execution produces a vanishing fraction of useful events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a propagation trace interval \(I\), let \(E(I)\) count propagator executions and let \(U(I)\) count executions that strictly contract the domain store or detect inconsistency. A family of trace intervals \((I_k)_{k\geq1}\) exhibits propagation thrashing when \(E(I_k)\to\infty\) while \(U(I_k)/E(I_k)\to0\), with executions repeatedly generated by wake-up and rescheduling events rather than by new domain contractions. Thus the kernel crosses the thrashing boundary when arbitrarily much propagation work can occur per useful event, even though every individual propagator execution terminates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagation thrashes when executions grow without bound while the fraction producing pruning or failure tends to zero because wake-ups repeatedly reschedule ineffective work.
assumptions_latex: Every propagator execution in each \(I_k\) terminates.
A useful execution either strictly contracts the current store or detects inconsistency.

notation.meaning: Number of propagator executions in an interval.
Number of useful executions in an interval.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports a formal definition of propagation thrashing.
Usefulness and trace-family conventions require an authoritative propagation-kernel source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the propagation-thrashing container, but the proposed asymptotic definition is uncited and not established as a standard characterization. In particular, the definition of useful execution and the requirement that ineffective work arise from wake-up or rescheduling events need authoritative support with a specific locator.

children.title: Priority Overhead
children.top_down_role: Scheduling costs caused by priority maintenance, comparison, and queue organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Priority Overhead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic boundary where maintaining propagation priorities dominates propagator evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each propagation run \(R_k\), let \(C_{\mathrm{prio}}(R_k)\) be the cost of computing priorities and maintaining priority queues, and let \(C_{\mathrm{eval}}(R_k)\) be the cost of executing the selected propagators, measured in one fixed computation model. Priority handling crosses its overhead failure boundary on a family \((R_k)_{k\geq1}\) when \[\frac{C_{\mathrm{prio}}(R_k)}{C_{\mathrm{eval}}(R_k)+1}\longrightarrow\infty.\] At this boundary, prioritization is no longer a lower-order scheduling mechanism: asymptotically, the kernel spends unboundedly more work choosing and reorganizing propagators than evaluating them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Priority overhead fails to remain subordinate when queue maintenance and priority computation become asymptotically unbounded relative to propagator evaluation.
assumptions_latex: All costs are measured under the same computation model.
\(C_{\mathrm{prio}}(R_k),C_{\mathrm{eval}}(R_k)\geq0\).

notation.meaning: A propagation run in an asymptotic family.

Nevertheless, the divergence ratio is a bespoke threshold rather than a sourced standard result, while the accounting boundaries for priority computation, queue maintenance, and propagator evaluation remain source-dependent. children.title: State Overhead
children.top_down_role: Time and memory costs associated with incremental, reversible, or explanatory state.

knowledge_statements.title: State Overhead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic boundary where recording and restoring solver state dominates propagation work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each search-and-propagation run \(R_k\), let \(C_{\mathrm{state}}(R_k)\) denote the cost of copying, trailing, timestamping, and restoring mutable kernel state, and let \(C_{\mathrm{prop}}(R_k)\) denote the cost of propagator evaluation, under one fixed computation model. State management crosses its overhead failure boundary on a family \((R_k)_{k\geq1}\) when \[\frac{C_{\mathrm{state}}(R_k)}{C_{\mathrm{prop}}(R_k)+1}\longrightarrow\infty.\] Consequently, reversible-state machinery asymptotically dominates the inference it supports, irrespective of whether restoration remains logically correct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: State overhead crosses its boundary when copying, trailing, and restoration cost becomes asymptotically unbounded relative to propagator evaluation.
assumptions_latex: All costs are measured under the same computation model.
\(C_{\mathrm{state}}(R_k),C_{\mathrm{prop}}(R_k)\geq0\).

children.title: Kernel Overhead Interactions
children.top_down_role: Feedback among reactivation frequency, queue management, and maintained state costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Kernel Overhead Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compound boundary where interacting kernel mechanisms cause superadditive overhead despite bounded isolated costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a propagation run \(R\), let \(C_{\mathrm{joint}}(R)\) be the measured kernel cost when wake-up scheduling, priority maintenance, and reversible-state management operate together. Let \(C_{\mathrm{base}}(R)\) be propagator-evaluation cost plus the sum of the three mechanisms' costs measured in isolation on the same event trace. Define the interaction excess by \(X(R)=C_{\mathrm{joint}}(R)-C_{\mathrm{base}}(R)\). A family \((R_k)_{k\geq1}\) crosses the interaction failure boundary when every isolated overhead-to-evaluation ratio remains bounded but \[\frac{C_{\mathrm{joint}}(R_k)}{C_{\mathrm{base}}(R_k)+1}\longrightarrow\infty.\] Hence the blow-up is attributable to interactions rather than any isolated mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kernel interactions become pathological when their joint cost is unbounded relative to the isolated-cost baseline although every individual overhead ratio remains bounded.
assumptions_latex: Joint and isolated costs use the same computation model and event trace.
Each isolated overhead-to-evaluation ratio is uniformly bounded over \(k\).
